revisionCards.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
revisionCards.heroInsight: Use the first row and first column as storage instead of extra arrays.
revisionCards.problemStatement: Given an m x n matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0 in-place.
revisionCards.whyThisProblemMatters: This problem tests whether you can optimize brute force space usage into an elegant in-place marking system — a classic interview expectation.

slides.headline: Set Matrix Zeroes
slides.body:
⚡ Collapse rows and columns containing zeros to zero in-place.

`[1,1,1]`     `[1,0,1]`
`[1,0,1]`  ➔  `[0,0,0]`
`[1,1,1]`     `[1,0,1]`

🧠 Recall:
- Reuse first row and first column as markers
- Use `col0` separately to track column 0
- Traverse backwards to prevent early marker overwrites
slides.visualCue: Matrix explosion animation from a single zero.
slides.memoryHook: One zero infects its row and column.
slides.transition: So how do we remember which rows and columns must become zero without using extra arrays?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
When should this pattern instantly trigger in your head?

✅ Matrix modification done IN-PLACE
✅ Need constant auxiliary space
✅ Rows and columns depend on future information
✅ Brute force uses separate row[] and col[] arrays

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you see 'optimize space' in matrix problems, think about reusing the matrix itself as metadata storage.
slides.transition: Let's first understand the brute-force instinct before upgrading it.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The obvious solution:

1. Traverse the matrix
2. Store rows containing zero in row[]
3. Store cols containing zero in col[]
4. Traverse again and zero them out

⏱️ Time: O(N*M)
📦 Space: O(N+M)

This works perfectly... but we can compress the storage into the matrix itself.
slides.analogy: Why carry a notebook when the wall itself can be used for writing reminders?
slides.transition: Now comes the interview-level optimization.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Instead of using separate row[] and col[] arrays:

✅ Use matrix[i][0] to mark whether row i should become zero
✅ Use matrix[0][j] to mark whether column j should become zero

The matrix becomes its OWN storage system.

⚠️ But there is one conflict:
matrix[0][0] belongs to BOTH first row and first column.
slides.goldenLine: The first row and first column become a hidden control panel.
slides.transition: Now let's visualize the entire execution step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Found zero at (1,1): mark matrix[1][0]=0 and matrix[0][1]=0
Markers now guide update; traverse backwards to avoid overwriting
Finally, check col0 and zero out the first column
slides.keyObservation: Backward traversal protects markers from being overwritten too soon.
slides.transition: Why backward traversal specifically?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Reverse Traversal Matters
slides.body:
If we traverse forward while updating cells, we may accidentally destroy marker information before using it.

Backward traversal guarantees:

✅ Markers are consumed safely
✅ Original decisions remain intact
✅ No accidental cascading zeroes occur
slides.interviewerTrap: Most candidates fail because they overwrite markers too early.
slides.transition: Now the entire algorithm becomes surprisingly small.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: First Pass: Scan matrix and mark rows/cols using first row & col
First Column: Use separate col0 variable to avoid overlap conflicts
Second Pass: Traverse backwards to apply stored markers safely
slides.mentalCompression: First pass = store decisions. Second pass = apply decisions.
slides.transition: Now lock it into muscle memory with clean code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code (Part 1/2)
slides.body: Optimal in-place matrix marking solution.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code (Part 2/2)
slides.body: Optimal in-place matrix marking solution. (Continued)

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: First row and first column are secretly acting as hash maps storing future zero decisions.
slides.memoryHook: Matrix becomes its own notebook.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to handle col0 separately (overlap)
Forward traversal updates markers too early
interviewerQuestions: Why is col0 required instead of matrix[0][0]?
Why do we traverse backwards during updates?

recall.5sec: Use first row and col as markers.
recall.30sec: Use col0 separately; update backwards to protect markers.
recall.1min: Optimal O(N*M) in-place matrix marking reusing boundaries as metadata storage.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body:
Strong candidates don't just code this problem.

They explain WHY the matrix itself can safely become storage, WHY reverse traversal prevents corruption, and WHY matrix[0][0] creates ambiguity.

That depth of reasoning is what interviewers actually remember.
slides.closingLine: Optimization is often about reusing existing space intelligently.

revisionCards.explanation:
Given an `m x n` integer matrix, if any element is `0`, set its entire row and column to `0`'s. You must perform this modification **in-place** without using a duplicate matrix. The goal is to optimize the space complexity to constant **O(1)** auxiliary space.

🔢 **Example**:
Input: `[[1,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,1]]`
Output: `[[1,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,1]]`

revisionCards.title: Pascal's Triangle
revisionCards.explanation:
Given an integer `numRows`, generate and return the first `numRows` of Pascal's Triangle. In this triangle, every row starts and ends with the value `1`. Each middle element is constructed by summing the two adjacent parent numbers directly above it.

🔺 **Example**:
Input: `numRows = 4`
Output: `[[1], [1,1], [1,2,1], [1,3,3,1]]`

slides.headline: Pascal’s Triangle
slides.body:
🔺 Every element is formed using the TWO elements above it.

`[1]`
`[1,1]`
`[1,2,1]`
`[1,3,3,1]`

🧠 Recall:
- Boundary values are always `1`
- Middle = top-left + top-right
- Build current row from previous row
slides.visualCue: Growing pyramid structure starting from a single 1.
slides.memoryHook: Each brick sits on two parent bricks.
slides.transition: When should we instantly recognize this structure in coding tests?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Row-by-row structure dependency
✅ Current value relies on previous results
✅ Math grid built using preceding elements

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires cell computation based purely on adjacent neighbors from the line above, think Constructive DP.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The manual math way:

Compute each cell independently using the combinations formula:
`C(n, r) = n! / (r! * (n-r)!)`

⏱️ Time: O(N³) due to factorials
📦 Space: O(N²) storage

Highly sub-optimal! We can build it faster by adding adjacent elements.
slides.analogy: Summing adjacent numbers is faster than calculating massive factorials from scratch.
slides.transition: Now for the constructive DP optimization.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Save computational power by using previous answers:

✅ Pre-fill the row with `1`s to handle borders easily
✅ Update middle columns (`1` to `row-1`) using the parents

`triangle[row-1][col-1] + triangle[row-1][col]`

This turns factorial multiplication into a single addition.
slides.goldenLine: Row by row, we cache history to create the future.
slides.transition: Let's watch this execute step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Row 0 & 1: Boundaries are set to [1] and [1, 1] directly
Row 2 & 3: Compute middle cells from previous row (e.g. 1+1=2, 1+2=3)
Row 4: Yields [1, 4, 6, 4, 1] incrementally using addition
slides.keyObservation: Setting default array values to 1 completely bypassed border checks.
slides.transition: Why does math vs incremental building matter here?

slides.headline: 🔍 Combinatorics vs DP
slides.body:
Why is constructive DP the absolute standard?

✅ Addition has O(1) instruction cycles
✅ Factorials trigger integer overflow limits quickly
✅ Prevents exponential duplication of calculations

DP reduces factorial math into simple, safe memory updates.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by calculating permutations instead of dynamic addition.
slides.transition: The blueprint of this logic is extremely compact.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Pre-allocate active row with length row+1 filled with 1s
Loop columns from index 1 to row-1
Apply parent sum logic: triangle[row-1][col-1] + triangle[row-1][col]
slides.mentalCompression: Pre-fill boundaries with 1s. Sum middle cells from the preceding row.
slides.transition: Lock this logic into memory with clean code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal row-by-row Constructive DP solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Pre-fill the entire row with 1s so boundaries are done, then overwrite the middle with sum of adjacent parents.
slides.memoryHook: Preallocate borders, add centers.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Off-by-one errors on inner loop boundaries
Invalid memory access on triangle[row-1]
interviewerQuestions: Can space be optimized to O(N) auxiliary space?
How is this related to Binomial Coefficients?

recall.5sec: Each element is the sum of two directly above.
recall.30sec: Initialize rows with 1; calculate middle cells from row-1.
recall.1min: Constructive O(N^2) Dynamic Programming row-by-row incrementally.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body:
Elite candidates don't just solve this problem.

They immediately mention how initializing boundaries avoids messy `if` conditions, how to optimize space to `O(N)` if only a single row is needed, and the direct links to Combinations.
slides.closingLine: Pre-allocating space is the key to elegant array codes.

revisionCards.title: Next Permutation
revisionCards.explanation: Rearrange numbers into the lexicographically next greater permutation of numbers. If no such arrangement is possible, the array must be rearranged in ascending order.

slides.headline: ⚡ Next Permutation Challenge
slides.body:
Find the lexicographically next greater permutation of an array of numbers.

Imagine the numbers in your array form a multi-digit value. You want to find the next larger value that can be formed using the exact same digits.

🎯 The real challenge:
Doing this in-place with `O(1)` auxiliary space without generating all permutations.
slides.visualCue: A sequence of numbers plotted on a graph, peaking and then dropping.
slides.memoryHook: Scan from right to find the first drop, swap with next-best, then flip the tail.
slides.transition: How do we spot the key mathematical turning point in interviews?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Problem asks for 'lexicographically next' configuration
✅ Elements are modified in-place with zero extra memory
✅ Involves finding mathematical permutations in order

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you see lexicographical ordering, look for the 'suffix of decreasing values' since a descending sequence cannot be increased further.
slides.transition: Let's explore the brute-force way to solve this.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
Generate every possible permutation:

1. Find all permutations of the array recursively
2. Sort them lexicographically
3. Find your current array, and return the next one in the sorted list

⏱️ Time: O(N! * N) to generate and sort permutations
📦 Space: O(N! * N) to store them

Completely unusable for larger inputs due to factorial growth.
slides.analogy: Searching through a massive library of all possible books just to find the next volume on a shelf.
slides.transition: How can we skip generating all permutations and find the next one instantly?

slides.headline: 🚀 The Suffix Breakthrough
slides.body:
Scan from right to left to find the 'pivot' (where order stops increasing):

✅ Find `i` such that `nums[i] < nums[i+1]` (first dip from the right)
✅ If no dip exists, the array is in reverse order; simply reverse it fully
✅ Find `j` from right such that `nums[j] > nums[i]`, swap them
✅ Reverse the suffix from `i+1` to end to make it as small as possible

This swaps the pivot with the next-best digit and minimizes the remaining tail.
slides.goldenLine: A local swap followed by a tail reverse transforms the suffix into its smallest form.
slides.transition: Let's run a dry run simulation to see this sequence in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Scan right-to-left: [5, 4, 3, 0] is decreasing. The dip is at index 1 (`nums[1] = 1`).
Find successor of 1 in the suffix: `nums[4] = 3` is the smallest value greater than 1.
Swap indices 1 and 4: array becomes [2, 3, 5, 4, 1, 0].
Reverse suffix from index 2: [5, 4, 1, 0] becomes [0, 1, 4, 5]. Result is [2, 3, 0, 1, 4, 5].
slides.keyObservation: Reversing the decreasing tail guarantees we get the absolute smallest increment.
slides.transition: Why does reversing the suffix mathematically yield the next permutation?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Suffix Reversal Works
slides.body:
Any suffix that is strictly decreasing is at its maximum possible permutation state.

To increase the overall value:
1. We must alter the element immediately to the left of this suffix (`nums[i]`).
2. We swap `nums[i]` with the next-larger number in the suffix to make the increment as small as possible.
3. Reversing the suffix changes it from descending (maximum) to ascending (minimum), minimizing the tail value.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates often search for swap candidates from the left instead of the right, leading to incorrect permutations.
slides.transition: Here is the exact step-by-step implementation blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Find first index `i` from right where `nums[i] < nums[i+1]`.
If `i < 0`, reverse entire array and return (it was the last permutation).
Otherwise, find first index `j` from right where `nums[j] > nums[i]`.
slides.mentalCompression: Find dip, swap with next-best on right, reverse suffix.
slides.transition: Let's look at the clean C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal in-place suffix scanning algorithm.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Locate the ascending hill from the right, swap the valley with its next greater climber, then reverse the entire descent.
slides.memoryHook: Hill dip, next-best swap, tail reverse.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Off-by-one errors while scanning from right-to-left.
Forgetting to handle arrays that are already in descending order (e.g. [3,2,1]).
interviewerQuestions: How would you adapt this to find the PREVIOUS permutation?
Can we optimize the scan for the next-larger element using binary search?

recall.5sec: Find dip from right, swap with next larger, reverse suffix.
recall.30sec: Locate pivot index i where nums[i] < nums[i+1]. Swap nums[i] with first nums[j] > nums[i] from right. Reverse from i+1 to end.
recall.1min: O(N) time and O(1) space in-place algorithm utilizing suffix peak analysis and minimal swaps.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates write the suffix reversal using std::reverse and point out that the suffix is always in descending order before swap, and remains in descending order after swap, making the suffix reversal O(N) simple and elegant.
slides.closingLine: True algorithmic control is knowing exactly when to reverse directions.

revisionCards.title: Kadane's Algorithm
revisionCards.explanation: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return its sum. Solve in O(N) time using dynamic programming.

slides.headline: ⚡ Contiguous Subarray Max Sum
slides.body:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum.

Imagine running a business where some days bring profits and other days bring losses. You want to find the consecutive days that give the maximum total net profit.

🎯 The real challenge:
Accomplishing this in a single `O(N)` pass without calculating all possible subsegments.
slides.visualCue: A slider window expanding and shrinking over an array of positive and negative numbers.
slides.memoryHook: If the current sum turns negative, dump it and start fresh.
slides.transition: When should Kadane's immediately come to mind during a dynamic subarray interview?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Identify the cues:

✅ Maximum or minimum sum of contiguous elements
✅ Subarray constraints (elements must be adjacent)
✅ Negative elements are present (positive-only would just be the sum of all elements)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you are asked to optimize contiguous array configurations and the current sum can drop below zero, think dynamic accumulation (Kadane's).
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
Check every possible subarray:

1. Try all starting indices `i`
2. Try all ending indices `j`
3. Calculate the sum of elements from `i` to `j` and track the maximum

⏱️ Time: O(N²) or O(N³)
📦 Space: O(1)

Extremely slow for large arrays because we re-sum overlapping segments repeatedly.
slides.analogy: Calculating your career profits by adding up every combination of start and end dates from scratch.
slides.transition: How can we make decisions on-the-fly and find the max sum in one pass?

slides.headline: 🚀 The 'Fresh Start' Breakthrough
slides.body:
At any element `nums[i]`, you have a critical choice:

✅ Add `nums[i]` to the existing running subarray sum.
✅ Start a brand-new subarray beginning at `nums[i]`.

💡 The Decision Rule:
If the running sum becomes negative, adding it to the next element will only drag it down. Dump the history and start a new subarray sum from the current element.
slides.goldenLine: Do not carry the burden of a negative past into a promising future.
slides.transition: Let's trace this decision rule in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: i=0: num=-2, curMax=-2, globalMax=-2
i=1: num=1, curMax=max(1, -2+1)=1, globalMax=1 (started fresh!)
i=2: num=-3, curMax=max(-3, 1-3)=-2, globalMax=1
i=3: num=4, curMax=max(4, -2+4)=4, globalMax=4 (started fresh!)
slides.keyObservation: When we hit 4 at index 3, we discarded the negative history (-2) to maximize current options.
slides.transition: Why is this greedy approach mathematically correct?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Kadane's is Correct
slides.body:
For any element `i`, the maximum subarray ending at `i` must either:
1. Be just `nums[i]` itself.
2. Be `nums[i]` plus the maximum subarray ending at `i-1`.

Since `maxSub(i) = max(nums[i], nums[i] + maxSub(i-1))`, this is pure Dynamic Programming with state-compression down to a single variable.

This guarantees all valid subarrays are evaluated without redundant scanning.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting that the array can contain all-negative numbers. Initializing the global max to 0 instead of nums[0] will fail for inputs like [-1, -2, -3].
slides.transition: Let's see the algorithm's simple structure.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize `maxSoFar` and `currentMax` to the first element `nums[0]`.
Iterate through the array starting from index 1.
For each element, update `currentMax = max(nums[i], currentMax + nums[i])`.
slides.mentalCompression: At each element, choose: join existing chain or start a new one.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Ultra-compact O(N) Kadane's algorithm.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Keep adding numbers; if the current sum becomes less than the current number itself, cut off the past and start fresh.
slides.memoryHook: Reset when current > current + past.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Initializing `maxSoFar` to 0 or `INT_MIN` instead of `nums[0]`, which fails when all numbers are negative.
Accidentally resetting `currentMax` to 0 instead of starting at `nums[i]`.
interviewerQuestions: How would you modify the code to print the actual subarray indices?
Can this be solved using Divide & Conquer? (Yes, in O(N log N) time)

recall.5sec: Keep adding elements. If sum goes negative, reset to current element.
recall.30sec: Track running currentMax and overall maxSoFar. Update currentMax as max(nums[i], currentMax + nums[i]).
recall.1min: Classic Dynamic Programming with O(N) time complexity and O(1) auxiliary space, ideal for contiguous subarray optimization.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates immediately ask if they need to return the indices of the subarray and write the index tracking effortlessly. They also explain the DP state reduction from dp[i] array to a single scalar variable.
slides.closingLine: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication in dynamic programming.

revisionCards.title: Sort Colors (Sort 0s, 1s, 2s)
revisionCards.explanation: Sort an array of red, white, and blue elements in-place using the Dutch National Flag 3-pointer partition algorithm.

slides.headline: ⚡ Sort Colors in One Pass
slides.body:
Given an array `nums` with `0`s, `1`s, and `2`s, sort them in-place so that objects of the same color are adjacent.

Imagine three piles of colored balls: Red (0), White (1), and Blue (2). You want to sort them into order using only swaps, without using any extra buckets.

🎯 The real challenge:
Solving this in a single pass with `O(1)` space, using only a three-way partition.
slides.visualCue: Three pointers partitioning the array into colored blocks: zeros on left, ones in middle, twos on right.
slides.memoryHook: Zeroes to the left, Twos to the right, Ones hang out in the middle.
slides.transition: What classic algorithm triggers this three-way partitioning logic?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Sorting an array of exactly 3 distinct keys/elements
✅ In-place sorting required without standard sort library
✅ Single pass constraint is specified

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you have exactly three categories of elements and need to group them in-place, think Dutch National Flag (3-Pointer partitioning).
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The two standard simple approaches:

1. Use built-in `sort()`: Time `O(N log N)`
2. Count elements (Counting Sort): Count zeroes, ones, twos, then rewrite array. Time `O(N)` but requires 2 full passes.

Can we do it in a single pass using pointers?
slides.analogy: Sorting laundry by going through the basket twice: first to count shirts, pants, socks, then distributing them.
slides.transition: Let's explore the single-pass 3-pointer partition breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Dutch National Flag Breakthrough
slides.body:
Maintain three pointers: `low` (boundary of 0s), `mid` (current scanner), and `high` (boundary of 2s).

✅ `nums[mid] == 0`: Swap with `low`, advance both `low` and `mid`.
✅ `nums[mid] == 1`: Leave it, just advance `mid`.
✅ `nums[mid] == 2`: Swap with `high`, decrement `high` (do not advance `mid` yet, as the swapped element must be inspected).

This ensures 0s move left, 2s move right, and 1s remain in the middle automatically.
slides.goldenLine: A triple pointer dance sweeps elements to their respective ends.
slides.transition: Let's see this elegant swap dance in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initial: low=0, mid=0, high=5. nums[mid] = 2. Swap with high: [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2]. high=4.
mid=0, low=0. nums[mid] = 0. Swap with low: [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2]. low=1, mid=1.
mid=1, low=1. nums[mid] = 0. Swap with low: [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2]. low=2, mid=2.
mid=2. nums[mid] = 2. Swap with high (index 4): [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]. high=3.
slides.keyObservation: When swapping with high, we don't increment mid because the element brought from the back is uninspected.
slides.transition: Why is this single-pass pointer arrangement perfectly safe?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why mid is not advanced after a high swap
slides.body:
When swapping `nums[mid]` with `nums[low]`, the element at `low` is guaranteed to be a `1` (since `mid` has already passed it and left only `1`s behind). Thus, it's safe to increment `mid`.

However, when swapping with `nums[high]`, the element coming from `high` is completely unknown (could be `0`, `1`, or `2`). We must evaluate it at `mid` in the next iteration.
slides.interviewerTrap: Advancing mid after swapping with high, which leaves unsorted elements stranded.
slides.transition: The blueprint is clean, precise, and easily memorized.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Set `low = 0`, `mid = 0`, and `high = nums.size() - 1`.
While `mid <= high`:
If `nums[mid] == 0`, swap `nums[low]` and `nums[mid]`, increment `low` and `mid`.
slides.mentalCompression: 0s swap left (low++), 2s swap right (high--), 1s step forward.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: In-place single pass Dutch National Flag implementation.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Keep low pointing to the first non-0, high pointing to the first non-2 from right, and sweep mid through the middle.
slides.memoryHook: Left-low swaps zeros, right-high swaps twos.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Incrementing `mid` when swapping with `high`.
Setting loop condition to `mid < high` instead of `mid <= high` (misses the last element inspection).
interviewerQuestions: What if there are K different colors instead of 3?
Is this sorting algorithm stable? (No, swaps can change original relative order of equal elements)

recall.5sec: 3 pointers: low, mid, high. Swap 0s to low, 2s to high.
recall.30sec: If nums[mid]==0 swap with low and low++, mid++. If nums[mid]==2 swap with high and high--. Else mid++.
recall.1min: O(N) single-pass partitioning algorithm with O(1) space, avoiding counting sort's double pass.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates explain the invariant of the three-way partition: nums[0...low-1] are all 0s, nums[low...mid-1] are all 1s, and nums[high+1...N-1] are all 2s. Stating this invariant demonstrates deep computer science maturity.
slides.closingLine: Code is clean when your invariants are rock solid.

revisionCards.title: Stock Buy and Sell
revisionCards.explanation: Find the maximum profit possible by buying and selling a single stock in-place, scanning prices exactly once.

slides.headline: ⚡ Maximizing Single Transaction Profit
slides.body:
You are given an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a given stock on the `i`-th day.

Find the maximum profit you can achieve by choosing a single day to buy one stock and choosing a different day in the future to sell that stock.

🎯 The real challenge:
Finding the optimal peak and valley combination in one linear pass.
slides.visualCue: A stock price chart showing valleys and peaks with a green profit arrow spanning from a local minimum to a subsequent global maximum.
slides.memoryHook: Buy at the absolute lowest price seen so far, sell today, keep tracking the max difference.
slides.transition: How do we model this decision-making process mathematically?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Look for these triggers:

✅ Maximizing differences between two elements in an array
✅ Strict ordering constraint: buy day must precede sell day
✅ Single transaction maximum yield

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you need to track dynamic relationships between future states and past minimums, think valley tracking.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
Check every possible pair of days:

1. Loop `i` from `0` to `N-1` (buy day)
2. Loop `j` from `i+1` to `N-1` (sell day)
3. Calculate profit `prices[j] - prices[i]` and track the maximum

⏱️ Time: O(N²) due to nested loops
📦 Space: O(1)

Too slow for highly volatile stocks with millions of data points.
slides.analogy: Checking every receipt of lifetime purchases against subsequent sales to see the best deal.
slides.transition: How can we do this instantly in a single pass?

slides.headline: 🚀 The Valley Tracking Breakthrough
slides.body:
To make the maximum profit on any day, you should have bought the stock at its lowest price in the past.

✅ Maintain a running `minPrice` representing the cheapest buying option seen so far.
✅ For each daily price, calculate the potential profit if we sold today: `price - minPrice`.
✅ Update `maxProfit` if today's profit is higher than previous records.

This completely eliminates the second nested loop.
slides.goldenLine: Keep your eyes on the lowest valley to capture the highest peak.
slides.transition: Let's watch this minimal scanner in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Day 0: price = 7. minPrice = 7, maxProfit = 0.
Day 1: price = 1. Update minPrice = 1, maxProfit = 0.
Day 2: price = 5. Potential profit = 5 - 1 = 4. Update maxProfit = 4.
Day 3: price = 3. Potential profit = 3 - 1 = 2. maxProfit remains 4.
slides.keyObservation: Even when prices dropped to 3 on Day 3, we retained our purchase price of 1, unlocking the peak of 6 on Day 4.
slides.transition: Why is this single-pass approach foolproof?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Valley Tracking is Optimal
slides.body:
Every potential sell day `j` has a unique optimal buy day `i` (where `i < j`).

By tracking the minimum price from index `0` to `j-1`, we guarantee that for each sell day, we are comparing it with its best possible match.

Thus, scanning the array once is mathematically sufficient to explore all optimal pairs.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates sometimes write nested loops or try sorting, which breaks the chronological order of transactions.
slides.transition: The code is incredibly neat and concise.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize `minPrice` to a very large value (e.g. `INT_MAX`).
Initialize `maxProfit` to 0.
Iterate through prices: if current price is less than `minPrice`, update `minPrice`.
slides.mentalCompression: Track the lowest price; measure profit on all other days.
slides.transition: Let's lock this down with C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal single-pass valley tracking solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Slide through the days, always updating the historical minimum price and checking if selling at the current price yields a new record.
slides.memoryHook: Minimum buying anchor, maximum selling profit.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Confusing buy/sell order (e.g., trying to sell before buying).
Initializing `minPrice` to 0 instead of a high boundary value.
interviewerQuestions: What if you are allowed to buy and sell multiple times? (Stock Buy & Sell II)
How do we handle a transaction fee on each sell?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Track running minPrice, update maxProfit whenever price - minPrice is larger.
recall.30sec: Loop prices once. If price < minPrice, update minPrice. Else, maxProfit = max(maxProfit, price - minPrice).
recall.1min: O(N) time complexity and O(1) space complexity algorithm relying on one-way minimum tracking and greedy maximization.

patternConnections: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out that this is a simplified version of the maximum subarray problem (Kadane's) where prices are converted to differences, demonstrating an advanced ability to map different problem families together.
slides.closingLine: Valleys exist to make the peaks feel even higher.

revisionCards.title: Rotate Image/Matrix
revisionCards.explanation: Rotate a square 2D matrix representing an image by 90 degrees clockwise in-place using Transpose and Flip symmetries.

slides.headline: ⚡ Rotate 2D Grid by 90° Clockwise
slides.body:
You are given an `n x n` 2D matrix representing an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise in-place.

Imagine rotating a square chessboard by a quarter turn. You must do this without using any helper chessboard.

🎯 The real challenge:
Performing this complex coordinate shift in-place without overwriting cell values before they are moved.
slides.visualCue: A matrix splitting into diagonals, elements swapping across, then rows reversing.
slides.memoryHook: Transpose the grid first, then reverse each row.
slides.transition: How do we break down the complex geometry of a 90-degree rotation?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Look for these signs:

✅ 2D Matrix rotation or mirroring operations
✅ Strict requirement for `O(1)` in-place space complexity
✅ Symmetric grid structures (N x N)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you see matrix rotation or reflection, think of linear algebra operations like Transpose and Flip.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
Create an auxiliary matrix:

For a matrix of size `N x N`, cell at `(i, j)` in the original matrix must move to `(j, N - 1 - i)` in the rotated matrix.
Copy all elements to a temp matrix, then copy back.

⏱️ Time: O(N²) operations
📦 Space: O(N²) helper storage

Not allowed in interviews since the goal is constant auxiliary space.
slides.analogy: Taking a photo of a chessboard, printing a rotated copy, and throwing the old board away.
slides.transition: How can we do this in-place using simple matrix symmetries?

slides.headline: 🚀 Transpose & Flip Breakthrough
slides.body:
A 90-degree clockwise rotation is mathematically equivalent to two simple operations:

✅ **Transpose**: Swap elements across the main diagonal (`matrix[i][j]` with `matrix[j][i]`).
✅ **Horizontal Flip**: Reverse each row individually.

Both operations are easily performed in-place with zero extra memory!
slides.goldenLine: Transpose the grid to swap rows with columns, then reverse the rows to point them in the right direction.
slides.transition: Let's visualize the dry run step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps:
Transpose (swap across diagonal): 
[[1, 4, 7],
 [2, 5, 8],
 [3, 6, 9]]

Horizontal Flip (reverse each row):
[[7, 4, 1],
 [8, 5, 2],
 [9, 6, 3]]
slides.keyObservation: The diagonal elements [1, 5, 9] remained completely fixed during the transpose step, acting as anchors.
slides.transition: Why is transpose followed by flip mathematically sound?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Math Behind Rotation
slides.body:
Mathematically, rotating `(i, j)` by 90 degrees clockwise puts it at index `(j, n - 1 - i)`.

1. Transpose shifts `(i, j)` to `(j, i)`.
2. Reversing the row shifts `(j, i)` to `(j, n - 1 - i)`.

By chaining these two basic symmetries together, we achieve the exact coordinate transformation without any complicated rotation formulas.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates often swap elements in the transpose loop twice, which swaps them back to their original positions. Ensure the inner loop starts at j = i + 1.
slides.transition: Let's review the clean blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Loop through rows `i` from `0` to `N-1`.
For each row, loop columns `j` from `i + 1` to `N-1` and swap `matrix[i][j]` with `matrix[j][i]`.
Loop through each row and reverse its elements in-place.
slides.mentalCompression: Transpose (diagonal swap) + Reverse (horizontal flip) = 90° rotation.
slides.transition: Here is the clean interview-ready C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: In-place matrix rotation using Transpose and Reverse.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Shatter the matrix across the main diagonal to transpose, then flip each row like a page in a book.
slides.memoryHook: Fold diagonally, flip horizontally.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Starting the inner transpose loop from `j = 0` instead of `j = i + 1` (cancels out the transpose).
Reversing columns instead of rows (which rotates 90 degrees counter-clockwise instead of clockwise).
interviewerQuestions: How would you rotate the matrix counter-clockwise?
How would you rotate a non-square (M x N) matrix in-place? (Highly complex, usually requires extra space)

recall.5sec: Transpose the matrix, then reverse each row.
recall.30sec: Swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for j > i. Then call reverse on every row of the matrix.
recall.1min: O(N^2) time and O(1) space in-place transformation exploiting basic geometric symmetries.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates explain both options: the Transpose + Reverse approach, and the direct 4-way cyclic swap. They discuss cache locality advantages.
slides.closingLine: Mastering symmetry is mastering efficiency.

revisionCards.title: Merge Overlapping Subintervals
revisionCards.explanation: Merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of non-overlapping intervals, sorted chronologically.

slides.headline: ⚡ Consolidate Time Intervals
slides.body:
Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]`, merge all overlapping intervals.

Imagine scheduling meetings in a conference room. If one meeting runs from 1 PM to 3 PM and another from 2 PM to 4 PM, they overlap and block the room from 1 PM to 4 PM.

🎯 The real challenge:
Correctly identifying overlaps when intervals are given in arbitrary order.
slides.visualCue: A timeline of segments sliding and merging together into continuous blocks.
slides.memoryHook: Sort by start times, then stretch the current interval as long as overlaps continue.
slides.transition: What is the crucial prerequisite to make overlap detection trivial?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Triggers to look out for:

✅ Input contains ranges, intervals, or start/end pairs
✅ Tasks, scheduling, or timeline overlaps
✅ Need to merge or find intersections of segments

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you see intervals, think SORTING first. Sorting by the start time converts a multi-dimensional search into a simple linear scan.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
Compare every interval with all other intervals:

1. Select an interval and scan all other intervals to see if they overlap.
2. If they do, merge them and start the search over again.
3. Repeat until no more merges are possible.

⏱️ Time: O(N²) or worse due to repeated scanning and indexing
📦 Space: O(N) to hold merged results

Highly sub-optimal because intervals can be scattered out of order.
slides.analogy: Trying to merge scattered diary entries without putting them in chronological order first.
slides.transition: How does sorting by start times unlock an elegant linear solution?

slides.headline: 🚀 Chronological Scan Breakthrough
slides.body:
If intervals are sorted by their start times, overlapping intervals are guaranteed to be adjacent in the array!

✅ Sort intervals based on start time.
✅ Maintain the first interval in the `merged` list.
✅ Iterate through subsequent intervals: if `current[start] <= last_merged[end]`, they overlap! Merge them by updating `last_merged[end] = max(last_merged[end], current[end])`.
✅ Otherwise, no overlap exists; append `current` as a new interval.
slides.goldenLine: Sorting converts a scattered 2D overlap problem into a single chronological sweep.
slides.transition: Let's watch this sweep step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initialize: merged = [[1,3]]
Inspect [2,6]: 2 <= 3 (overlap!). Merge: last element becomes [1, max(3,6)] = [1,6]. merged = [[1,6]]
Inspect [8,10]: 8 > 6 (no overlap). Add [8,10] to merged. merged = [[1,6], [8,10]]
slides.keyObservation: By sorting, we only ever need to compare the current interval with the last interval in our merged output.
slides.transition: Why is sorting the start time sufficient instead of sorting end times?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Sort by Start Times?
slides.body:
If we sorted by end times, a very long interval like `[1, 100]` could appear at the very end, despite overlapping with every single previous interval. We would have to backtrack and merge everything.

Sorting by start times guarantees that if a new interval does not overlap with the current merged range, it cannot possibly overlap with any future intervals either. This unlocks O(N) single-pass merging.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to use max() when updating the end time. An interval like [1, 4] followed by [2, 3] should end at 4, not 3!
slides.transition: Let's lay out the implementation blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: If intervals size is <= 1, return intervals immediately.
Sort intervals in ascending order based on start values.
Initialize output vector `merged` with the first interval.
slides.mentalCompression: Sort intervals. Compare current start with previous end. Merge or append.
slides.transition: Let's examine the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal interval merging after sorting.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Lay the intervals along a timeline from left to right; if a segment starts before the current block ends, melt them together.
slides.memoryHook: Sort, melt overlaps, print clean path.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to sort the input intervals first.
Using `current[1]` to overwrite `last[1]` directly instead of using `max(last[1], current[1])` (e.g., fails for nested interval `[1, 4]` and `[2, 3]`).
interviewerQuestions: Can we solve this without modifying the input array?
How would you insert a new interval and merge on-the-fly? (Insert Interval)

recall.5sec: Sort by start times, sweep and merge overlapping neighbors.
recall.30sec: Sort intervals. Push first to merged. If intervals[i][0] <= merged.back()[1], merge by updating end with max. Else append.
recall.1min: O(N log N) sorting dominant algorithm with O(N) output space, highly applicable to scheduling and range query scenarios.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates discuss in-place merging to optimize auxiliary space complexity. They explain how to overwrite elements in-place on the sorted input array, reducing auxiliary space to O(1) (excluding sorting overhead).
slides.closingLine: A sorted timeline resolves all temporal chaos.

revisionCards.title: Merge Sorted Array Without Extra Space
revisionCards.explanation: Merge two sorted arrays into one sorted array in-place inside the first array without using extra memory.

slides.headline: ⚡ In-place Sorted Array Merge
slides.body:
You are given two sorted integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2`. Merge them into a single sorted array in-place inside `nums1`.

`nums1` has enough buffer space at the end to hold all elements from `nums2`.

🎯 The real challenge:
Merging them without shifting elements repeatedly, which would cause an expensive `O(N*M)` execution time.
slides.visualCue: Two pointers at the end of valid elements in both arrays, and a third pointer filling elements from back-to-front in the blank buffer.
slides.memoryHook: Fill from the back of nums1 to prevent overwriting your own valid elements.
slides.transition: Why is back-to-front filling the ultimate trick here?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Merging two already sorted sequences
✅ In-place requirement with zero auxiliary space
✅ One array contains a trailing empty buffer matching the other array's size

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you merge two sorted structures in-place and one has a trailing blank buffer, think reverse two-pointer merging to avoid shifting overhead.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple forward brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive forward approach:

1. Use a standard merge step from merge-sort by writing elements into a temporary array.
2. Copy the temporary array back to `nums1`.

⏱️ Time: O(N + M)
📦 Space: O(N + M) extra memory

If extra space is forbidden, a forward in-place merge would require shifting elements right on every insertion, taking `O(N * M)` time.
slides.analogy: Merging lines of people by making everyone in main line step back every time someone from second line joins.
slides.transition: How do we merge in O(N+M) time with O(1) space?

slides.headline: 🚀 The Back-to-Front Breakthrough
slides.body:
Since the tail of `nums1` is completely empty buffer space, it's safe to write elements there without losing any data!

✅ Start comparison from the largest elements (the ends of both sorted lists).
✅ Place the largest element at the very end of `nums1` (`k = m + n - 1`).
✅ Move pointers backward.

This guarantees we never overwrite any elements in `nums1` that haven't been processed yet!
slides.goldenLine: By building the sequence backward from the largest elements, we turn buffer space into a safe haven.
slides.transition: Let's watch this reverse fill step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Pointers: i = 2 (element 3), j = 2 (element 6), k = 5 (target cell).
Compare 3 and 6: 6 is larger. Place at nums1[5] = 6. j decrements to 1, k to 4.
Compare 3 and 5: 5 is larger. Place at nums1[4] = 5. j decrements to 0, k to 3.
slides.keyObservation: No elements in nums1 were shifted, and we didn't use a single byte of extra storage.
slides.transition: Why is this reverse pointer algorithm completely safe?

slides.headline: 🔍 Safety of Reverse Merge
slides.body:
Why are we guaranteed not to overwrite unprocessed elements in `nums1`?

Because the number of empty slots at the end of `nums1` is exactly `n`.
At any point, the number of elements written to the back is `(m + n - 1 - k)`.
The number of elements read from `nums1` is `(m - 1 - i)`.
Since we always write faster or equal to the rate we read from `nums1`, the write pointer `k` will never overtake the read pointer `i`.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to copy remaining elements of nums2 when nums1 elements run out first (e.g. nums1 = [4, 5, 6, 0, 0, 0], nums2 = [1, 2, 3]).
slides.transition: Let's review the step-by-step blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize `i = m - 1` (end of active nums1 elements).
Initialize `j = n - 1` (end of nums2 elements).
Initialize `k = m + n - 1` (end of nums1 buffer capacity).
slides.mentalCompression: Iterate from the end. Place the larger element at the back. Copy remaining nums2.
slides.transition: Let's review the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Elegant reverse two-pointer in-place merge.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Start from the back of the bus where all the empty seats are, and invite the biggest passengers in first.
slides.memoryHook: Buffer at back, biggest to the rear.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Writing loop condition as `i >= 0 && j >= 0` and forgetting to copy leftover `nums2` elements.
Using forward pointers and overwriting elements at the start of `nums1`.
interviewerQuestions: What if nums1 does not have extra buffer space? (Requires Shell Sort / Gap method or swapping)
What is the time complexity if we have to shift elements? (O(N*M))

recall.5sec: Merge from back-to-front comparing the largest elements.
recall.30sec: Set pointers i=m-1, j=n-1, k=m+n-1. While j>=0, place larger of nums1[i] or nums2[j] at nums1[k] and move pointers back.
recall.1min: Optimal O(N+M) time and O(1) space in-place merging leveraging trailing empty space to completely bypass cell-shifting.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates explain clearly why checking j >= 0 is the only termination condition needed. If i < 0 first, we copy the rest of nums2. If j < 0 first, the remaining elements of nums1 are already sorted.
slides.closingLine: Real efficiency is knowing when you can stop copying.

revisionCards.title: Find the Duplicate Number
revisionCards.explanation: Find the single duplicate number in an array of size N+1 containing integers between 1 and N in O(N) time and O(1) space, without modifying the array.

slides.headline: ⚡ Detect the Duplicate Element
slides.body:
Given an array `nums` containing `n + 1` integers where each integer is in the range `[1, n]` inclusive.

There is only one duplicate number in `nums`, but it could be repeated multiple times. Find this duplicate.

🎯 The real challenge:
Solving this in `O(N)` time and `O(1)` space without modifying the array or using a hash set.
slides.visualCue: A directed graph where indices point to cell values, forming a cycle, with two runners traversing the cycle.
slides.memoryHook: Treat the array as a linked list where values are next pointers, and find the cycle's entrance.
slides.transition: How does a simple array hide a secret cyclic linked list?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Identify these triggers:

✅ N+1 elements with values strictly between 1 and N
✅ Read-only array constraint (cannot modify/sort)
✅ constant O(1) space and linear O(N) time bounds

💡 Interview Signal:
When an array contains indices mapping directly to its values and a duplicate exists, it creates a cyclic graph. Think Floyd's Cycle Detection (Tortoise and Hare).
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
Naive ways to solve:

1. Sorting: Sort the array and find adjacent duplicates. Time `O(N log N)`, but modifies the array.
2. Hash Set: Store visited elements in a set. Time `O(N)` but requires `O(N)` auxiliary space.

We need to find the duplicate while maintaining read-only access and constant space.
slides.analogy: Finding duplicate pages in a book by scanning over and over, or making xerox copies of every page.
slides.transition: How can we find the cycle entrance in constant space?

slides.headline: 🚀 Floyd's Cycle Breakthrough
slides.body:
Since each number is between `1` and `n`, we can treat the array as a linked list where the value at `nums[i]` is the pointer to the next node `i`.

✅ Because there is a duplicate, multiple nodes will point to the same index, creating a loop!
✅ Use a slow pointer (moves 1 step: `slow = nums[slow]`) and a fast pointer (moves 2 steps: `fast = nums[nums[fast]]`).
✅ Once they meet, reset `slow` to the start, and move both pointers at a speed of 1 step. The point where they meet again is the duplicate!
slides.goldenLine: The duplicate value is the gateway to the infinite cycle.
slides.transition: Let's trace this tortoise and hare chase.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Indices map: 0->1, 1->3, 2->4, 3->2, 4->2. Note that both indices 3 and 4 point to value 2.
Phase 1 (Meeting): slow starts at 0, fast at 0.
Step 1: slow = nums[0] = 1, fast = nums[nums[0]] = nums[1] = 3.
Step 2: slow = nums[1] = 3, fast = nums[nums[3]] = nums[2] = 4.
slides.keyObservation: The convergence point of Phase 2 is mathematically guaranteed to be the start of the cycle, which is the duplicate number.
slides.transition: Why is this mathematical meeting point guaranteed to be correct?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Math of Floyd's Cycle
slides.body:
Let `F` be distance from start to cycle entrance, `C` be cycle length, and `a` be meeting point inside cycle.

During Phase 1 meeting:
`Distance(Fast) = 2 * Distance(Slow)`
`F + k*C + a = 2 * (F + m*C + a)`
This simplifies to `F = (k - 2m)*C - a`.

This means the distance from the start to cycle entrance (`F`) is equal to the distance from meeting point to cycle entrance traveling forward. Thus, resetting one pointer and moving both at speed 1 guarantees they meet at the entrance!
slides.interviewerTrap: Using index 0 as a value check. Since values are in range [1, n], index 0 is never part of any cycle, which makes it the perfect starting point.
slides.transition: Let's review the clean code blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize `slow = nums[0]` and `fast = nums[0]`.
Run a `do-while` loop: set `slow = nums[slow]` and `fast = nums[nums[fast]]`.
Loop until `slow == fast`.
slides.mentalCompression: Phase 1: Chase until meet. Phase 2: Reset slow, walk together to find cycle entrance.
slides.transition: Let's examine the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal Floyd's cycle detection algorithm.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Hop from value to index like a linked list chain; when two travelers crash, reset one to the beginning and walk until they meet again at the loop's gate.
slides.memoryHook: Tortoise and Hare meeting at the loop gate.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Initializing `slow = 0` and `fast = 0` (this triggers an infinite loop if nums[0] == 0, though values are 1-indexed here).
Modifying the array (e.g. marking negative values) when array is read-only.
interviewerQuestions: What if there are multiple duplicates? (Floyd's still finds one of them)
Can we solve this using binary search? (Yes, in O(N log N) time and O(1) space)

recall.5sec: Treat array as linked list. Use slow and fast pointers to find cycle entrance.
recall.30sec: Find meeting point using slow = nums[slow] and fast = nums[nums[fast]]. Reset slow = nums[0], advance both by 1 step until they meet.
recall.1min: O(N) time and O(1) space cycle detection algorithm mimicking linked list node traversal on read-only memory.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates present all three approaches: Binary Search on range [1, N], Bit Manipulation, and Floyd's Cycle Detection. They explain trade-offs.
slides.closingLine: A cycle is just a straight line that learned how to loop.

revisionCards.title: Repeat and Missing Number
revisionCards.explanation: Find the repeating and missing numbers in an array of size N containing values from 1 to N, in O(N) time and O(1) space using algebraic equations.

slides.headline: ⚡ Find Missing & Repeating Values
slides.body:
You are given a read-only array of size `N` containing integers from `1` to `N`.

Each integer appears exactly once, except for one value `X` which appears twice, and one value `Y` which is missing. Find `X` and `Y`.

🎯 The real challenge:
Finding both variables in a single pass with `O(1)` auxiliary space without modifying the read-only input.
slides.visualCue: Two mathematical balance scales comparing actual sums vs expected sums.
slides.memoryHook: Use sum and sum-of-squares equations to isolate the two unknown values.
slides.transition: How do basic algebraic equations solve this search problem?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the signals:

✅ Size N array containing numbers from 1 to N
✅ One element is repeated, one is missing
✅ Strict O(1) auxiliary space and O(N) time complexity

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you are dealing with a permutation of 1 to N with exactly two errors (one missing, one repeating), think Algebraic Sum Equations or XOR bit manipulation.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
Using a frequency tracker:

1. Maintain a frequency array or hash map of size `N+1` initialized to 0.
2. Iterate and count occurrences of each element.
3. The element with count 2 is repeating (`X`), and count 0 is missing (`Y`).

⏱️ Time: O(N) linear time
📦 Space: O(N) auxiliary space

Not allowed if the interviewer demands constant `O(1)` space.
slides.analogy: Finding a missing book by printing a brand-new copy of the entire catalog to tick them off.
slides.transition: How can we do this in O(1) space using pure mathematics?

slides.headline: 🚀 The Algebraic Balance Breakthrough
slides.body:
Let `X` be the repeating number and `Y` be the missing number. We can set up two mathematical equations using actual sums vs expected sums:

✅ **First Equation (Sum Difference)**:
`Sum(Actual) - Sum(Expected) = X - Y = diff`

✅ **Second Equation (Sum of Squares Difference)**:
`SumSq(Actual) - SumSq(Expected) = X² - Y² = sqDiff`

Since `X² - Y² = (X - Y)(X + Y)`, we can easily find `X + Y = sqDiff / diff`. With both `X - Y` and `X + Y`, we solve for `X` and `Y` using simple arithmetic!
slides.goldenLine: Two equations, two unknowns, zero extra space.
slides.transition: Let's trace this math wizardry in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Input: nums = [3, 1, 2, 5, 3], N = 5. Expected numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
Expected Sum = 15. Expected Square Sum = 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 + 5^2 = 55.
Actual Sum = 3+1+2+5+3 = 14. Actual Square Sum = 9+1+4+25+9 = 48.
Equation 1: X - Y = 14 - 15 = -1.
slides.keyObservation: Using 64-bit integers (`long long` in C++) is absolutely vital to prevent integer overflow when calculating sum of squares.
slides.transition: Why does integer overflow happen and how do we prevent it?

slides.headline: 🔍 Defeating Integer Overflow
slides.body:
For `N = 10^5`, the expected sum of squares is roughly:
`N * (N + 1) * (2N + 1) / 6 ≈ 3.3 * 10^14`.

This far exceeds the maximum limit of a standard 32-bit signed integer (`2 * 10^9`).

✅ Always perform accumulations using 64-bit types (`long long` in C++).
✅ Cast individual products like `num * num` to 64-bit before addition.
slides.interviewerTrap: Using 32-bit integers, which causes silent overflows and wrong answers for large inputs.
slides.transition: Let's review the clean blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize 64-bit variables `sum = 0` and `sqSum = 0`.
Compute expected sum `(N * (N + 1)) / 2` and expected square sum `(N * (N + 1) * (2 * N + 1)) / 6`.
Iterate through input and accumulate actual sums using 64-bit casting.
slides.mentalCompression: Use (X - Y) and (X^2 - Y^2) to find (X + Y), then solve for X and Y.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Overflow-safe algebraic math solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Subtract actual values from standard ranges to build a two-equation system that separates the double-counter from the ghost-number.
slides.memoryHook: Math scales balance double vs missing.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to use 64-bit integers (`long long`), leading to runtime crashes on large arrays.
Swapping the output order of repeating and missing numbers.
interviewerQuestions: Can we solve this using XOR? (Yes, by separating set and unset bits, which avoids overflow entirely)
What if array is read-only and math equations are not allowed?

recall.5sec: Use sum and square-sum equations to solve for X and Y.
recall.30sec: Calculate actual vs expected sum of values and squares. Solve system: X - Y = diff, X + Y = sqDiff / diff.
recall.1min: O(N) time and O(1) space mathematical solution leveraging 64-bit algebraic identities for high efficiency.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates discuss the trade-offs between the Math approach (which is fast but can overflow if not careful) and the XOR approach (which is completely safe from overflow but requires bit manipulation logic), displaying comprehensive systems maturity.
slides.closingLine: Equations are the shortest path to silent optimizations.

revisionCards.title: Inversion of Array
revisionCards.explanation: Count the number of inversions in an array. Two elements form an inversion if a[i] > a[j] and i < j. Solve in O(N log N) using modified Merge Sort.

slides.headline: ⚡ Count Array Inversions
slides.body:
Inversion Count for an array indicates how far the array is from being sorted. Two elements `a[i]` and `a[j]` form an inversion if `a[i] > a[j]` and `i < j`.

Imagine ranking movies. If your ranking is completely opposite to the public ranking, you have a high inversion count. If they match perfectly, it's zero.

🎯 The real challenge:
Counting all such pairs in `O(N log N)` time without resorting to slow `O(N²)` comparisons.
slides.visualCue: A divide-and-conquer merge tree splitting arrays, comparing left and right portions, and accumulating crossover counts.
slides.memoryHook: During merge step, if left-side element is greater than right-side, ALL remaining left elements are also greater!
slides.transition: How does Merge Sort secretly keep track of array sortedness?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Look for these indicators:

✅ Counting pairs `(i, j)` where `i < j` and `arr[i] > arr[j]`
✅ Finding 'how out of order' a list of elements is
✅ High-efficiency constraints (must be faster than quadratic `O(N²)`)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you need to count pairs in an array where left element is larger than right element, think Divide and Conquer (Merge Sort crossover tracking).
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
Compare every element with every element to its right:

1. Loop `i` from `0` to `N-1`.
2. Loop `j` from `i+1` to `N-1`.
3. If `arr[i] > arr[j]`, increment inversion counter.

⏱️ Time: O(N²) quadratic time
📦 Space: O(1) space

Unusable when analyzing large databases of rankings (e.g. N = 10^5).
slides.analogy: Checking if a deck of cards is sorted by pulling out every single possible pair one-by-one.
slides.transition: How can we count inversions during a merge sort recursion?

slides.headline: 🚀 The Merge Sort Crossover Breakthrough
slides.body:
When dividing the array into two sorted halves (Left and Right):

✅ If `Left[i] <= Right[j]`: No inversion. Move `Left[i]` to temporary array.
✅ If `Left[i] > Right[j]`: Inversion detected! Since `Left` is sorted, if `Left[i]` is greater than `Right[j]`, then all elements from `Left[i]` to `Left[mid]` are also greater than `Right[j]`!

💡 The Formula:
Add `(mid - i + 1)` directly to your inversion count in one step!

This counts thousands of inversions simultaneously without visiting individual pairs.
slides.goldenLine: A sorted sublist lets us multiply our discoveries instead of counting them one-by-one.
slides.transition: Let's watch this crossover counting in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Let's trace merge of Left = [4, 8] (mid=1, i=0) and Right = [1, 2] (right=3, j=2).
Compare Left[0] (4) and Right[2] (1): 4 > 1. Inversion! Elements [4, 8] are both > 1. Count += (1 - 0 + 1) = 2. Take 1. j becomes 3.
Compare Left[0] (4) and Right[3] (2): 4 > 2. Inversion! Elements [4, 8] are both > 2. Count += (1 - 0 + 1) = 2. Take 2. j becomes 4.
Right exhausted. Copy remaining Left [4, 8]. Total crossovers in this merge = 4.
slides.keyObservation: Because the Left array was sorted, seeing 4 > 1 allowed us to instantly count 8 > 1 as well without comparing them.
slides.transition: Why is this divide-and-conquer counting mathematically complete?

slides.headline: 🔍 Completeness of Crossover Count
slides.body:
Every inversion pair `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `arr[i] > arr[j]` must fall into one of three categories during recursion:
1. Both `i` and `j` are in the Left half.
2. Both `i` and `j` are in the Right half.
3. `i` is in Left half and `j` is in Right half.

Categories 1 & 2 are counted during recursive calls. Category 3 is captured during the merge crossover step. This guarantees 100% correct counting without duplicates.
slides.interviewerTrap: Returning count as regular 32-bit integer. For N = 5 * 10^5, maximum inversions can be near N*(N-1)/2, causing overflow. Always return 64-bit long long.
slides.transition: Let's look at the clean implementation structure.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Implement recursive `mergeSort` returning a 64-bit count.
Split array at `mid = left + (right - left) / 2`.
Sum inversions: `leftCount + rightCount + mergeCrossoverCount`.
slides.mentalCompression: Perform merge-sort. If left element > right element, add remaining left size to count.
slides.transition: Let's review the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code (Part 1/2)
slides.body: Recursive merge crossover tracker helper.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code (Part 2/2)
slides.body: Recursive merge crossover tracker helper. (Continued)

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: As we zipper-merge two sorted halves, every time a right-side card jumps ahead of a left-side card, count all remaining cards in the left hand as inverted.
slides.memoryHook: Right jumps left card = left-tail added to count.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Using standard 32-bit `int` instead of `long long`, leading to integer overflow.
Off-by-one errors during range partitioning (`mid` vs `mid + 1`).
interviewerQuestions: Can we count inversions using a Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick Tree) or Segment Tree? (Yes, in O(N log N) time)
How does this relate to bubble sort swap count? (It is exactly equal)

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.30sec: Divide array recursively. In merge, if arr[i] > arr[j], add (mid - i + 1) to count because all elements after i in the sorted left half are also > arr[j].
recall.1min: O(N) space and O(N log N) time divide-and-conquer algorithm ideal for large-scale disorder profiling.
