slides.closingLine: In-place modifications are about writing only when necessary.

revisionCards.title: Max consecutive ones
revisionCards.explanation: Find the maximum number of consecutive 1s in a binary array.
examples: nums = [1,1,0,1]. At 0, maxCount=2, current resets to 0. Next 1, current=1. Max is 2.

slides.headline: Max Consecutive Ones
slides.body:
⚡ Given a binary array `nums`, return the maximum number of consecutive `1`s in the array.

This is a classic stream calculation problem.

By tracking a running counter and updating a global maximum, we can solve this in a single scan.
slides.visualCue: A running tally counter incrementing on 1s and resetting to zero on 0s.
slides.memoryHook: Count consecutive matches, and reset to zero when the streak breaks.
slides.transition: Let's explore when greedy tracking is the absolute optimal choice.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
✅ Finding the longest continuous streak of a specific target element.
✅ Linear single-pass requirements.

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks for the maximum length of adjacent matching elements, a simple greedy running counter is always the most efficient approach.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force instinct before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The obvious approach:
Use nested loops to check the length of consecutive ones starting at every index.

⏱️ Time: O(N²) due to nested checks.
📦 Space: O(1) constant auxiliary space.
This is slow because we are repeatedly checking the same sequences of ones multiple times.
slides.analogy: Counting consecutive sunny days by resetting and counting from day one every single morning.
slides.transition: Let's maintain a running streak counter instead.

slides.headline: 🚀 Running Streak Breakthrough
slides.body:
We can track the streak in a single pass:

✅ Maintain a `currentCount` (current streak) and `maxCount` (longest streak).
✅ Loop through `nums`:
  - If `nums[i] == 1`, increment `currentCount`.
  - Update `maxCount = max(maxCount, currentCount)`.
  - If `nums[i] == 0`, reset `currentCount = 0`.

This captures the maximum streak with minimal state tracking.
slides.goldenLine: A single reset is enough to protect the global history.
slides.transition: Let's dry run the streak calculation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Init: maxCount=0, currentCount=0.
Val 1: currentCount=1. maxCount=max(0, 1) = 1.
Val 1: currentCount=2. maxCount=max(1, 2) = 2.
Val 0: currentCount resets to 0. maxCount stays 2.
slides.keyObservation: We update the maxCount *inside* the 1-condition so we never miss a trailing streak ending at the very last index.
slides.transition: Why is updating the maximum inside the 1-condition so robust?

slides.headline: 🔍 Preventing Trailing Streak Bugs
slides.body:
Many candidates only update `maxCount` when they encounter a `0` (the streak breaks).

However, if the array ends with a streak of `1`s (e.g. `[1, 1, 0, 1, 1]`), the streak never breaks before the loop ends, causing the algorithm to miss updating the maximum for the final streak!

Updating `maxCount` at every `1` completely avoids this bug.
slides.interviewerTrap: Resetting the counter on 0 and only updating the max then, which drops the trailing streak.
slides.transition: Let's outline the algorithm blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize maxCount = 0, currentCount = 0.
Loop through nums from i = 0 to nums.size() - 1.
If nums[i] == 1, increment currentCount and update maxCount = max(maxCount, currentCount).
slides.mentalCompression: Increment count on 1 and update max. Reset count to 0 on 0.
slides.transition: Lock this logic into memory with clean code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Highly optimal single-pass streak counter.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: A pedometer counting steps. Keep counting as long as you are walking; freeze the record if you trip, and start over.
slides.memoryHook: Step counts build records, trips reset counters.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Updating the maximum count only when a 0 is met, losing the last sequence if it ends with 1.
Not resetting `currentCount` to 0, which sums all 1s in the array.
interviewerQuestions: What if you can flip at most one 0 to a 1? Yes, use a sliding window tracking the count of 0s.
What is the time complexity? Strictly O(N) time with O(1) space.

slides.body: Elite candidates point out that this is the perfect base problem for more complex sliding window challenges (like Max Consecutive Ones III, where you can flip K zeros). They show they see the progressive difficulty ladder of the problem.
slides.closingLine: Streaks are easily built, but mastering the rules of their breaks is where elegance lies.

revisionCards.title: Reverse a Linked List
revisionCards.explanation: Reverse a singly linked list in-place by flipping the arrow directions of each node.

slides.headline: 🔄 The Core Challenge
slides.body:
You are given a singly linked list and need to reverse it in-place.

Imagine a line of people holding hands, where each person only knows who is *ahead* of them. We want them to flip their orientation completely.

🎯 The real challenge:
Doing this without losing track of the rest of the list while updating the current connection.
slides.visualCue: A chain of nodes with arrows pointing right, transforming into arrows pointing left.
slides.memoryHook: Flip the arrow before stepping onto the next stone.
slides.transition: How do we instantly recognize when a list needs in-place modification?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the pattern instantly:

✅ Request for in-place reordering (e.g. reverse, reorder, group)
✅ Reversing a sub-portion of a sequence
✅ Standard linear list modifications with O(1) auxiliary space

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires processing elements from back-to-front in a singly linked list, reversing is the primary helper tool.
slides.transition: Let's look at the basic brute-force way before doing it in-place.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The simple buffer approach:

1. Traverse the linked list and copy node values into an array/vector.
2. Reconstruct the linked list backwards or write values back in reverse.

⏱️ Time: O(N) traversal
📦 Space: O(N) memory storage

Slow and memory-intensive! We can redirect pointers in-place instead.
slides.analogy: Writing down a list of names, reading them backwards, and rewriting them on new paper, rather than just turning the line around.
slides.transition: Let's discover how the three-pointer slide works.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Track three contiguous nodes simultaneously:

✅ `prev`: The already reversed sub-list
✅ `curr`: The node currently being processed
✅ `nextNode`: The remaining sub-list

By keeping a reference to the next node before overwriting `curr->next`, we never break the chain.
slides.goldenLine: Save the future, redirect the present, step into the past.
slides.transition: Let's watch this dynamic dance step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initialize: prev = null, curr = Node 1
Step 1: Save nextNode = 2. Flip 1->next to prev (null). Move prev = 1, curr = 2.
Step 2: Save nextNode = 3. Flip 2->next to prev (1). Move prev = 2, curr = 3.
Step 3: Save nextNode = null. Flip 3->next to prev (2). Move prev = 3, curr = null. Return prev (3).
slides.keyObservation: Saving `curr->next` before reassigning it is the only thing preventing us from losing the list.
slides.transition: Why is this three-pointer approach mathematically robust?

slides.headline: 🔍 Loop Invariant Safety
slides.body:
Why is this completely safe and leak-proof?

At the start of every iteration, `prev` points to the head of the reversed portion, and `curr` points to the head of the unreversed portion. We never lose access to any node, and no cycle is created.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates often write `curr->next = prev` before saving `nextNode`, causing a segmentation fault or infinite loop.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the code blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize pointers: prev = nullptr, curr = head
While curr is not null: save nextNode = curr->next
Point curr->next to prev (redirecting arrow)
slides.mentalCompression: Three pointers: prev, curr, and a temporary next pointer to secure the link.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Classic, optimal in-place singly linked list reversal.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Save nextNode, flip current next pointer to prev, move prev and curr one step forward.
slides.memoryHook: Secure next, flip link, shift right.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Losing reference to the rest of the list by forgetting nextNode
Returning curr instead of prev (curr will be nullptr at termination)
interviewerQuestions: Can you write this recursively?
What is the space complexity of the recursive solution? (O(N) stack space)

recall.5sec: Reverse in-place using three pointers (prev, curr, next).
recall.30sec: Loop through, save curr->next, flip curr->next to prev, move prev and curr forward.
recall.1min: Linear O(N) time and constant O(1) space in-place reversal by redirecting links node-by-node.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates write the iterative solution first due to constant space, then proactively mention the O(N) recursive stack overhead. They also call out that returning `prev` works flawlessly even for an empty list (`head == nullptr`).
slides.closingLine: True mastery is choosing the space-optimal iterative approach over recursion.

revisionCards.title: Find the Middle of a Linked List
revisionCards.explanation: Find the middle node of a singly linked list. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node.

slides.headline: 🎯 The Midpoint Hunt
slides.body:
Find the middle node of a singly linked list.

If the list length is odd, return the exact middle. If it is even, return the second middle.

🎯 The real challenge:
Finding it in a single pass without knowing the list length beforehand.
slides.visualCue: A walker taking single steps and a runner taking double steps on a straight path.
slides.memoryHook: Fast runner reaches the end; slow walker rests exactly at the middle.
slides.transition: When does this Fast & Slow pointer pattern trigger in interviews?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the pattern instantly:

✅ Locating midpoints or division points in lists
✅ Cycle detection (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare)
✅ Splitting a linked list in two for Merge Sort

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem mentions 'middle', 'halfway', or requires splitting, immediately think Fast & Slow Pointers.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple two-pass approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Double-Pass approach:

1. Traverse the entire list to count the total length `L`.
2. Traverse again from the head up to `L / 2` steps to get the middle node.

⏱️ Time: O(N) time (takes 1.5N passes)
📦 Space: O(1) space

Can we do it in exactly one pass (0.5N steps for the slow pointer)?
slides.analogy: Counting the pages of a book to find the middle page, then flipping from page 1 again to reach it.
slides.transition: Enter the dynamic ratio optimization.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Speed Ratio Hook
slides.body:
Use the ratio of speeds:

✅ Move `fast` pointer by 2 steps
✅ Move `slow` pointer by 1 step

Since `fast` travels exactly twice as fast as `slow`, when `fast` reaches the end of the list, `slow` must be exactly in the middle.
slides.goldenLine: Harnessing relative velocities to divide distance in half.
slides.transition: Let's trace this beautiful coordination.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initialize slow = 1, fast = 1.
Step 1: slow moves to 2, fast moves to 3. (Both valid)
Step 2: slow moves to 3, fast moves to 5. (fast->next is null)
Termination: Loop ends because fast->next is nullptr. Slow is at 3. Return 3.
slides.keyObservation: For an even list like [1,2,3,4,5,6], fast starts at 1, moves to 3, then 5, then fast becomes null. Slow stops at 4 (second middle) perfectly!
slides.transition: Why is this loop boundary safe?

slides.headline: 🔍 Safe Boundary Guards
slides.body:
Why does `while (fast != nullptr && fast->next != nullptr)` prevent crash?

If `fast` is null (even length list), the loop stops immediately. If `fast->next` is null (odd length list), the second check stops us from dereferencing a null pointer with `fast->next->next`. The order of conditions is vital.
slides.interviewerTrap: Reversing the check order to `fast->next != nullptr && fast != nullptr` causes crash on null list.
slides.transition: Let's look at the algorithm blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize: slow and fast both at head pointer
Loop: while fast and fast->next are both not null
Advance slow by 1 step (slow = slow->next)
slides.mentalCompression: Slow steps 1, Fast steps 2. Stop when Fast hits the wall.
slides.transition: Here is the clean interview C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal single-pass Fast & Slow pointer solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Start slow and fast together, advance slow by 1 and fast by 2 until fast or fast->next becomes null.
slides.memoryHook: Fast runs double, Slow lands in middle.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Null reference on fast->next if fast is nullptr
Forgetting fast->next != nullptr check, causing null pointer dereference on odd-length lists
interviewerQuestions: How would you modify this to return the first middle in even length list?
Can this be used to split a list for Merge Sort?

recall.5sec: Fast and slow pointers: slow moves 1, fast moves 2.
recall.30sec: Start slow/fast at head. Move fast by 2, slow by 1. Return slow when fast or fast->next hits null.
recall.1min: Single-pass O(N) time and O(1) space midpoint finder using 1:2 velocity ratio.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out that the fast-and-slow approach has excellent cache locality compared to doing a double-pass that spans memory twice, and explain exactly why the short-circuiting `&&` operator prevents segment faults.
slides.closingLine: Double the speed, half the traversal, zero memory overhead.

revisionCards.title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists
revisionCards.explanation: Merge two sorted linked lists into a single sorted list in-place.

slides.headline: ⛓️ Merging Two Chains
slides.body:
You have two sorted linked lists.

You want to splice them together in-place so that the final list is also sorted.

🎯 The real challenge:
Doing it without allocating any new nodes, simply rewiring existing pointers to maintain O(1) space.
slides.visualCue: Two sorted columns of values being zipped together into a single sorted column.
slides.memoryHook: Compare the heads, stitch the smaller, advance the pointer.
slides.transition: When does this zipping pattern be useful?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Combining multiple sorted sequences
✅ Merge step of Merge Sort on lists
✅ Building a unified list from sorted partitions

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires merging two structures that are already sorted, think two-pointer linear traversal.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force way.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Node-Copy approach:

1. Create a brand new linked list.
2. Compare heads of both lists and copy the smaller node value into the new list.
3. Move pointers and repeat.

⏱️ Time: O(N + M) time
📦 Space: O(N + M) space due to creating N+M new node allocations.

Inefficient! We can reuse existing node pointers to do it in-place.
slides.analogy: Building a new train from scratch by copying passenger lists rather than just decoupling and reattaching the actual train cars.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the dummy node technique.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Dummy Node Hook
slides.body:
Use a fake temporary starting node:

✅ `dummy` node serves as the anchor point of our merged list
✅ `curr` pointer stitches the next link dynamically

This completely eliminates edge case checks for empty lists or deciding which list's head becomes the new return head.
slides.goldenLine: A dummy anchor absorbs all edge cases, leaving pointer rewiring simple.
slides.transition: Let's dry run the stitching process.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initialize dummy node. curr points to dummy. l1=1, l2=2.
Step 1: l1 (1) <= l2 (2). Stitch curr->next = l1. Advance l1 to 4. Advance curr to 1.
Step 2: l2 (2) < l1 (4). Stitch curr->next = l2. Advance l2 to 3. Advance curr to 2.
Step 3: l2 (3) < l1 (4). Stitch curr->next = l2. l2 becomes null. Advance curr to 3.
slides.keyObservation: Once one list runs out, we can directly attach the rest of the other list in O(1) time without looping.
slides.transition: Why is this dummy-node approach so robust?

slides.headline: 🔍 Memory Safety & In-Place Splicing
slides.body:
Why is this in-place method superior?

It updates only the `next` pointers of existing nodes. No heap allocations are done (except the single temporary dummy node). This avoids memory fragmentation and is cache-friendly.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to attach the non-null remainder after the while loop terminates is a classic error.
slides.transition: Let's review the exact code blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create a dummy node to act as the head anchor
Set a tracking pointer 'curr' to point to dummy
While both l1 and l2 are not null: compare values
slides.mentalCompression: Compare heads, attach the smaller to curr, shift forward, attach the remainder at the end.
slides.transition: Here is the clean interview C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal in-place zipping of two sorted lists.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Compare the heads of both lists, link the smaller node to the merged chain, and tack on the remainder at the end.
slides.memoryHook: Stitch the smaller head, append the leftover.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to advance `curr` inside the while loop, causing infinite replacement
Forgetting the remainder attachment after the while loop finishes
interviewerQuestions: Can you solve this recursively? (Yes, O(N+M) recursive stack space)
How does this scale to K sorted lists?

recall.5sec: Use dummy node and compare heads of l1 and l2.
recall.30sec: Iterate, attach the smaller node to dummy's chain, advance pointers. Attach the leftover list at the end.
recall.1min: In-place linear O(N+M) time, O(1) auxiliary space merge using a dummy pointer and simple redirection.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out that the temporary dummy node can be allocated on the stack (`ListNode dummy(-1)`) instead of the heap (`new ListNode(-1)`) to avoid memory leaks and overhead in C++, returning `dummy.next`.
slides.closingLine: Stack-allocated dummy nodes are the hallmark of production-grade C++ developers.

revisionCards.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
revisionCards.explanation: Remove the N-th node from the end of a singly linked list in a single pass.

slides.headline: ✂️ Retrospective Deletion
slides.body:
You need to delete the N-th node *from the end* of a singly linked list.

Singly linked lists only let us walk forward. How do we measure distance from the *end* before we even get there?

🎯 The real challenge:
Completing this in exactly a single pass, without storing nodes or measuring length first.
slides.visualCue: Two pointers moving together, separated by a fixed distance like a rigid measuring rod.
slides.memoryHook: Keep a fixed gap between fast and slow; when fast hits the end, slow is just before the target.
slides.transition: Let's explore why standard approaches require two passes.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ K-th element from the end of a list
✅ Node removal based on relative distance from termination
✅ Single-pass boundary-based traversals

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks for elements relative to the end of a singly linked list, think Two-Pointer Sliding Window.
slides.transition: Let's examine the brute-force two-pass way.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Length-Subtraction approach:

1. Traverse the list from start to end to find the total length `L`.
2. Perform a second pass from head to target index `L - N - 1`.
3. Delete the next node.

⏱️ Time: O(N) (takes 2N steps)
📦 Space: O(1) space

But can we solve it using a single traversal, visiting each node exactly once?
slides.analogy: Counting the total number of steps in a dark corridor, turning back, and walking N steps back, rather than using a measuring stick.
slides.transition: Let's discover the sliding gap technique.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Gap Window Hook
slides.body:
Maintain a fixed gap of size `N` between two pointers:

✅ Advance `fast` pointer by `N + 1` steps first
✅ Then advance `fast` and `slow` together at the same speed

When `fast` becomes `nullptr`, `slow` is pointing exactly to the node *before* the target node. We can delete `slow->next` directly!
slides.goldenLine: A constant offset window makes the tail visible from the head.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this offset technique.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
array: Both moved till fast is null
steps: Initialize dummy node pointing to head (1). Set slow = dummy, fast = dummy.
Advance fast pointer by N + 1 = 3 steps (dummy -> 1 -> 2 -> 3).
Slide both slow and fast step-by-step: slow -> 1 (fast -> 4), slow -> 2 (fast -> 5), slow -> 3 (fast -> null). Stop.
Re-link: slow->next = slow->next->next (3's next becomes 5). Return dummy->next (1->2->3->5).
slides.keyObservation: Using a dummy node handles the edge case of deleting the head node (e.g. n = length of list) seamlessly.
slides.transition: Why is the dummy node crucial for safety here?

slides.headline: 🔍 Edge Case Protection
slides.body:
Why is the dummy node so vital?

If we need to remove the first node (`head`), `slow` must stop *before* the head node. By using a dummy node, `slow` starts one step behind `head`. This prevents a segmentation fault and keeps the algorithm completely uniform.
slides.interviewerTrap: Failing to handle lists of size 1 or removing the head node leads to crashes without a dummy node.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create dummy node pointing to head, initialize slow and fast to dummy
Move fast pointer N + 1 steps forward
Move slow and fast together until fast reaches nullptr
slides.mentalCompression: Move fast by N+1 steps, then slide slow and fast together. Bypass slow->next.
slides.transition: Here is the clean interview C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Single-pass optimal sliding-window node deletion.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Send the fast pointer N+1 steps ahead, then step slow and fast together until fast is null, and delete slow's next node.
slides.memoryHook: Fast gap of N+1, slide to the end, skip next.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Off-by-one errors while advancing fast pointer initially
Crashing when deleting the head node if dummy node isn't used
interviewerQuestions: Can this be done without a dummy node? (Yes, but requires extra `if` checks)
What happens if N is larger than the list length?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Fast pointer goes N+1 steps ahead, then slide slow and fast together.
recall.30sec: Use dummy node. Advance fast N+1 times. Slide slow/fast together until fast is null. slow->next = slow->next->next.
recall.1min: Single-pass O(N) time and O(1) space node deletion using a fixed-gap sliding pointer pair.

patternConnections: Swapping Nodes in a Linked List

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates write the stack-allocated dummy node `ListNode dummy(0); dummy.next = head;` and explicitly delete the target node in C++ to prevent memory leaks, showing they write production-ready code.
slides.closingLine: A single pass with garbage hygiene is the hallmark of senior candidates.

revisionCards.title: Add Two Numbers as Linked Lists
revisionCards.explanation: Add two numbers represented as linked lists in reverse order.

slides.headline: ➕ List Arithmetic
slides.body:
You have two numbers represented as linked lists. The digits are stored in *reverse order*, and each node contains a single digit.

Add the two numbers and return the sum as a new linked list.

🎯 The real challenge:
Handling unequal lengths and tracking carry-overs gracefully across node transitions.
slides.visualCue: Two vertical stacks of nodes being summed column-by-column with a carry value hopping left.
slides.memoryHook: Add columns from left to right, push the tens digit as a carry to the next column.
slides.transition: How do we map standard grade-school addition to pointer traversal?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Big integer arithmetic using custom structures
✅ Column-wise digit-by-digit summation
✅ Sequential element-by-element processing with carry rules

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks to perform math operations on linked lists or string representations, think digit-by-digit simulation with a carry state.
slides.transition: Why is the reversed format of lists a massive hidden benefit?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Value-Reconstruction trap:

1. Traverse both lists to construct the two integer values (e.g. `342` and `465`).
2. Add them mathematically to get `807`.
3. Convert the sum back to a linked list node-by-node.

⏱️ Time: O(N + M)
📦 Space: O(max(N, M)) for result

❌ Fatal Flaw: Big integer overflow! Linked lists can represent numbers with hundreds of digits, which will easily exceed standard integer or long-long storage limits.
slides.analogy: Converting a massive train into a single number just to add another train, rather than linking individual matching compartments.
slides.transition: Let's discover the elegant digit-by-digit carry loop.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Carry-Forward Hook
slides.body:
Because the digits are *already reversed*, the least significant digit is at the head. This matches how we add manually!

✅ Sum corresponding digits and the current `carry`
✅ Compute new carry: `carry = sum / 10`
✅ Create new node with: `sum % 10`

This streams addition in one direction without any numerical overflow.
slides.goldenLine: Reversed order is a gift: addition flows naturally from head to tail.
slides.transition: Let's trace this arithmetic simulation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initialize dummy node, curr = dummy, carry = 0.
Col 1: sum = 2 (l1) + 5 (l2) + 0 (carry) = 7. carry = 0. New node (7). Advance.
Col 2: sum = 4 (l1) + 6 (l2) + 0 (carry) = 10. carry = 1. New node (0). Advance.
Col 3: sum = 3 (l1) + 4 (l2) + 1 (carry) = 8. carry = 0. New node (8). Advance. Return 7->0->8.
slides.keyObservation: Even if one list finishes early, the `while (l1 || l2 || carry)` loop handles leftover digits and a final carry seamlessly.
slides.transition: Why does the loop condition solve three edge cases at once?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Loop Condition Mastery
slides.body:
Why is `while (l1 != nullptr || l2 != nullptr || carry)` so clean?

If one list is shorter, it treats its value as `0`. If both lists end but we have a leftover `carry = 1` (e.g. `99 + 1 = 100`), the `carry` flag keeps the loop active for one more cycle to attach the final `1` node.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to append the final carry node after both lists are exhausted is the most common bug.
slides.transition: Let's view the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create dummy node and set curr to point to dummy
Initialize carry = 0
Loop while l1 is not null, or l2 is not null, or carry is non-zero
slides.mentalCompression: Sum l1 + l2 + carry. New digit is sum % 10. Carry is sum / 10.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal digit-by-digit simulation code.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Sum elements and carry column by column, save units digit as a new node, and carry over the tens digit to the next iteration.
slides.memoryHook: Sum, split carry, attach unit.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to check the `carry` in the loop condition, losing the leading 1 (e.g. 9 + 1 => 0 instead of 0->1)
Dereferencing null pointer on shorter list when accessing `l1->val` directly
interviewerQuestions: What if the digits are stored in direct order? (Must reverse lists first, add, and reverse result)
Can we do this recursively?

recall.5sec: Digit summation with carry propagation on a combined loop.
recall.30sec: Loop `while (l1 || l2 || carry)`. sum = val1 + val2 + carry, create node `sum % 10`, carry = `sum / 10`.
recall.1min: Linear O(max(N, M)) time and space solution using elementary addition simulation on a single-pass traversal.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out that we could optimize memory by reusing the original lists' nodes to store the sum in-place, but call out that this mutates the inputs, which might not be thread-safe or desirable in actual systems.
slides.closingLine: Balancing space optimization with clean functional design is senior behavior.

revisionCards.title: Delete Node in a Linked List
revisionCards.explanation: Delete a given node in a singly linked list without access to the head pointer.

slides.headline: 🕵️ The Blind Deletion
slides.body:
You are asked to delete a node in a singly linked list, but you are only given access to *that specific node*.

You have no access to the `head` pointer of the list!

🎯 The real challenge:
Deleting a node requires updating its predecessor's `next` pointer. Without the head, how can we possibly find the predecessor?
slides.visualCue: A person in a line copying the face of the person ahead of them, then telling that person to step out.
slides.memoryHook: If you can't bypass yourself, steal your neighbor's identity and discard them.
slides.transition: Let's see why traditional deletion fails here.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Node deletion request without list context or head
✅ Constant time O(1) structural modification
✅ Value-copying based deletion hacks

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a singly linked list question gives you a node reference directly and guarantees it is not the tail, think Value Shuffling.
slides.transition: Let's review why this seems mathematically impossible at first.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Backwards-Search failure:

Usually, to delete node `N`, we find the parent node `P` where `P->next == N`, and update `P->next = N->next`.

Without a `head` or `prev` reference, finding `P` requires searching backwards, which is impossible in a singly linked list.

⏱️ Time: Impossible to do conventionally
📦 Space: O(1)
slides.analogy: Trying to remove a link from a heavy locked chain when you can only touch that link and the ones ahead of it, not the ones behind.
slides.transition: Behold the optimal identity-theft breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Identity Theft Hook
slides.body:
If you can't delete yourself, become your neighbor!

✅ Copy the value of the next node into the current node
✅ Bypass the next node by pointing `node->next = node->next->next`

This makes the current node indistinguishable from the next node, and effectively deletes the next node's shell.
slides.goldenLine: To erase a node, we copy the future and erase the duplicate shell.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this magical swap.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initialize: target node is 5. Next node is 1.
Step 1: Copy value of next node (1) into current node. The list is now [4, 1, 1, 9].
Step 2: Bypass the duplicate next node. Update current node's next pointer to point to 9. List is [4, 1, 9].
Result: Node 5 is completely deleted from the observer's perspective!
slides.keyObservation: We didn't actually delete the target node's memory cell; we deleted the cell *after* it after stealing its data.
slides.transition: What are the hidden interviewer traps of this method?

slides.headline: 🔍 Semantic Drawbacks & Traps
slides.body:
Why is this trick popular but controversial?

1. It fails if the node to delete is the tail (no `next` node exists to copy from).
2. Any outside pointers referencing the next node are now pointing to a deleted/bypassed shell, causing dangling pointer issues.
3. Mutates values instead of references, which triggers errors in read-only nodes.
slides.interviewerTrap: The interviewer will ask: 'What if the node is the tail?' Always explicitly state that this method requires the node not to be the tail.
slides.transition: Let's check the code blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Locate the next node: temp = node->next
Copy the value: node->val = temp->val
Bypass the next node: node->next = temp->next
slides.mentalCompression: Copy value of next node into this node. Delete next node.
slides.transition: Here is the super-compact C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Constant time value-copy node deletion.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Copy the next node's value onto yourself and skip the next node in the chain.
slides.memoryHook: Copy value from next, point next to next-next.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Accessing node->next->val without checking if it's null (crashes on tail)
Forgetting to delete the duplicate node shell, causing memory leaks in C++
interviewerQuestions: What if the node to delete is the last node? (Need dummy/head to update parent to null)
Why does this fail in multi-threaded environments?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Copy next node's value, bypass next node.
recall.30sec: Given `node`, set `node->val = node->next->val`, and `node->next = node->next->next`.
recall.1min: Constant O(1) time and space deletion trick that simulates node removal by shifting values instead of changing preceding links.

patternConnections: Delete N Nodes After M Nodes

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out the garbage collection vs manual delete differences. In C++, they explicitly save `node->next`, bypass, and then call `delete` to prevent memory leaks. They also discuss reference preservation issues for external trackers.
slides.closingLine: Knowing when a hack is useful—and when it is dangerous—shows true seniority.

revisionCards.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
revisionCards.explanation: Find the node at which two singly linked lists intersect. Return null if there is no intersection.

slides.headline: 🛣️ Where Paths Collide
slides.body:
You have two singly linked lists that might merge at some point to form a Y-shaped structure.

Find the exact node where they first intersect.

🎯 The real challenge:
Solving this in O(N + M) time and O(1) auxiliary space, without knowing where the merge point is or how long the separate tails are.
slides.visualCue: Two roads of different lengths joining into a single highway.
slides.memoryHook: Swap tracks when you hit the end; the travel difference is wiped clean.
slides.transition: How do we instantly recognize where the pathways intersect?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Finding a common suffix in two chains
✅ Finding shared references between linear pathways
✅ Aligning two data streams of different offsets

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks for a common convergence point between two sequences, think Offset Alignment.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple hash-table approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Hash Map tracker:

1. Traverse List A and store every node pointer in a Hash Set.
2. Traverse List B and check if current node pointer exists in the set.
3. The first match is the intersection.

⏱️ Time: O(N + M) traversal
📦 Space: O(N) hash memory

Can we do it in constant O(1) space?
slides.analogy: Taking photos of every milepost on Road A, then driving on Road B and checking your photos, rather than just aligning your odometers.
slides.transition: Enter the brilliant track-switching technique.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Path-Symmetrizing Hook
slides.body:
Eliminate the length difference by zipping paths!

✅ Pointer `pA` traverses List A, then jumps to List B's head.
✅ Pointer `pB` traverses List B, then jumps to List A's head.

Because `len(A) + len(B) == len(B) + len(A)`, both pointers will travel exactly the same distance, aligning them perfectly at the intersection node!
slides.goldenLine: By swapping tracks, we make unequal journeys equal.
slides.transition: Let's trace this beautiful dance step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
array: pA reaches null. Jumps to B's head (5)
pB is at 8 (on A's joint path)
pB reaches null. Jumps to A's head (4)
Both pointers arrive at node 8 simultaneously
steps: Initialize: pA = headA (4), pB = headB (5). len(A)=5, len(B)=6.
pA moves 5 times to nullptr, then switches to B's head (5).
pB moves 6 times to nullptr, then switches to A's head (4).
After switching, both pointers are exactly 2 steps away from the joint node 8. They meet at 8. Return 8.
slides.keyObservation: If there is no intersection, they both reach nullptr at the exact same step, terminating the loop with pA == pB == nullptr.
slides.transition: Why is this track-switching mathematically sound?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Math of Track Switching
slides.body:
Why does this work flawlessly?

Let List A have non-shared length `a` and List B have non-shared length `b`, with shared length `c`. 
- Pointer A travels `a + c + b`
- Pointer B travels `b + c + a`

Since `a + c + b == b + c + a`, they meet exactly after that distance, which is the start of the shared segment `c`!
slides.interviewerTrap: Infinite loops if you check `pA->next == nullptr` to switch instead of `pA == nullptr`. Let the pointer hit nullptr itself before switching.
slides.transition: Let's check the code blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize: pA = headA, pB = headB
Loop while pA is not equal to pB
If pA is null, redirect to headB; else move to pA->next
slides.mentalCompression: Pointer A does A then B. Pointer B does B then A. They meet at the joint or at null.
slides.transition: Here is the elegant C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal track-switching intersection finder.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Traverse your list; when you hit the end, start at the other list's head; the pointers will meet at the collision point.
slides.memoryHook: Complete A then B, meet at the joint.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Redirecting pointers to the next node (`pA = headB`) rather than hitting the `nullptr` boundary, which causes infinite loops when there is no intersection
Using value equality (`pA->val == pB->val`) instead of pointer reference equality (`pA == pB`)
interviewerQuestions: What is the time complexity? (O(N + M))
Can we solve this by calculating list lengths? (Yes, find the difference `d = L1 - L2` and shift the longer list ahead by `d` steps)

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Switch list heads at the end of each traversal to align pointers.
recall.30sec: Iterate two pointers. If one hits null, redirect to the opposite list's head. They will meet at the intersection point.
recall.1min: Symmetric O(N + M) time and O(1) space intersection finder using self-aligning dual pointer traversal.
