slides.closingLine: Visualizing lists as circular alignment tracks is the hallmark of elite intuition.

revisionCards.title: Detect Cycle in a Linked List
revisionCards.explanation: Determine if a linked list contains a cycle.

slides.headline: 🌀 The Infinite Loop
slides.body:
You have a singly linked list. A cycle occurs if some node can be reached again by continuously following the `next` pointer.

Detect if a cycle exists.

🎯 The real challenge:
Detecting the loop in O(1) auxiliary space, without modifying the list structure or marking visited nodes.
slides.visualCue: A track with a straight segment leading into a circle where a runner laps a walker.
slides.memoryHook: In a circular race track, the fast runner will always lap the slow walker.
slides.transition: How does the runner-walker analogy translate into robust pointer arithmetic?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Checking for infinite loops in pointer structures
✅ Finding structural cycles in directed single-path graphs
✅ Determining if a process repeats state configurations

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem involves discovering cycles or repeats in sequential traversals, think Floyd's Tortoise and Hare algorithm.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple hash-set approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Visited Set approach:

1. Traverse the linked list node-by-node.
2. Store each node's memory address in a Hash Set.
3. If you encounter a node address already in the set, a cycle exists!

⏱️ Time: O(N) traversal
📦 Space: O(N) hash memory

This is memory-inefficient! Can we find the cycle using constant O(1) extra space?
slides.analogy: Leaving a trail of breadcrumbs to detect if you are walking in circles, which fails if you run out of crumbs.
slides.transition: Behold the velocity-ratio breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Tortoise & Hare Hook
slides.body:
Use relative velocities:

✅ Slow pointer (`slow`) advances 1 step
✅ Fast pointer (`fast`) advances 2 steps

If there is no cycle, `fast` will hit the end (`nullptr`). If there *is* a cycle, `fast` enters the loop first. Because `fast` reduces the distance to `slow` by 1 node in every step, they are guaranteed to meet inside the loop!
slides.goldenLine: Inside a loop, a velocity difference of 1 guarantees convergence without bypass.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this pursuit.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
array: slow moved to 2, fast moved to 0
slow moved to 0, fast looped to 2
slow moved to -4, fast moved to -4. Collision!
steps: Initialize slow = 3, fast = 3.
Step 1: slow moves 1 step to 2. fast moves 2 steps to 0. (No collision)
Step 2: slow moves 1 step to 0. fast loops around to 2. (No collision)
Step 3: slow moves 1 step to -4. fast moves 2 steps (from 2 to 0 to -4). Collision! Return true.
slides.keyObservation: No matter how large the loop is, the fast pointer can never jump over the slow pointer without landing on it because the relative gap closes by exactly 1 per step.
slides.transition: Why is this collision mathematically guaranteed?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Math of Loop Intersection
slides.body:
Why is collision guaranteed?

Let the distance from `slow` to `fast` inside a loop of length `C` be `D` nodes. In each step:
`New Distance = (D + 1 - 2) mod C = (D - 1) mod C`

The gap decreases by exactly 1 every step. Thus, they will meet in exactly `D` steps. This is simple modular arithmetic safety!
slides.interviewerTrap: Checking `fast->next->next` without first validating that `fast->next` is not null. Always double-guard the fast pointer.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the algorithm blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize slow and fast pointers to the head node
Loop while fast is not null and fast->next is not null
Advance slow by 1 step (slow = slow->next)
slides.mentalCompression: Slow advances 1, Fast advances 2. If they collide, there is a cycle.
slides.transition: Here is the clean interview C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal constant space cycle detection.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Advance slow pointer by 1 and fast by 2; if there's a loop, they will eventually crash into each other.
slides.memoryHook: Run tortoise & hare; collision means cycle.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Accessing `fast->next->next` when `fast` or `fast->next` is nullptr, causing segfault
Comparing node values (`slow->val == fast->val`) instead of pointers (`slow == fast`), which fails if the list has duplicate values
interviewerQuestions: How do you find the starting node of the cycle? (Floyd's starting point logic)
What is the maximum number of steps slow will take before they meet? (Less than the list length N)

recall.5sec: Fast & slow pointers collide if there is a cycle.
recall.30sec: Start slow/fast at head. Move slow by 1, fast by 2. If they meet, return true. If fast or fast->next becomes null, return false.
recall.1min: Floyd's Cycle Detection in O(N) time and O(1) space, using relative velocity ratios to force a pointer collision.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates don't just show the algorithm. They explain the modular arithmetic proof that guarantees they will meet within `N` steps, proving that slow will never complete a full lap of the loop before being caught.
slides.closingLine: Relative motion is the cleanest way to bound infinite loops.

revisionCards.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
revisionCards.explanation: Reverse the nodes of a linked list k at a time and return the modified list.

slides.headline: 🔄 Grouped Reversals
slides.body:
Given a linked list, reverse the nodes in groups of size `k` and return the modified list.

If the number of nodes is not a multiple of `k`, the leftover nodes at the end should remain in their original order.

🎯 The real challenge:
Performing this chunk-by-chunk reversal while cleanly stitching the sub-lists together in-place.
slides.visualCue: A chain segmented into blocks of k nodes, each block flipping direction, while keeping the connections between blocks intact.
slides.memoryHook: Reverse each segment of k nodes in-place, then stitch the tail to the next recursive group.
slides.transition: Why is this considered a top-tier Hard interview question?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Batch reordering or chunk-wise processing of sequences
✅ Multi-stage reversing with remaining constraints
✅ In-place node modifications with recursive block dependencies

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires applying a transformation to small, equal-sized subsets of a list, think Segmented Recursion.
slides.transition: Let's review the sub-optimal brute-force way.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Node Array approach:

1. Traverse the list and copy all nodes into an array.
2. Slice the array into chunks of size `k`.
3. Reverse each chunk that has size exactly `k`.
4. Re-link all nodes from start to finish by setting their `next` pointers.

⏱️ Time: O(N) time
📦 Space: O(N) array storage

Simple, but uses linear auxiliary space. Let's do it in-place.
slides.analogy: Uncoupling all train cars, parking them, sorting them in batches on separate tracks, and putting them back together.
slides.transition: Let's explore the recursive segment-stitching optimization.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Recursive Stitch Hook
slides.body:
Break the problem into sub-problems:

✅ First check if at least `k` nodes exist in the current block.
✅ If yes, reverse those `k` nodes in-place.
✅ The original `head` of this block becomes the *tail* after reversal.

Recursively call the function for the remaining list (`curr`), and link `head->next = reverseKGroup(curr, k)`!
slides.goldenLine: A reversed block's tail is the perfect anchor for the next block's head.
slides.transition: Let's trace a dry run with k=2.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
array: Only 1 node remains (5) < k. Keep as-is (5)
steps: Count N = 5 nodes. We have enough for first block [1, 2].
Reverse block [1, 2] in-place to [2, 1]. head (1) is now tail. prev (2) is head.
Recurse on remainder starting at 3. Next block is [3, 4].
Reverse [3, 4] to [4, 3]. head (3) is tail. prev (4) is head.
slides.keyObservation: By checking node count *before* reversing, we guarantee that the final sub-k block remains untouched.
slides.transition: Why is recursion so incredibly clean for stitching?

slides.headline: 🔍 Recursive vs Iterative Splitting
slides.body:
Why is recursion the cleanest way to solve this?

Reversing a block is easy, but holding onto the head of the *next* block while linking the tail of the *current* block iteratively requires tracking 4 pointers. Recursion uses the call stack to store these bridge connections, making the code elegant and bug-free.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to link the tail of the reversed group to the result of the recursive call.
slides.transition: Let's see the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Check if there are at least k nodes from the current head pointer
If there are fewer than k nodes, return head (no reversal needed)
If k nodes exist, reverse the next k nodes iteratively
slides.mentalCompression: Count k nodes. Reverse. Connect head->next to recursion on remainder.
slides.transition: Let's view the C++ implementation split into two slides.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Checking group boundaries and starting the reversal process.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Verify k nodes exist, reverse them in-place, and recursively link the group tail to the head of the next reversed block.
slides.memoryHook: Check k size, reverse chunk, stitch to next recursive head.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Reversing the leftover nodes when their count is less than k
Losing connection between adjacent blocks, causing disjoint list fragments
interviewerQuestions: Can you write this with O(1) auxiliary space? (Yes, requires iterative tracking)
How would you modify this to reverse the leftover nodes too?

recall.5sec: Check for k nodes, reverse them, link tail to next recursive call.
recall.30sec: Iterate to count k nodes. If found, reverse them. Set `head->next = reverseKGroup(curr, k)`. Return `prev`.
recall.1min: Segmented block reversal in O(N) time and O(N/k) recursive stack space using count-controlled local pointer flipping.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates call out the stack space complexity of O(N/k) and can explain how to write the fully iterative O(1) space version using a dummy node and a tracker for the previous block's tail, showcasing deep production-ready optimization skills.
slides.closingLine: Clean recursion builds clarity; optimal iteration builds enterprise speed.

revisionCards.title: Check if a Linked List is Palindrome
revisionCards.explanation: Check if a singly linked list is a palindrome by reversing its second half.

slides.headline: 🔁 Symmetric Lists
slides.body:
You have a singly linked list. You want to determine if the list is a palindrome (reads the same forward and backward).

🎯 The real challenge:
Singly linked lists can only be traversed forward. How do we check symmetry from the tail back to the head in-place with O(1) auxiliary space?
slides.visualCue: A list split in half at the middle, with the second half's arrows reversed to point back towards the middle.
slides.memoryHook: Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare it with the first half.
slides.transition: Let's look at why standard linear space techniques are sub-optimal.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Structural symmetry validation in linked lists
✅ Mirror-image comparisons of sequences
✅ Multi-stage list transformations (split, reverse, compare)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires checking symmetry on a singly linked list with O(1) space, think Midpoint Reversal.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force way.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Array-Mirror approach:

1. Traverse the linked list and copy all values to an array/vector.
2. Use a standard two-pointer check on the array to verify symmetry.

⏱️ Time: O(N) time
📦 Space: O(N) space due to extra array allocation

Too much memory! We can do it in-place by reversing the second half.
slides.analogy: Writing a long message on paper, photocopying it, and folding the copy to check if the ends match, instead of just folding the original paper.
slides.transition: Enter the three-stage list optimization.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Midpoint Reversal Hook
slides.body:
Combine three simple primitives:

✅ **Find middle**: Use fast and slow pointers.
✅ **Reverse second half**: Reverse the list starting from the middle node in-place.
✅ **Compare**: Use two pointers starting at the head and the reversed middle to compare values.

This achieves perfect mirror-matching without any extra space!
slides.goldenLine: Reversing the second half flips the tail into a head, enabling simple forward comparisons.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this tripartite logic.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
array: slow = Node 2 (index 2), fast = null. Mid found!
Reverse starting from slow: 2 -> 1 becomes 1 -> 2 -> null
p1=head(1), p2=prev(1). Compare: 1==1, move to 2. 2==2. Match!
steps: Initialize slow = head, fast = head. Advance: slow goes to 2, fast goes to null. slow represents the second half head.
Reverse second half in-place starting at slow (2->1) to get (1->2). prev is now 1.
Initialize p1 = head (1), p2 = prev (1).
Loop compare: p1->val (1) == p2->val (1). Shift both. p1->val (2) == p2->val (2). Shift. p2 is null. Loop ends. Return true.
slides.keyObservation: For odd lengths (e.g. 1->2->3->2->1), slow stops at 3. The reversed second half is 1->2. The comparison finishes when the second half ends, bypassing the odd center node perfectly!
slides.transition: Why is this three-stage process safe?

slides.headline: 🔍 Symmetry Safety & Odd Lengths
slides.body:
Why does the odd center node not break the comparison?

For an odd list, the first half is slightly longer (e.g., `1->2->3` vs `1->2` reversed). Since we only loop while `p2` (the reversed second half pointer) is not null, we stop before comparing the center node `3` with itself, which is logically correct since the center of an odd palindrome is always symmetric.
slides.interviewerTrap: Leaving the list permanently modified at the end of the algorithm. Proactively suggest restoring the original list state.
slides.transition: Let's see the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Find the middle of the linked list using slow and fast pointers
Reverse the second half of the list starting from the slow pointer
Initialize two pointers: p1 at head, p2 at the head of the reversed half
slides.mentalCompression: Find mid, reverse second half, compare two pointers. Clean and linear.
slides.transition: Let's write the C++ code split into two parts.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Finding the midpoint and reversing the second half.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Cut the list in half using slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, and compare it forward with the first half.
slides.memoryHook: Siphon the middle, flip the tail, run match.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Using value modifications instead of pointer operations, which changes node keys
Crashing on empty or single-node lists (need basic checks at top)
interviewerQuestions: Can we restore the list before returning? (Yes, reverse the second half again)
Is this thread-safe? (No, since it mutates the list pointer structure)

recall.5sec: Find middle, reverse second half, compare both halves.
recall.30sec: Find middle using fast/slow. Reverse starting from middle. Compare head with reversed second half. If they match, return true.
recall.1min: O(N) time and O(1) space in-place palindrome verification using midpoint pointer reversing and linear verification.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates always ask the interviewer: 'Should I restore the original list structure before returning?' This shows they are thoughtful of other consumers of the data structure, who would be surprised to find a mutilated list after a boolean check.
slides.closingLine: Restoring mutated state is the mark of a true software engineer.

revisionCards.title: Find starting point of the Cycle
revisionCards.explanation: Find the node where the cycle begins in a linked list. Return null if no cycle exists.

slides.headline: 🌀 Loop Entry Point
slides.body:
You have a linked list that contains a cycle.

Your task is to find the *exact node* where the cycle begins. If no cycle exists, return `null`.

🎯 The real challenge:
Finding the entry point in O(1) space, without storing nodes or using external visited markers.
slides.visualCue: A straight path leading into a circular loop, with two pointers starting at different locations and meeting exactly at the loop entrance.
slides.memoryHook: Once fast and slow collide, reset slow to head, move both at 1x speed; they will crash exactly at the entrance.
slides.transition: Let's discover why resetting slow to head works with mathematical precision.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Locating cycle or loop entries in sequence traversals
✅ Finding repeated states in state-machine paths
✅ Aligning cyclic paths with non-cyclic lead-in paths

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks for the starting node of a loop or cycle in a singly linked structure, think Floyd's Cycle Detection Phase II.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple hash-table approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Visited Address Set:

1. Traverse the linked list node-by-node.
2. Store each node's memory address in a Hash Set.
3. The first node you encounter that is *already* in the Hash Set is the starting point of the cycle!

⏱️ Time: O(N) time
📦 Space: O(N) space

This is memory-inefficient! We can find it in-place using simple mathematical alignments.
slides.analogy: Leaving a colored flag on every stone you step on. The first stone you step on that already has a flag is the loop entry.
slides.transition: Let's discover the beautiful math behind Floyd's Phase II.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Math Alignment Hook
slides.body:
Let distance from head to loop entry be `L1`, and loop entry to collision point be `L2`. The loop has length `C`.

✅ At collision, `slow` traveled `L1 + L2`.
✅ `fast` traveled `L1 + L2 + k*C`.
✅ Since `fast` is twice as fast: `2*(L1 + L2) = L1 + L2 + k*C` => `L1 = k*C - L2`!

This means the distance from head to entry (`L1`) is exactly equal to the distance from the collision point to the entry going forward!
slides.goldenLine: The math dictates: head-to-entry equals collision-to-entry modulo loop size.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this magical alignment.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
array: slow and fast collide at Node -4
Reset slow to head (3). Keep fast at collision (-4)
Move both 1 step: slow to 2, fast to 2. Collision!
steps: Initialize slow = 3, fast = 3. Phase 1 runs: slow moves by 1, fast by 2.
First Collision occurs at node -4. Phase 1 ends.
Reset slow to head (3). Keep fast at collision node (-4).
Advance both slow and fast by 1 step: slow goes to 2, fast goes to 2 (from -4). Collision! They meet at 2. Return 2.
slides.keyObservation: Even if the loop was cycled multiple times by the fast pointer, the algebraic formula `L1 = k*C - L2` holds perfectly true.
slides.transition: Why is this algebraic alignment so robust?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Algebraic Proof
slides.body:
Why is this always correct?

`L1 = k*C - L2` can be rewritten as `L1 = (k-1)*C + (C - L2)`. 
- `C - L2` is exactly the distance from the collision point to the loop start. 
- `(k-1)*C` represents full laps around the loop.

So a pointer starting at head (`L1` steps) and a pointer starting at collision will meet *exactly* at the loop entry!
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to check if a cycle actually exists before resetting slow. If fast hits null, return nullptr immediately.
slides.transition: Let's check the code blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Detect cycle using fast and slow pointers (Phase 1)
If fast or fast->next becomes null, there is no cycle; return nullptr
If slow equals fast, reset slow pointer to the head of the list
slides.mentalCompression: Detect collision. Reset slow to head. Move both at 1x speed. Meet at entrance.
slides.transition: Let's view the C++ implementation split into two slides.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Phase 1: Finding the initial collision point.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Reset slow to head on loop collision, and walk slow and fast step-by-step together; they will meet exactly at the loop entrance.
slides.memoryHook: Collide, head-reset tortoise, step together to entry.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Resetting slow to head but keeping fast moving at 2x speed in Phase 2
Forgetting to verify `fast` is not null, causing dereference crash on linear lists
interviewerQuestions: How does this prove there is no infinite loop inside Phase 2? (Phase 2 is guaranteed linear time)
Can we calculate the loop length? (Yes, count steps until slow meets itself again while keeping fast stationary)

recall.5sec: Detect collision. Reset slow to head. Move both 1 step at a time. Meet at entry.
recall.30sec: Move fast at 2x, slow at 1x. On collision, reset slow to head. Move both slow and fast at 1x speed until they meet. The meeting node is the cycle start.
recall.1min: O(N) time and O(1) space two-phase Floyd's entry finder based on loop-modulus path algebra.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates don't just state the code; they draw the algebraic variable segments (`L1`, `L2`, `C`) on the board and derive `L1 = k*C - L2` from first principles, demonstrating deep mathematical mastery to the interviewer.
slides.closingLine: Deriving the mathematics proves you understand the code, rather than just memorizing it.

revisionCards.title: Flattening a Linked List
revisionCards.explanation: Flatten a multi-level linked list where each node has next and bottom pointers into a single sorted list.
examples: Hierarchical list -> single flattened list sorted by values

slides.headline: 🥞 Structural Flattening
slides.body:
You have a 2D linked list. Each node has a `next` pointer (to the next list) and a `bottom` pointer (downwards to a sorted column).

Flatten this multi-level list into a single, completely sorted vertical linked list using `bottom` pointers.

🎯 The real challenge:
Merging multiple sorted vertical segments efficiently in-place without copying node memory.
slides.visualCue: A 2D grid of sorted columns, collapsing row-by-row into a single sorted vertical column.
slides.memoryHook: Recursively flatten the right lists first, then merge the current column with the flattened right list.
slides.transition: Why is this hierarchical structure so cleanly sorted recursively?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Flattening nested hierarchical structures in-place
✅ Pairwise zipping of sorted columns
✅ 2D pointer maps with orthogonal linkages (next and bottom)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires zipping sorted sub-structures into a single sequential layout, think Divide and Conquer with Sorted Merge.
slides.transition: Let's review the sub-optimal global sort approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Global Collector:

1. Traverse the entire 2D grid of nodes and copy all values into an array.
2. Sort the array globally using QuickSort.
3. Create a brand new linked list from the sorted array.

⏱️ Time: O(K log K) where K is total nodes
📦 Space: O(K) memory storage

Sub-optimal! We can exploit the fact that each individual column is *already sorted* to merge them in-place.
slides.analogy: Dumping multiple sorted stacks of files into a giant pile, shuffling them, and re-sorting, instead of just zipping adjacent stacks together.
slides.transition: Enter the column-by-column recursive merge breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Right-To-Left Merge Hook
slides.body:
Solve from right to left using recursion:

✅ Recursively flatten the list to the right of the current node first.
✅ This leaves you with the current column (`root`) and the single merged vertical column (`root->next`).
✅ Merge these two sorted vertical lists using a standard sorted merge algorithm!

This zips the columns one-by-one from the end to the start.
slides.goldenLine: Recursion handles the tail columns, leaving us to merge just one column at a time.
slides.transition: Let's trace a dry run of this collapse.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Start at head (Col 1: 5). Recurse on `root->next` (Col 2: 7). Recurse on `root->next` (Col 3: 30).
Base case: Col 3 has no next. Returns Col 3 [30].
Merge Col 2 [7->8] with returned Col 3 [30] recursively to form sorted [7->8->30].
Merge Col 1 [5->10] with resulting [7->8->30] to form final sorted vertical list: [5->7->8->10->30]. Return 5.
slides.keyObservation: Severing the `next` pointers of nodes during the merge ensures that the final list is purely 1D (linked via `bottom` pointers).
slides.transition: Why is recursive merging mathematically optimal here?

slides.headline: 🔍 Two-Way Sorted Merge Mechanics
slides.body:
Why is this divide-and-conquer optimal?

By zipping columns pairwise from right to left, we never have to compare more than two nodes at a time. The merge helper operates on `bottom` pointers, and explicitly sets the `next` pointers to `nullptr` to avoid structural corruption, creating a clean 1D list.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to set `result->next = nullptr` inside the merge function, which leaves dangling horizontal paths.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Base cases: if root is null or root->next is null, return root
Recursively call flatten on root->next to get the merged right side
Merge the current vertical list (root) with the merged right list
slides.mentalCompression: Recursively flatten the right, then merge it with the current column via bottom pointers.
slides.transition: Let's review the C++ implementation split into two slides.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: The recursive merge helper for sorted columns.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Recursively flatten adjacent columns from right to left, zipping them together via bottom pointers into a single vertical column.
slides.memoryHook: Flatten from right, zip bottom-up, snap next.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to set `next = nullptr` during the merge, leaving garbage pointers
Using standard `next` pointers instead of `bottom` pointers to link elements of the flattened list
interviewerQuestions: How would you solve this iteratively? (Use a Min-Heap/Priority Queue of column heads, similar to Merge K Sorted Lists)
What is the space complexity of the iterative Min-Heap version? (O(N) space)

recall.5sec: Flatten right side recursively, then merge it with current column.
recall.30sec: Base case: if no next column, return. Else: `root->next = flatten(root->next)`. Merge `root` and `root->next` using 2-way sorted list merge. Return merged head.
recall.1min: O(N * M) time and O(N) space right-to-left recursive reduction that zips sorted orthogonal columns.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates call out the stack memory usage and immediately present the iterative Priority Queue approach for production scale. They show how a heap containing at most `N` column-heads flattens the list without deep recursion overhead.
slides.closingLine: Moving from recursion to heap-based iteration is the calling card of a systems architect.

revisionCards.title: Rotate a Linked List
revisionCards.explanation: Rotate a linked list to the right by k places.
examples: List = [1,2,3,4,5], k=2 -> Connect 5 to 1. Traverse 3 steps. newHead = 4. 3->next = null. Result: [4,5,1,2,3]

slides.headline: 🎡 Cyclic Rotation
slides.body:
Given a linked list, rotate the list to the right by `k` places.

🎯 The real challenge:
Handling `k` values that are far larger than the list length, and performing the rotation in-place without copying nodes or allocating new space.
slides.visualCue: A straight chain bending into a closed ring, then snapping open at a different point to form a new straight chain.
slides.memoryHook: Form a circular ring, calculate effective steps, cut the ring at the new tail.
slides.transition: Why does measuring list length first optimize cyclic wraps?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Cyclic shifts of sequence structures
✅ Splitting a list and swapping the order of the halves
✅ Large rotation factors requiring modular reductions

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem involves wrapping, shifting, or rotating elements in a singly linked list, think Circular Ring Connection.
slides.transition: Let's review the sub-optimal brute-force way.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The One-by-One Shift:

For `k` times:
1. Traverse to the second-to-last node of the list.
2. Detach the last node and make it the new head.

⏱️ Time: O(K * N) where N is list length
📦 Space: O(1) space

❌ Fatal Flaw: If `k = 10^9`, this will run forever! We must optimize using modular arithmetic.
slides.analogy: Rotating a carousel one seat at a time 1000 times, rather than calculating the final offset modulo seats and doing a single rotation.
slides.transition: Enter the modular snap breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Snapped Ring Hook
slides.body:
Turn the list into a circular ring:

✅ Connect the `tail->next` back to the `head` node.
✅ Calculate the actual rotation offset: `k = k % len`.
✅ The new tail is located at `len - k` steps from the original head.

Walk to the new tail, save its next pointer as `newHead`, and break the circle by setting `newTail->next = nullptr`!
slides.goldenLine: A circular loop allows us to shift any distance in a single snapping action.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this snappy rotation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
array: steps = 5 - 2 = 3 steps from head. Tail walks: 1 -> 2 -> 3
steps: Traverse list to count len = 5. tail is at node 5.
Link `tail->next = head` (5 points to 1) to make list circular.
Reduce k: `2 % 5 = 2`. Steps to walk to new tail = `5 - 2 = 3`.
Walk 3 steps from head: tail stops at Node 3. New head is 3's next: Node 4.
slides.keyObservation: Reducing `k % len` completely neutralizes cases where `k` is a massive number.
slides.transition: Why is this ring method so structurally safe?

slides.headline: 🔍 Modular Math & Edge Cases
slides.body:
Why is the modular snap so bulletproof?

If `k` is a multiple of `len` (e.g. `k = len`), `k % len = 0`. Steps to new tail = `len`. Walking `len` steps brings us back to the original tail, and breaking it there returns the original list unchanged, which is correct since rotating a list of size N by N places yields the original list!
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to handle `k = 0` or empty/single-node lists, which leads to division by zero on `k % len` or null pointer crashes.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Handle edge cases: empty list, single node, or k = 0
Traverse to find the length (len) and the tail node
Connect tail->next = head to form a circular list
slides.mentalCompression: Make circular, count len, shift len - (k%len) steps, cut the link.
slides.transition: Let's view the C++ implementation split into two slides.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Finding list length and forming a circular ring.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Connect tail to head, move forward by len - (k % len) steps from tail, snap the link at the new tail.
slides.memoryHook: Loop the tail to head, snap the chord at len - (k%len).

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Division by zero if length is not tracked and `k % len` is run on empty list
Walking `len - k` steps from `head` instead of `tail`, which causes an off-by-one error
interviewerQuestions: Can we do this without making the list circular? (Yes, but requires more pointer tracking)
What is the time complexity? (O(N) traversal)

recall.5sec: Connect tail to head, walk `len - k` steps, snap the link.
recall.30sec: Find length and tail. Set `tail->next = head`. Move `len - (k % len)` steps from `tail`. Identify `newHead = tail->next`, set `tail->next = nullptr`. Return `newHead`.
recall.1min: O(N) time and O(1) space circular-connect and cut strategy that handles arbitrary rotation factors with modular safety.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates immediately write the circular ring method because it is incredibly elegant, and proactively mention how starting the walk to the new tail from `tail` (rather than resetting to `head`) saves them a pointer variable, demonstrating high-quality code minimalism.
slides.closingLine: Minimizing pointer variables is the best way to write bug-free code under interview pressure.

revisionCards.title: Clone a Linked List with Random Pointer
revisionCards.explanation: Deep clone a linked list where each node contains an extra random pointer pointing to any node.
examples: Clone a list with randomized references without map search.

slides.headline: 👥 The Carbon Copy
slides.body:
You have a linked list where each node has a standard `next` pointer and a `random` pointer that can point to *any* node in the list, or `null`.

Create a deep copy of this list.

🎯 The real challenge:
Mapping the random pointers to their corresponding copied nodes in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space, without using a Hash Map lookup table.
slides.visualCue: A sequence of original nodes interleaved with copied nodes, forming a double-zipped chain.
slides.memoryHook: Interweave copy nodes, copy random pointers, separate the chains.
slides.transition: Why is the standard Hash Map lookup space-inefficient?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Cloning graph-like structures with arbitrary cross-references
✅ Deep copying pointers without standard sequential indexes
✅ Constant-space complex pointer mapping challenges

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires mapping relations between original and copied nodes with O(1) memory constraints, think Node Interweaving.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple Hash Map approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Hash Map Mapper:

1. First pass: Traverse original list and create copy nodes, storing the mapping `Map[OriginalNode] = CopiedNode`.
2. Second pass: Set `CopyNode->next = Map[OriginalNode->next]` and `CopyNode->random = Map[OriginalNode->random]`.

⏱️ Time: O(N) time
📦 Space: O(N) auxiliary hash memory

Simple, but fails the O(1) space constraint! Can we store this mapping in the pointer structure itself?
slides.analogy: Building a directory database to find match pairings, instead of just standing each twin directly behind their original counterpart.
slides.transition: Enter the brilliant triple-pass interweaving breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Interweaving Hook
slides.body:
Store the map directly inside the list structure:

✅ **Phase 1 (Interweave)**: Place copy nodes *directly after* their original nodes (`original -> copy -> original -> copy`).
✅ **Phase 2 (Random Mapping)**: Set `copy->random = original->random->next`!
✅ **Phase 3 (Untangle)**: Separate the interwoven chains back into their original and copied forms.

This turns random-pointer search into a simple O(1) local lookup.
slides.goldenLine: By placing copies adjacent to originals, we bypass the need for hash memory.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this magical interweaving.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Phase 1: Create copies 1' and 2', splice them in: 1 -> 1' -> 2 -> 2' -> null.
Phase 2: Since 1's random is 2, set 1'->random = 1->random->next = 2->next = 2'. Done!
Phase 3: Set dummy copy tail. Siphon off copies: dummy -> 1' -> 2'. Restore original list: 1 -> 2 -> null.
Result: Cloned list is successfully detached and returned. Original list restored.
slides.keyObservation: Because `original->random->next` points exactly to the copy of the target, we do not need to search for it!
slides.transition: Why is this three-pass interweaving so elegant and robust?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Power of Adjacency
slides.body:
Why is this structural trick so reliable?

By weaving copy nodes directly adjacent to the originals, we temporary hijack the `next` pointer of the original node. This creates a hard-coded physical association between the original and the clone. We extract this relation in Phase 2 and cleanly untangle them in Phase 3, leaving zero side effects.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to restore the original list's `next` pointers. Interleaving mutates the input; you *must* cleanly separate them before returning.
slides.transition: Let's see the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Phase 1: Insert copy of each node directly after that node
Phase 2: Set copy->random = original->random->next (if original->random is not null)
Phase 3: Create a dummy node to act as the head of the copied list
slides.mentalCompression: Interweave copy nodes, link randoms locally, separate the dual chains.
slides.transition: Let's review the C++ code split into two parts.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Phase 1 and Phase 2: Interweaving and mapping random pointers.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Weave copy nodes right after originals, connect their randoms locally, and then untangle the interleaved chains.
slides.memoryHook: Weave copies, link randoms locally, untangle twins.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Accessing `curr->random->next` when `curr->random` is null, causing segfault
Failing to restore the original list's pointers, causing destructive side effects
interviewerQuestions: Can we do this in a single pass using a hash map? (Yes, O(N) space)
What are the garbage collection implications in languages like C++? (Must clean up dummy node, though here we ignore it to avoid leaks)

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Interweave copies, copy random pointers, separate the lists.
recall.30sec: Splice a copy node next to each original. Map copy->random = original->random->next. Untangle original->next and copy->next chains.
recall.1min: O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space cloning method based on direct spatial pointer interweaving.

patternConnections: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out that while the interweaving method is O(1) space, it is not thread-safe. If multiple threads read the list, interweaving will corrupt it temporarily. A Hash Map method, although O(N) space, is thread-safe. This trade-off analysis is what interviewers love.
slides.closingLine: Architectural scale means thinking about concurrency, not just complexity.

revisionCards.title: N Meetings in One Room
revisionCards.explanation: Find the maximum number of meetings that can be held in a single meeting room.
examples: start=[1,3,0,5,8,5], end=[2,4,6,7,9,9]. Sort by end times. Pick meeting 1 (ends 2). Pick meeting 2 (ends 4). Skip 3. Pick meeting 4. Total = 4.

slides.headline: N Meetings in One Room
slides.body:
⚡ Coordinate maximum meetings in a single room without any time clashes!

`Meeting 1: [1, 2]`
`Meeting 2: [3, 4]`
`Meeting 3: [0, 6]`

🧠 Intuitive Recall:
- Greedy choice: Sort by **end times**
- Finish meetings early to open slots for others
- If start time > last end time, accept the meeting!
slides.visualCue: Timeline slot block visualization with color-coded intervals.
slides.memoryHook: First finished, first served.
slides.transition: How do we prove that finishing earliest is always the optimal choice?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
When should this pattern instantly trigger in your head?

✅ Interval scheduling / activity selection
✅ Maximizing non-overlapping segments
✅ Single resource shared by multiple requests

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you are asked to 'maximize activities' or 'minimize clashes' on a timeline, immediately think about sorting by endpoints.
slides.transition: Let's first inspect the brute force approach before optimizing.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

1. Generate all `2^N` subsets of meetings.
2. For each subset, check if any meetings overlap.
3. Keep track of the maximum size of a non-overlapping subset.

⏱️ Time: `O(2^N)`
📦 Space: `O(N)` recursive stack

This is extremely slow because we repeat overlap checks for identical subproblems.
slides.analogy: Trying every possible combo of clothes in your closet to see which ones match instead of sorting them by color.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal O(N log N) greedy strategy.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Why sort by end times instead of start times?

✅ Sort by Start Time: A meeting starting at 1 AM and ending at 11 PM would block the room all day.
✅ Sort by End Time: Finishes the room resource as early as possible, maximizing leftover time for subsequent meetings.

💡 Golden Rule:
Always pick the meeting that finishes first!
slides.goldenLine: The earlier a meeting ends, the more time remains for future meetings.
slides.transition: Let's trace this logic with a visual timeline simulation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Step 2: Pick [1,2] (limit=2, count=1).
Step 3: Check [3,4] (start 3 > 2) -> Pick [3,4] (limit=4, count=2).
Step 4: Check [0,6] (start 0 < 4) -> Clash! Skip.
slides.keyObservation: Clashing meetings are easily skipped since the list is sorted by end times.
slides.transition: Why is this greedy approach mathematically correct?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why It Works
slides.body:
Sorting by end times is optimal because at any point, choosing the meeting that ends earliest leaves the maximum possible duration free for subsequent choices.

Any other choice would either leave the same amount of time or less. Thus, the greedy choice is guaranteed to be part of the optimal global solution.
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer: 'Can you sort by start times instead?' Trap: No, because a long meeting starting early can block multiple short meetings.
slides.transition: Let's translate this into our implementation blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Define a custom structure to hold start time, end time, and original 1-based meeting index.
Sort meetings in ascending order of end times. Resolve ties using original index position.
Pick the first meeting, set the end-time boundary limit.
slides.mentalCompression: Sort by end time. Pick non-overlapping intervals left-to-right.
slides.transition: Let's look at the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Meeting structure and custom sorting comparator.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Visualize squeezing block items onto a timeline from left to right; the shorter the end blocks, the more blocks you fit.
slides.memoryHook: Early bird gets the meeting slot.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting that input array index positions must be preserved.
Using start time comparator instead of end time comparator.
interviewerQuestions: What if two meetings end at the same time? (Order by original index)
Can we solve this using dynamic programming? (Yes, O(N^2) but Greedy is O(N log N) optimal)

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Sort by end times.
recall.30sec: Pack meetings left to right by picking the one that finishes earliest.
recall.1min: Optimal O(N log N) greedy algorithm that sorts by end time and takes non-clashing meetings sequentially.
