slides.closingLine: Standard solutions show you know heaps; stream scaling shows you know systems.

revisionCards.title: Merge K Sorted Arrays
revisionCards.explanation: Merge K sorted arrays into a single sorted array.
examples: Merge multiple sorted arrays using a K-sized heap tracker.

slides.headline: ⛓️ Zipping K Chains
slides.body:
You have `K` sorted arrays. You want to merge them into a single sorted array.

🎯 The real challenge:
Doing this in `O(N log K)` time and `O(K)` auxiliary space, bypassing the need to merge them one-by-one or do a global re-sort.
slides.visualCue: K parallel lines of sorted elements moving forward, their front elements being pulled into a central sorting funnel.
slides.memoryHook: Keep a Min-Heap of size K holding the head of each active array. Pop the minimum, then push its array successor.
slides.transition: Let's see why merging them sequentially is sub-optimal.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Merging multiple sorted sources in real-time
✅ N-way merge steps in distributed sorting
✅ Processing dynamic sorted input feeds

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires zipping K sorted streams into a single sorted sequence, think Min-Heap of size K containing head elements.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Flat Sort approach:

1. Copy all `N` elements from all `K` arrays into a single array.
2. Sort this global array using standard QuickSort.

⏱️ Time: O(N log N) sorting time
📦 Space: O(N) storage space

Sub-optimal! It completely ignores that the individual arrays are *already sorted*. We can do it in O(N log K) time using a Min-Heap.
slides.analogy: Dumping K stacks of sorted letters into a giant pile, shuffling them, and sorting them alphabet-by-alphabet from scratch.
slides.transition: Enter the active-pointer Min-Heap breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Active-Pointer Hook
slides.body:
Since each array is sorted, the globally smallest element *must* be among the first elements of the `K` arrays!

✅ Push the first element of each array along with its coordinates `(arrIdx, valIdx)` into a Min-Heap.
✅ Pop the smallest element (`curr`).
✅ Push the next element from the *same* array into the heap.

This keeps the heap size capped at `K`, and streams sorted elements dynamically!
slides.goldenLine: A size-K heap funnels the next absolute minimum from K sorted sources in logarithmic time.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this zipping funnel.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Push first element of each array: 1 (from arr 0), 2 (from arr 1), 3 (from arr 2). Heap is [1, 2, 3].
Pop min: 1 (arr 0, index 0). Add to result. Push next from arr 0: 4. Heap is [2, 3, 4].
Pop min: 2 (arr 1, index 0). Add to result. Push next from arr 1: 5. Heap is [3, 4, 5].
Pop min: 3 (arr 2, index 0). Add to result. Array 2 exhausted.
slides.keyObservation: The heap size never exceeds K, meaning each step of inserting and popping takes exactly O(log K) operations.
slides.transition: Why is tracking coordinates of popped elements mandatory?

slides.headline: 🔍 Context Preservation Safety
slides.body:
Why do we need a custom struct or index pairing?

When we pop an element, we must know *which array* it came from so we can fetch its successor. Without saving `arrIdx`, we would have no way to know whether to advance array 0, 1, or 2, breaking the streaming chain. This index tracking ensures perfect alignment.
slides.interviewerTrap: Not checking if the next index `valIdx + 1` exceeds the bounds of its array before pushing, causing a segmentation fault.
slides.transition: Let's check the code blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Define an Element struct storing value, array index, and element index, with greater-than operator
Initialize a Min-Heap of Elements
Push the first element of each non-empty array into the heap
slides.mentalCompression: Min-heap stores first elements. Pop minimum, add successor from same array. Keep size <= K.
slides.transition: Let's review the C++ code split into two slides.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Defining the state structure and initializing the Min-Heap.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Maintain the lead elements of all arrays in a Min-Heap; pop the absolute minimum, and immediately push its array successor to continue the zip.
slides.memoryHook: Heap stores array fronts; pop minimum, feed its sibling.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Pushing items from empty sub-arrays on startup
Out-of-bounds array access on the successor query by forgetting size checks
interviewerQuestions: Can we solve this using Divide and Conquer? (Yes, merge arrays pairwise. Same O(N log K) time, but uses O(N) space instead of O(K))
How is this used in external merge sorting?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Min-heap stores head of each array. Pop min, push next from same array.
recall.30sec: Create struct `Element {val, arr, valIdx}`. Push first cell of each array to min-heap. Pop, add to result, push `arr[valIdx+1]` if it exists.
recall.1min: O(N log K) time and O(K) space streaming zipping funnel using a coordinate-aware Min-Priority Queue.

patternConnections: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out the spatial trade-off. While the Divide and Conquer approach also achieves O(N log K) time, it requires storing temporary merged arrays of size O(N). The Min-Heap approach requires only O(K) auxiliary space, making it highly optimal for systems processing disk-backed massive data streams.
slides.closingLine: In enterprise streaming, saving space is as critical as saving cycles.

revisionCards.title: K Most Frequent Elements
revisionCards.explanation: Find the K most frequent elements in an array.

slides.headline: 📊 The Frequency Peak
slides.body:
Given an integer array, return the `K` most frequent elements.

🎯 The real challenge:
Doing this in `O(N log K)` time and `O(N)` space, preventing a full sorting of unique frequencies.
slides.visualCue: A bar chart representing element counts, with a size-K boundary slicing off only the top K tallest bars.
slides.memoryHook: Count frequencies with a Hash Map. Keep a Min-Heap of size K based on frequency; pop the least frequent.
slides.transition: Let's explore why sorting unique elements is sub-optimal.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Requesting top elements sorted by occurrence count
✅ Data analytics dashboards ranking high-frequency items
✅ Bounded selection of popular tags or logs

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires finding high-frequency or popularity extremes, think Hash Map + Bounded Min-Heap.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The Map-and-Sort approach:

1. Count frequencies using an unordered map.
2. Copy map elements to a vector and sort the vector based on frequency descending.
3. Return the first `K` elements.

⏱️ Time: O(D log D) sorting where D is unique elements (up to N)
📦 Space: O(N) storage space

Can we do it in O(N log K) time, which is highly optimal if `K` is much smaller than `D`?
slides.analogy: Counting votes for all parties, sorting all 100 parties globally, instead of just keeping track of the top 3 vote-getters in real-time.
slides.transition: Enter the frequency-bounded Min-Heap breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Frequency Filter Hook
slides.body:
Count frequencies, then filter using a Min-Heap of size `K`:

✅ Store pairs of `{frequency, element}` in the heap.
✅ If size exceeds `K`, pop the top element (which has the *lowest* frequency).

Since the heap constantly expels the least frequent element, it retains exactly the `K` highest frequency elements. Pop remaining elements for the result!
slides.goldenLine: A Min-Heap sorted by frequency filters out rare values, keeping only the popular peaks.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this popularity contest.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Build frequency map: `count[1]=3, count[2]=2, count[3]=1`.
Iterate over map. Push {3, 1} (element 1, freq 3). Heap: [{3, 1}].
Push {2, 2} (element 2, freq 2). Heap: [{2, 2}, {3, 1}].
Push {1, 3} (element 3, freq 1). Heap size is 3 (exceeds k=2). Pop minimum frequency: {1, 3}. Heap is [{2, 2}, {3, 1}].
slides.keyObservation: Sorting pairs by frequency ensures that the min-heap naturally bubbles the lowest-frequency item to the top, making it easy to prune.
slides.transition: Why does a Min-Heap work better than a Max-Heap here?

slides.headline: 🔍 Min vs Max Heap Trade-offs
slides.body:
Why not use a Max-Heap?

If we use a Max-Heap, we can push all `D` unique elements into it and pop `K` times. 
- Time: `O(D log D)` heap construction.
- Space: `O(D)` heap storage.

With a Min-Heap of size `K`, the heap size is capped at `K`. 
- Time: `O(D log K)` operations, which is significantly faster when `K` is small. Space stays bounded at `O(K)` in the heap!
slides.interviewerTrap: Incorrectly ordering the pair as `{element, frequency}` in the C++ queue, which sorts by element value instead of occurrence count.
slides.transition: Let's check the code blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Build a frequency hash map from the input numbers
Declare a Min-Heap storing pairs of {frequency, element}
Iterate through the hash map: push each pair into the heap
slides.mentalCompression: Hash map counts frequencies. Min-heap of size k stores {freq, val}. Pop if size > k.
slides.transition: Let's review the C++ code split into two slides.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Hashing counts and filling the size-constrained Min-Heap.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Index occurrence counts in a map, push `{frequency, value}` into a Min-Heap of size K, popping the bottom elements to leave only the K top giants.
slides.memoryHook: Map occurrences, Min-heap size K of {freq, element}, extract peaks.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Declaring the pair as `{element, frequency}` inside the Min-Heap, sorting by the wrong property
Using a standard Max-Heap of size N, which takes larger memory
interviewerQuestions: Can we solve this in O(N) time? (Yes, using Bucket Sort, where array index represents frequency)
What is the space complexity of the Bucket Sort approach? (O(N) space, which might be higher if N is large but unique numbers are few)

recall.5sec: Count frequencies with hash map. Keep min-heap of size k based on frequencies.
recall.30sec: Build count map. Push `{freq, val}` to min-heap of pairs. If size > k, pop. Extract remaining keys into result vector.
recall.1min: O(N log K) time and O(N) space frequency ranker utilizing a map and a size-bounded Min-Priority Queue.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out both the Min-Heap O(N log K) and Bucket Sort O(N) solutions. They discuss the memory trade-offs: Bucket Sort is faster but requires allocating an array of lists of size N, which wastes massive space if frequencies are sparse, whereas the heap maintains high efficiency with O(K) extra space.
slides.closingLine: True mastery means matching the memory footprint of your algorithm to the sparsity of your dataset.

revisionCards.title: Implement Stack using Arrays
revisionCards.explanation: Implement a stack using a standard array.
examples: Push elements, check indexing bounds, verify LIFO output on pop.

slides.headline: Implement Stack using Arrays
slides.body:
⚡ A Stack is a LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) data structure.

Imagine a stack of plates: you can only add a plate to the top, and you can only remove the topmost plate. If you try to take one from the middle, the whole stack crashes!

🧠 Recall:
- Push adds element to `arr[++top]` 
- Pop retrieves element from `arr[top--]`
- Peek returns the element at index `top` without removing it
slides.visualCue: Stray arrows showing elements pushing in and popping out of a linear array container.
slides.memoryHook: A stack of heavy cafeteria trays.
slides.transition: How do we translate this simple physical LIFO model into an optimized array implementation?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot when a custom LIFO array stack is needed:

✅ Need constant O(1) operations with absolute minimum overhead
✅ System-level programming where standard library containers like `std::vector` are restricted
✅ Predictable size limits where heap allocation needs to be avoided

💡 Interview Signal:
If the interviewer asks to avoid dynamic scaling or heap allocation to prevent memory fragmentation, build a static array-backed stack.
slides.transition: Let's first think about the raw mechanics of an array stack.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The basic way:

Create a dynamic array. Every time you push, if the array is full, resize it by doubling. Resizing requires copying elements which takes O(N) in the worst case.

⏱️ Time: O(1) amortized, but O(N) worst-case.
📦 Space: O(N) auxiliary space.

For a fixed-capacity system, we can optimize this to guaranteed O(1) worst-case time by using a static size array.
slides.analogy: Resizing an array is like buying a whole new bigger house just to fit one more plate, then moving everything over.
slides.transition: Now, let's look at the optimal constant-time static array breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
The ultimate optimization:

✅ Pre-allocate a static array of size `capacity`
✅ Maintain a single integer pointer `topIdx` initialized to `-1`

This simple integer acts as the guard of the boundaries: 
- `push(x)`: Increment `topIdx` and insert: `arr[++topIdx] = x`
- `pop()`: Read `arr[topIdx]` and decrement: `topIdx--`

No dynamic allocation, no shifting elements, just pure pointer arithmetic.
slides.goldenLine: A single index pointer transforms a passive array into a high-speed LIFO machine.
slides.transition: Let's trace this index pointer movement in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initialize stack of capacity 3: arr = [_, _, _], topIdx = -1
push(5): topIdx incremented to 0. arr[0] = 5. Array state: [5, _, _]
push(10): topIdx incremented to 1. arr[1] = 10. Array state: [5, 10, _]
pop(): Returns arr[1] (10). topIdx decremented to 0. Logical state: [5, _, _]
slides.keyObservation: Elements are never physically erased on pop; we simply move the topIdx boundary down.
slides.transition: Why is this boundary strategy so incredibly efficient?

slides.headline: 🔍 Static Boundaries & Memory
slides.body:
Why does the static array stack dominate in performance-critical environments?

✅ Glibc & Kernels utilize static buffers to avoid dynamic allocation overhead
✅ Array elements reside in contiguous memory, maximizing cache line utilization
✅ No garbage collection or heap fragmentation risks

This is why real-time embedded systems implement stacks exactly this way.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forget to check for overflow (topIdx >= capacity - 1) before pushing, or underflow (topIdx < 0) before popping.
slides.transition: Let's translate this clean logic into high-grade C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create a class ArrayStack with fields `arr`, `topIdx`, and `capacity`
In constructor, allocate raw array of size `capacity` and set `topIdx = -1`
Implement push: check for overflow first, then increment topIdx and insert
slides.mentalCompression: topIdx tracks the boundary. Pre-allocate once, insert with pre-increment, retrieve with post-decrement.
slides.transition: Let's write the clean production-grade C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Class layout, constructor, and boundary variables.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: An elastic tape measure where you only look at the tip and pull it back to hide elements.
slides.memoryHook: Guard the boundary index.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Off-by-one error: Checking topIdx > capacity instead of >= capacity - 1
Calling pop() on an empty stack leading to negative index out-of-bounds crash
interviewerQuestions: How would you make this stack dynamically resizable?
What are the benefits of an array-based stack over a linked-list stack?

recall.30sec: Implement stack with static array to get O(1) worst-case time, avoiding vector resizing copies.

Highlight that a contiguous array stack is dramatically faster in practice than a linked-list stack because it avoids CPU cache misses and heap allocations. Mentioning destructor memory management also demonstrates junior-vs-senior level maturity.
slides.closingLine: Hardware-friendly code is always elite code.

slides.headline: Implement Queue using Arrays
slides.body:
⚡ A Queue is a FIFO (First-In, First-Out) data structure.

Imagine a ticket counter line. The first person to arrive gets their ticket first and leaves the front of the line. Newcomers must join the back of the line.

🧠 Recall:
- Enqueue (push) adds to the back
- Dequeue (pop) removes from the front
- Circular wrapping maximizes array space utilization
slides.visualCue: A conveyor belt showing items arriving at the back and leaving from the front.
slides.memoryHook: A ticket line at the movies.
slides.transition: How do we implement a queue using arrays without wasting space after elements are popped?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Need strict FIFO message processing
✅ Fixed capacity buffer queue is required (e.g., ring buffers in hardware drivers)
✅ Need O(1) operations without any dynamic resizing delays

💡 Interview Signal:
When designing networking buffers or message queues that require constant time throughput and memory stability, always opt for a circular array queue.
slides.transition: Let's first understand why a basic array implementation is terribly slow.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive way:

Every time you pop from the front (index 0), shift all other elements left by 1 index to fill the gap. This makes popping extremely expensive.

⏱️ Time: push = O(1), pop = O(N) due to shifting.
📦 Space: O(N) capacity.

Shifting elements is a performance killer. We must find a way to pop in O(1) time.
slides.analogy: Shifting elements is like forcing everyone in a long line to step forward one-by-one every single time a ticket is sold.
slides.transition: Here is where the circular ring buffer breakthrough comes in.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Circular Breakthrough
slides.body:
The ultimate optimization:

✅ Treat the array as a closed loop using modulo arithmetic: `next = (index + 1) % capacity`
✅ Maintain two pointers: `front` and `rear`
✅ Store the current `size` to easily distinguish between empty and full states

- `push(x)`: Write `arr[rear] = x`, then `rear = (rear + 1) % capacity`
- `pop()`: Read `arr[front]`, then `front = (front + 1) % capacity`

No shifting, no wasted space. Pure mathematical wrapping.
slides.goldenLine: Modulo arithmetic bends a straight array into an endless circular track.
slides.transition: Let's watch the queue wrap around the array boundaries.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Queue cap 3. Push 5, Push 10. Front=0, Rear=2, Size=2. State: [5, 10, _]
pop(): retrieves 5 at front (0). Front becomes (0+1)%3 = 1. Size=1. State: [_, 10, _]
push(15): writes at rear (2). Rear becomes (2+1)%3 = 0. Size=2. State: [15, 10, _] (wrapped!)
slides.keyObservation: The rear pointer wraps back to index 0, reusing the space vacated by popped elements.
slides.transition: Let's explore why circular queues are widely used in operating systems.

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Circular Queues Are Elite
slides.body:
Circular queues (ring buffers) are the gold standard for high-frequency systems:

✅ Zero shifting overhead ensures constant O(1) execution latency
✅ Crucial for OS scheduling, keyboard input streams, and network sockets
✅ Lock-free implementations are possible using atomic index updates

By decoupling head and tail movements, we get stable, deterministic performance.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to update the `currSize` tracker, or letting `rear` overwrite `front` when capacity is exceeded.
slides.transition: Let's implement this elegant circular model in C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize fields: `arr`, `frontIdx = 0`, `rearIdx = 0`, `currSize = 0`, `capacity`
push: check if currSize == capacity. If not, write at `rearIdx` and advance `(rearIdx + 1) % capacity`
pop: check if currSize == 0. If not, read from `frontIdx` and advance `(frontIdx + 1) % capacity`
slides.mentalCompression: Wrap around borders via modulo. Keep size counter to verify capacity status.

slides.headline: Implement Stack using Queues
slides.body:
⚡ Can you reverse a flow using a sequence that strictly preserves order?

This classic design problem tests your ability to think adaptively under rigid interface constraints. You are given a Queue (FIFO) and must build a Stack (LIFO).

🧠 Recall:
- Stack: Last In First Out (LIFO)
- Queue: First In First Out (FIFO)
- Solvable elegantly using a SINGLE queue by rotating elements!
slides.visualCue: A circular tube showing balls pushed in, then rotated around so the newest ball stays in front.
slides.memoryHook: A rotating cylinder of bullets.
slides.transition: Let's explore the simple two-queue approach first before looking at the optimal single-queue solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the core interview triggers:

✅ Building a LIFO API under pure FIFO device interfaces
✅ Testing deep mental visualization of container state transitions
✅ Algorithmic optimization from two utility objects down to a single container

💡 Interview Signal:
This is a favorite 'sandbox' question for top tier companies. They want to see if you can transition from using auxiliary memory to a smart self-contained rotational pattern.
slides.transition: How do we start thinking about this? Let's check the traditional two-queue approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The standard Two-Queue approach:

Use two queues, `q1` and `q2`. On `push(x)`:
1. Insert `x` into `q2`
2. Dequeue all elements from `q1` and enqueue them to `q2`
3. Swap the names of `q1` and `q2`

⏱️ Time: push = O(N), pop = O(1)
📦 Space: O(N) utilizing two queues

This works perfectly... but we are using twice the space. We can optimize this by performing rotations in a single queue.
slides.analogy: Using two queues is like having two cups, pouring all water from cup A to cup B just to put a drop in the bottom of A, then pouring it back.
slides.transition: Let's look at the optimal single-queue rotation breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Single Queue Rotation Hook
slides.body:
The elegant single-queue breakthrough:

✅ Push the new element `x` to the back of the queue
✅ Dequeue each existing element and immediately re-enqueue it at the back
✅ Do this exactly `size - 1` times

This shifts the new element all the way from the back to the front of the queue, making it immediately accessible for the next LIFO operation.

Push becomes O(N), but Pop is a super-fast O(1) front extraction.
slides.goldenLine: A queue can reverse its own order if you let it chase its tail.
slides.transition: Let's watch this loop rotation step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Queue currently contains [1, 2] (1 is front). Push(3) enqueues to back. Queue: [1, 2, 3]
Size was 2 before push. We rotate 2 times: Dequeue 1 and enqueue to back. Queue: [2, 3, 1]
Second rotation: Dequeue 2 and enqueue to back. Queue: [3, 1, 2]
3 is now at the front! Calling pop() immediately returns 3. FIFO becomes LIFO!
slides.keyObservation: The number of rotations must be exactly size - 1. One extra rotation corrupts the LIFO state.
slides.transition: Why is the single queue implementation superior in system designs?

slides.headline: 🔍 Single Queue Efficiency
slides.body:
Why is the single-queue approach standard in code reviews?

✅ Cuts memory allocation overhead in half by avoiding a second container
✅ Eliminates the need for pointer swapping, which can cause CPU cache thrashing
✅ Clean, elegant, and shows a deep grasp of circular structures

This highlights that space optimization is about thinking recursively.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to handle the empty queue condition inside pop() or top(), causing undefined behavior.
slides.transition: Let's look at the clean and compact C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Declare a class QueueStack with a single `std::queue<int>`
push(x): append `x` to back, record size, then loop `size - 1` times popping and pushing
pop(): read front element, pop from queue, and return it
slides.mentalCompression: Enqueue the newcomer, then cycle all older elements around to stack them behind it.
slides.transition: Let's look at the clean, production-grade code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Single queue declaration and the rotation-based push operation.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Roll a snowball into a tunnel, then sweep everyone else in front of it around to its back.
slides.memoryHook: Rotate existing elements behind the new.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Rotating `size` times instead of `size - 1`, which keeps the newcomer at the back
Using an O(N) pop strategy instead of push, which is slower for lookup-heavy workloads
interviewerQuestions: Can you implement this with O(1) push and O(N) pop instead?
What is the call stack overhead if we solved this recursively?

recall.5sec: Push: q.push(x), then pop and push front sz-1 times.
recall.30sec: Single-queue stack uses rotational enqueues during push to enforce LIFO ordering in O(N) time.
recall.1min: Single container stack simulation that shifts elements in place. Simplifies the standard two-queue model to minimize memory footprints.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Stand out by analyzing the workload! Explain that if the system performs a massive number of push operations but very few pop operations, a two-stack layout with O(1) push and O(N) pop might actually be superior, whereas the single-queue approach is perfect for pop-heavy or balanced LIFO streams.
slides.closingLine: Great engineers always choose their complexity based on the workload.

slides.headline: Implement Queue using Stacks
slides.body:
⚡ Two negatives make a positive. Two stack reversals restore original order!

This problem asks you to implement a FIFO Queue using LIFO Stacks. It is a fundamental lesson in amortized analysis and data flow restoration.

🧠 Recall:
- Stack: LIFO (reverses order on pop)
- Queue: FIFO (preserves order)
- Using two stacks: one for inputs, one for outputs
slides.visualCue: Two dynamic stacks where pouring elements from stack 1 into stack 2 flips the top/bottom order.
slides.memoryHook: Two cups of sand poured back and forth.
slides.transition: Let's explore the brute-force way first before unlocking the elite O(1) amortized method.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Recognize the triggers instantly:

✅ RESTRICTED to LIFO API, but need to process elements in strict chronological order
✅ Testing deep comprehension of amortized complexity (constant time average cost)
✅ Simulating read-heavy or write-heavy buffering systems

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever an interviewer mentions 'amortized O(1)' in stack/queue design, think about transferring elements only when necessary rather than on every operation.
slides.transition: Let's first analyze the standard O(N) push approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The basic way:

Maintain two stacks: `s1` and `s2`. For every `push(x)`:
1. Move all elements from `s1` to `s2` (reversing them)
2. Push `x` onto `s1`
3. Move all elements back from `s2` to `s1` (reversing again)

⏱️ Time: push = O(N), pop = O(1)
📦 Space: O(N) capacity

This is highly sub-optimal because every single push triggers two full stack transfers. We can do better by delaying the transfer.
slides.analogy: Moving all boxes from room A to room B just to put a new box at the back of A, then moving everything back.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal delayed-transfer amortized breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Amortized Breakthrough
slides.body:
The double stack delayed-transfer optimization:

✅ Use two stacks: `input` (for push) and `output` (for pop/peek)
✅ `push(x)` is always constant time `input.push(x)` (O(1))
✅ `pop()` / `peek()`: if `output` is empty, move ALL elements from `input` to `output` at once. Then pop from `output`.

Since each element is transferred at most once, the average (amortized) cost of every operation becomes a blazing fast O(1)!
slides.goldenLine: Reversing the flow only when empty turns worst-case costs into average-case bargains.
slides.transition: Let's watch this lazy transfer sequence in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: push(1), push(2), push(3). input = [1, 2, 3] (3 is top), output = []
pop(): output is empty, so transfer. pop from input, push to output. input = [], output = [3, 2, 1] (1 is top)
output.pop() returns 1. output state becomes [3, 2]. input = []
Next pop() returns 2 instantly in O(1) time because output is not empty!
slides.keyObservation: Transfer ONLY occurs when the output stack is completely empty, ensuring order is preserved.
slides.transition: Why is amortized O(1) highly prized in professional software development?

slides.headline: 🔍 Inside Amortized O(1)
slides.body:
Let's prove why the average cost is O(1):

- Each element is pushed onto `input` once: 1 op
- Each element is popped from `input` once: 1 op
- Each element is pushed onto `output` once: 1 op
- Each element is popped from `output` once: 1 op

Total operations for N elements is 4N. The average cost per element is exactly 4 operations, which mathematically is constant time O(1) amortized!
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to check if `output` is empty before transferring, which scrambles the chronological order.
slides.transition: Let's implement this elegant double-stack architecture in C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Define classes using two stacks: `input` and `output`
push: push value directly to `input` stack (always O(1))
Create private helper `transfer()`: while `input` is not empty, push `input.top()` to `output` and pop it
slides.mentalCompression: Write to input, read from output. Refill output from input ONLY when output runs dry.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the clean C++ implementation.

slides.body: Class definition and the transfer helper.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code (Part 2/2)
slides.body: Class definition and the transfer helper. (Continued)

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: A double hourglass: sand falls into upper chamber (input), then flips completely into lower chamber (output) to flow out.
slides.memoryHook: Delayed flip restores chronological flow.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Transferring input elements to output on every push (destroys O(1) amortized performance)
Checking `!input.empty()` instead of `output.empty()` inside pop() before transferring
interviewerQuestions: What is the worst-case time complexity of a single pop operation?
How does amortized time differ from average-case time?

recall.30sec: Amortized O(1) Queue uses s1 for buffering writes and s2 for reversing reads on-demand.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates clearly articulate the difference between worst-case cost (O(N) when refilling) and amortized cost (O(1) overall). Mentioning real-world applications like read/write separation in database logs shows that you understand the architectural patterns behind simple coding exercises.
slides.closingLine: Efficiency is the art of delaying expensive work until absolutely necessary.

revisionCards.title: Valid Parentheses
revisionCards.explanation: Verify if bracket pairs are correctly nested and closed.
examples: s = "([])". Stack: [(, [] -> pop [ matches ] -> pop ( matches ). Stack is empty -> true.

slides.headline: Valid Parentheses
slides.body:
⚡ Symmetry and balance: matching pairs must close in the exact reverse order of their opening.

Given a string containing brackets `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[`, `]`, determine if the input string is valid.

🧠 Recall:
- Open brackets must close in LIFO order
- Open brackets must be closed by the same type
- Solved beautifully using a dynamic Stack
slides.visualCue: A bracket pair system expanding and nesting. A stack pushes openers, pops on matching closers.
slides.memoryHook: Nested Russian dolls.
slides.transition: Why do simple counters fail here, and why is a stack mandatory?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Brackets, tags, or delimiters that open and close in nested layers
✅ Matching pairs where closer must match the most recently opened symbol
✅ Expression parsing or syntax validation constraints

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you see recursive nesting where the inner-most boundary must be solved or matched first, a LIFO stack is your weapon of choice.
slides.transition: Let's first analyze why basic counting variables are insufficient.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The count-based approach:

Keep three counters for `(`, `{`, `[`. Increment when seen, decrement when closed. Fails completely for overlapping cases like `[(])` where counts match but nesting is illegal.

⏱️ Time: O(N) but incorrect correctness.
📦 Space: O(1) space.

To ensure correct chronological order, we must remember the exact identity of the opened brackets, not just their counts.
slides.analogy: Counting is like tracking how many men and women entered a room without checking who is married to whom.
slides.transition: Let's look at the optimal stack validation breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The LIFO Matching Breakthrough
slides.body:
The stack validation breakthrough:

✅ Push every opening bracket onto the stack
✅ For every closing bracket, look at the stack top. It MUST match the current closing bracket.
✅ If it matches, pop it. If not (or stack is empty), the string is invalid!

This ensures that brackets are closed in the exact reverse order of opening, preserving nesting integrity.
slides.goldenLine: The stack top always represents the currently active open frontier.
slides.transition: Let's watch this dynamic open frontier match and collapse.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Input: '{[ ]}'. st = []. Scan '{': opener -> push. st = ['{']
Scan '[': opener -> push. st = ['{', '[']
Scan ']': closer -> check st.top() which is '['. Match! Pop. st = ['{']
Scan '}': closer -> check st.top() which is '{'. Match! Pop. st = []. Empty means valid!
slides.keyObservation: Every match annihilates the top of the stack, shrinking the validation frontier.
slides.transition: Why is stack safety crucial during this matching process?

slides.headline: 🔍 Boundary Safety & Nested States
slides.body:
Why does the stack work so flawlessly for nested rules?

✅ It mirrors the nested activation records of recursion
✅ Any closer must resolve the absolute nearest open tag
✅ Handles arbitrary combinations of bracket types without overlap bugs

This is the core foundation behind compiler scanners and HTML/JSON parsers.
slides.interviewerTrap: Accessing `st.top()` when the stack is empty (e.g., input starts with `]`), which triggers a segment fault.
slides.transition: Let's implement this safe bracket matching in clean C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Declare a `std::stack<char>`
Iterate through each character `c` of string `s`
If `c` is opener `(`, `{`, `[`, push onto stack
slides.mentalCompression: Push openers. Pop on match. Empty stack at the end means absolute validity.

mistakes: Forgetting `st.empty()` check before calling `st.top()` (causes runtime crash)
Returning `true` prematurely inside the loop before scanning the entire string

revisionCards.title: Next Greater Element
revisionCards.explanation: Find the next greater element for every index in an array.
examples: nums = [1,2,1]. Trace index calculations backwards. Next greater of 1 is 2. Next greater of 2 is -1. Next greater of 1 is 2.

slides.headline: Next Greater Element
slides.body:
⚡ Look to the right: who is the first taller building in your line of sight?

Given an array, find the next greater element for each index. If it does not exist, return `-1`.

🧠 Recall:
- Nearest greater element to the right
- Monotonic Stack stores elements in sorted order
- Processing right-to-left simplifies future lookups!
slides.visualCue: A series of building silhouettes showing vision lines skipping over shorter roofs to hit the first taller tower.
slides.memoryHook: Shadows cast by skyscrapers.
slides.transition: Let's first understand the obvious nested-loop way before upgrading to optimal monotonic time.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Nearest greater or smaller element queries
✅ Finding boundaries or vision limits in a linear sequence
✅ Nested loop logic searching right or left with O(N^2) time

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires querying immediate larger/smaller bounds for every element in an array, think Monotonic Stack immediately.
slides.transition: Let's see why the double loop is too slow for large inputs.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The double loop method:

For each element `nums[i]`, iterate through elements `j = i + 1` to `N-1`. The first element where `nums[j] > nums[i]` is the answer. If none found, write `-1`.

⏱️ Time: O(N^2) due to nested scans
📦 Space: O(1) auxiliary space

This is highly redundant. Shorter elements are scanned repeatedly, wasting computations. We can store the future in a sorted stack.
slides.analogy: A nested loop is like asking every single person in front of you how tall they are, instead of just looking over the heads of the short people.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal right-to-left monotonic stack breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Monotonic Breakthrough
slides.body:
The right-to-left monotonic decreasing stack:

✅ Traverse the array backwards (from `N-1` down to `0`)
✅ Keep a stack of potential next greater elements in strictly decreasing order
✅ Pop all elements from stack that are `<= current` (they are blocked/shadowed by current)
✅ The stack top is now the next greater element! Push current onto stack.

Every element is pushed once and popped at most once, achieving a brilliant O(N) time complexity!
slides.goldenLine: Traversing backward builds the future first, letting the stack shadow obsolete choices.
slides.transition: Let's watch this shadow-masking stack execute in a simulation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Input: [4, 5, 2, 25]. Traverse backwards. i = 3 (25): st is empty -> nge = -1. Push 25. st = [25]
slides.keyObservation: When scanning 5, the element 2 becomes obsolete for anything further left, so we safely popped it.
slides.transition: Why does the backward traversal strategy work so cleanly?

slides.headline: 🔍 Shadowing & Monotonicity
slides.body:
Why is the monotonic stack so incredibly powerful?

✅ The 'Shadowing' Effect: if `A[i] >= A[j]` and `i < j`, then `A[j]` can never be the next greater element for any element to the left of `A[i]`
✅ Stack maintains a strictly decreasing order from bottom to top
✅ Amortized O(1) per element because each index enters the stack exactly once

This turns a quadratic search into a smooth, single-pass sweep.
slides.interviewerTrap: Using `<` instead of `<=` when popping duplicate elements, which causes incorrect NGE values.
slides.transition: Let's check the clean C++ implementation of this monotonic sweep.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize an array `nge` of size `N` filled with `-1`
Declare a `std::stack<int> st`
Loop `i` from `N - 1` down to `0`
slides.mentalCompression: Scan backward. Pop smaller or equal elements. Top is the answer. Push current.

revisionCards.title: Next Smaller Element
revisionCards.explanation: Find the next smaller element for every index in an array.
examples: A = [4, 5, 2]. 2 is smaller than 5 and 4. Stack pops and registers next smaller values.

slides.headline: Next Smaller Element
slides.body:
⚡ The exact mirror: looking to the right for the first shorter building.

Given an array, find the next smaller element for each index. If none exists, return `-1`.

🧠 Recall:
- Nearest smaller element to the right
- Monotonic Increasing Stack stores elements in sorted order
- Eliminating larger elements simplifies future lookups
slides.visualCue: A series of building silhouettes looking right to find the first shorter house nestled under their gaze.
slides.memoryHook: Finding the first step down on a staircase.
slides.transition: Let's explore the brute-force nested search before upgrading to optimal monotonic time.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Nearest smaller element query in an array
✅ Finding limits of minimum extension (crucial for Histogram & Water Trapping)
✅ Right-side search with O(N^2) time constraints

💡 Interview Signal:
If the problem requires finding a lower boundary to compute spans or rectangles, immediately reach for the Monotonic Increasing Stack.
slides.transition: Let's review why the double loop is highly inefficient.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The double loop method:

For each index `i`, run a forward scan `j = i + 1` to `N-1`. The first index where `nums[j] < nums[i]` is the answer. If no smaller value is found, write `-1`.

⏱️ Time: O(N^2) due to double iterations
📦 Space: O(1) auxiliary space

This is highly wasteful because larger elements are repeatedly scanned. We can optimize this by keeping a sorted stack of future prospects.
slides.analogy: Walking down every single step of a staircase individually to see where the next drop is, rather than looking at the profile of the stairs.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal right-to-left monotonic increasing stack.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Monotonic Breakthrough
slides.body:
The right-to-left monotonic increasing stack:

✅ Traverse the array backwards (from `N-1` down to `0`)
✅ Keep a stack of potential next smaller elements in strictly increasing order
✅ Pop all elements from stack that are `>= current` (they are blocked/shadowed by current)
✅ The stack top is now the next smaller element! Push current onto stack.

Since every element enters and leaves the stack at most once, the total time complexity is a guaranteed O(N)!
slides.goldenLine: A smaller element blocks out all future views of larger elements behind it.
slides.transition: Let's trace this step-by-step through a simulation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Input: [4, 8, 5, 2]. Scan backwards. i = 3 (2): stack is empty -> nse = -1. Push 2. st = [2]
i = 2 (5): top is 2 < 5 -> nse = 2. Push 5. st = [2, 5]
slides.keyObservation: When scanning 4, the larger elements 8 and 5 are permanently popped because 4 is smaller and closer to any future left elements.
slides.transition: Why is the monotonic stack so robust against duplicate elements?

slides.headline: 🔍 Inside Monotonic Increasing Stacks
slides.body:
Why does this solution guarantee safe linear execution bounds?

✅ Monotonicity ensures stack values are always sorted in increasing order from bottom to top
✅ Eliminating larger elements ensures that only valid, closer minima remain in contention
✅ Prevents quadratic redundant checks by caching future state limits

This is the absolute cornerstone for solving advanced rectangle bounds problems.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to pop equal elements (>=), which can lead to incorrect limits when duplicates are present.
slides.transition: Let's write this clean monotonic logic in C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize an array `nse` of size `N` filled with `-1`
Declare a `std::stack<int> st`
Loop `i` from `N - 1` down to `0`
slides.mentalCompression: Scan backward. Pop larger or equal elements. Top of stack is next smaller. Push current.
slides.transition: Let's review the clean C++ code.

slides.body: Init arrays and reverse loop setup.

slides.memoryHook: Shorter steps block taller stairs.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting the `st.empty()` guard during pop loops, causing illegal memory reads
Popping only strictly greater elements (>) which leaves duplicate greater elements in the stack
interviewerQuestions: How do we modify this code if we need the nearest smaller element on the LEFT?
How is this problem directly connected to the Largest Rectangle in Histogram?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.30sec: Monotonic increasing stack filters out larger elements from the right, ensuring O(1) access to the nearest smaller value.

revisionCards.title: LRU Cache
revisionCards.explanation: Design a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with O(1) get and put operations.
examples: Put keys. Move accessed keys to the head of the list. Evict nodes from the tail of the list when capacity is exceeded.

slides.headline: LRU Cache
slides.body:
⚡ Limited space, high frequency: keep the most recently used items at hand.

Design a Least Recently Used (LRU) Cache that supports `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` operations in constant **O(1)** time.

🧠 Recall:
- Fast key-value lookup: Hash Map
- Ordered chronological eviction: Doubly Linked List (DLL)
- MRU (Most Recently Used) at Head, LRU at Tail
slides.visualCue: A horizontal train of DLL nodes with a hash map pointing directly to individual cars for rapid extraction.
slides.memoryHook: A dynamic desk space with old papers falling into a drawer.
slides.transition: How do we combine a hash map and a linked list to achieve O(1) time for all operations?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Need key-value caching with a fixed capacity limit
✅ Eviction policy must target the least recently accessed item
✅ Requirement for absolute O(1) time complexity on both reads and writes

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever an interviewer asks for a cache with O(1) retrieval and a chronology-based eviction policy, reach for the Map + DLL combo immediately.
slides.transition: Let's first understand why single containers fail.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The basic way:

Use a standard `std::vector` of pairs. On `get(key)`, iterate through vector to find key (O(N)). On eviction, scan to find oldest timestamp (O(N)).

⏱️ Time: get = O(N), put = O(N)
📦 Space: O(N) capacity

This is far too slow for real-world databases. We need a way to move nodes in constant time.
slides.analogy: Searching an unsorted pile of papers on your desk one-by-one every time you need a document.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal Map + DLL breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Map + DLL Breakthrough
slides.body:
The ultimate optimization:

✅ Use a **Doubly Linked List (DLL)** to track chronological order (Head = MRU, Tail = LRU)
✅ Use an **Unordered Hash Map** mapping `key` to `DLL Node*` pointers

- `get(key)`: Lookup node pointer via map (O(1)). Detach node from DLL and insert at Head (MRU) (O(1)).
- `put(key, val)`: If key exists, update value and move to Head (O(1)). If cap full, evict Tail node (LRU), erase from map, and insert new node at Head (O(1))!

This is pure algorithmic harmony.
slides.goldenLine: A hash map provides immediate sight, while a doubly linked list provides immediate motion.
slides.transition: Let's watch this dynamic dance of pointers in simulation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: get(1): Map finds node [1] instantly. Detach [1] from list and insert at Head. DLL: Head <-> [1] <-> [2] <-> Tail.
put(3, 30): Capacity full! Evict tail->prev which is [2]. Erase key 2 from map. Delete node [2].
Insert [3] at Head. DLL: Head <-> [3] <-> [1] <-> Tail. Map: {1->[1], 3->[3]}.
slides.keyObservation: Sentinel Head and Tail nodes permanently bypass null pointer checks during detaching and inserting.
slides.transition: Why is a Doubly Linked List mandatory rather than a Singly Linked List?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Doubly Linked List is Mandatory
slides.body:
Why does a Singly Linked List (SLL) fail to achieve O(1)?

✅ To delete a node in O(1), we must connect its predecessor directly to its successor
✅ SLL does not contain a backward pointer to its predecessor, forcing an O(N) scan to locate it
✅ DLL provides both `prev` and `next` pointers, allowing instant O(1) removal of any node from the middle

DLL turns deletion into a localized, constant-time pointer swap.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to delete evicted nodes from memory or failing to remove their keys from the hash map, leading to memory leaks.
slides.transition: Let's construct this production-grade C++ class.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Define struct Node with `key`, `val`, `prev`, `next` pointers
Maintain Hash Map `key` -> `Node*` and integer `cap`
Use sentinel dummy `head` and `tail` nodes connected to each other
slides.mentalCompression: Map provides sight. DLL provides movement. Sentinel nodes eliminate null checks. Put to head, delete from tail.

Failing to connect sentinel pointers correctly in insert() (results in circular crashes)

revisionCards.title: LFU Cache
revisionCards.explanation: Design a Least Frequently Used (LFU) cache.
examples: Track minimum frequency level. Evict keys from the frequency list corresponding to `min`.

slides.headline: LFU Cache
slides.body:
⚡ Beyond time: caching by actual utility frequency!

Design a Least Frequently Used (LFU) Cache that supports `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` operations in **O(1)** time.

🧠 Recall:
- Evicts the item used the least number of times
- Ties broken by LRU policy
- Achieved using two nested hash maps and doubly linked lists!
slides.visualCue: A vertical staircase of frequency levels, each containing a horizontal train of DLL nodes representing items.
slides.memoryHook: A multi-tier sorting rack in a high-speed sorting warehouse.
slides.transition: How do we build a frequency cache that runs in constant time without scanning keys?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Eviction policy must prioritize popularity (access count) over chronology
✅ Requirement for constant O(1) complexity across both lookups and updates
✅ Handling dual priority constraints (frequency first, recency as a tiebreaker)

💡 Interview Signal:
When an interviewer mentions 'popularity-based eviction' and demands strict O(1) performance, reach for the Double Map + Frequency DLL combo.
slides.transition: Let's first understand why a simple sorted list is too slow.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The basic way:

Keep key-value pairs in a single list. Track `accessCount` on each node. On `get(key)`, increment counter and sort the list. On eviction, scan to find min `accessCount`.

⏱️ Time: get = O(N log N) or O(N), put = O(N)
📦 Space: O(N) capacity

This is far too slow for database caching. We need a way to update frequency groups in constant time.
slides.analogy: Having to completely re-sort a massive warehouse catalog by sales rank every single time someone buys a single pencil.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal double-map frequency-staircase breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Frequency Staircase Breakthrough
slides.body:
The ultimate nested map optimization:

✅ Maintain a hash map `keyToIter` mapping key to a Node iterator inside a specific frequency list
✅ Maintain a hash map `freqToList` mapping frequency count to a DLL of all nodes sharing that frequency
✅ Maintain a single integer `minFreq` representing the absolute lowest frequency currently populated

When a key is accessed, we detach it from `freqToList[f]` and push it to `freqToList[f+1]` (O(1)).
Evictions target `freqToList[minFreq].back()` (O(1))!
slides.goldenLine: Grouping elements by exact popularity bands turns sorting into constant-time level shifts.
slides.transition: Let's trace this level-up movement step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Capacity = 2. put(A), put(B). freqToList[1] = [B, A] (B is MRU). keyToIter has both. minFreq = 1.
get(A): Increment A's frequency to 2. Detach A from freqToList[1]. Push front of freqToList[2].
Now freqToList[1] = [B], freqToList[2] = [A]. minFreq remains 1.
put(C): Cap full! Evict from freqToList[minFreq (1)]. List back is B. Erase B from map. Insert C at freq 1. minFreq = 1.
slides.keyObservation: By grouping nodes in separate lists by frequency, we bypass sorting entirely.
slides.transition: Why is tracking `minFreq` so essential during updates?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why minFreq Tracking Matters
slides.body:
Why is LFU cache design highly prized in FAANG interviews?

✅ `minFreq` is the ONLY way to locate the eviction target in O(1) time
✅ If an element at `minFreq` is accessed, its frequency becomes `minFreq + 1`
✅ If the list at `minFreq` is now empty, we increment `minFreq` by 1
✅ On a fresh `put()`, `minFreq` is always reset to 1 because the new item has freq 1

This simple integer pointer maintains absolute constant-time synchronization.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to increment `minFreq` when the last element at that minimum frequency is accessed and promoted.
slides.transition: Let's implement this elegant C++ design.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Define struct Node containing `key`, `val`, and `freq`
Use `std::list<Node>` for Doubly Linked Lists
Maintain map `keyToIter` mapping `key` to `std::list<Node>::iterator`
slides.mentalCompression: Nested maps map key to iterator and frequency to list. Promote on read, evict from minFreq on write.
slides.transition: Let's look at the clean, split C++ code.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to increment `minFreq` when the promotion leaves the minimum frequency list empty
Creating a new node in `put` but forgetting to insert its iterator into `keyToIter`

Clearly explain why standard sorting algorithms are disastrous for caching, and describe how list iterators act as constant-time pointers directly into DLL nodes.

revisionCards.title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
revisionCards.explanation: Find the largest rectangular area possible in a histogram.
examples: heights = [2,1,5,6,2,3]. Pop heights, calculate areas. Maximum area is 10.

slides.headline: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
slides.body:
⚡ Find the largest rectangular area under a series of vertical bars.

Given an array of integers `heights` representing the histogram's bar heights, find the area of the largest rectangle that can be formed within the boundaries.

🧠 Recall:
- Area = height * width
- A bar can extend left and right as long as adjacent bars are taller
- Optimized using a Monotonic Stack!
slides.visualCue: A profile of skyline columns. A rectangular box expands horizontally until it hits shorter columns.
slides.memoryHook: An expanding block between concrete walls.
slides.transition: Let's first understand the double-loop search before looking at the optimal linear stack.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Recognize the triggers instantly:

✅ Maximizing rectangular area under a curve or dynamic boundaries
✅ Finding left and right limits of values that are strictly greater than or equal to current
✅ Nested loop scans seeking boundary limits with O(N^2) time

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires calculating dynamic bounds where an element's influence terminates at the first smaller neighbor, reach for the Monotonic Stack.
slides.transition: Let's review why the brute force approach is too slow for large inputs.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The basic way:

For each bar `i`, scan left to find the first bar smaller than `heights[i]` (`pse`). Scan right to find the first bar smaller (`nse`). The width is `nse - pse - 1`. Area = `heights[i] * width`.

⏱️ Time: O(N^2) due to double scanning
📦 Space: O(1) auxiliary space

This is slow because we are searching for boundaries repeatedly. We can find all boundaries in a single pass using a stack.
slides.analogy: An expanding balloon that has to walk and touch the left and right walls individually every single time it expands.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal single-pass monotonic stack breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Monotonic Stack Breakthrough
slides.body:
The single-pass area calculation breakthrough:

✅ Maintain a **Monotonic Increasing Stack** storing indices of bars
✅ If the current bar is smaller than stack top, the stack top's right limit (`nse`) is found!
✅ Pop the stack top. Its height `h` is the rectangle height. The new stack top is its left limit (`pse`)!
✅ Width is `current_index - new_stack_top - 1`. Calculate area and update maximum!

This calculates the optimal bounds for every popped bar on the fly!
slides.goldenLine: Popping a bar from the stack represents the exact moment its boundary is fully realized.
slides.transition: Let's watch this dynamic area calculation sweep through an array.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Heights = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2]. Add sentinel 0 to end: [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 0]. st = []
slides.keyObservation: Adding a sentinel value of 0 at the end of the heights array guarantees that the stack is fully flushed, calculating all areas without cleanup loops.
slides.transition: Why does the stack top represent the left limit so perfectly?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Monotonicity works
slides.body:
Why is the monotonic stack mathematically correct here?

✅ Every element in the stack is strictly greater than the element below it
✅ Therefore, when a bar `st.top()` is popped, the element directly below it in the stack is guaranteed to be the FIRST bar to its left that is smaller than it
✅ The current element `i` triggers the pop because it is smaller, meaning it is the FIRST bar to its right that is smaller

We get both limits instantly without scanning!
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to handle elements remaining in the stack if no sentinel 0 is used, which misses several potential maximum area rectangles.
slides.transition: Let's translate this elegant math sweep into clean C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Push a sentinel `0` to the end of the `heights` array
Declare a `std::stack<int> st` storing indices
Loop `i` from `0` to `heights.size() - 1`
slides.mentalCompression: Sentinel 0 flushes the stack. Pop height, compute width between boundary indices, maximize area.
slides.transition: Let's review the clean, split C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Sentinel appending and loop setup.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: An expanding bridge between two pillars: the bridge collapses when a shorter pillar is encountered, calculating its span width immediately.
slides.memoryHook: Encountering a step down collapses the span.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Failing to push a sentinel 0 or write a cleanup loop, leaving uncalculated heights in the stack
Incorrect width calculation: using `i - st.top()` instead of `i - st.top() - 1` when stack is not empty
interviewerQuestions: How would you solve Maximal Rectangle in a 2D binary matrix using this problem?
Can this be solved using Divide and Conquer? What would be the complexity?

recall.30sec: Monotonic increasing stack tracks indices, calculating a bar's maximum rectangle as soon as its right-hand smaller neighbor is found.
recall.1min: Single pass O(N) time and O(N) space algorithm. Replaces O(N^2) boundary scans with a highly optimized linear index sweep.

revisionCards.title: Sliding Window Maximum
revisionCards.explanation: Find the maximum value inside every sliding window of size k.
examples: nums = [1,3,-1], k=3. Queue holds indices. Return maximums.

slides.headline: Sliding Window Maximum
slides.body:
⚡ A moving spotlight: tracking the tallest actor as the frame slides along.

Given an array `nums` and a window size `k`, find the maximum element inside each sliding window configuration of size `k`.

🧠 Recall:
- Sliding window limits: `i - k + 1` to `i`
- Need fast query and update: Monotonic Queue
- Solved beautifully in linear **O(N)** time using a Deque!
slides.visualCue: A moving brackets window sweeping over an array, with a helper container filtering out obsolete values.
slides.memoryHook: A dynamic leaderboard of the current tallest.
slides.transition: How do we query the maximum in constant time without doing a linear sweep of the window?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Scanning maximums or minimums within a sliding frame or fixed interval
✅ Continuous stream analysis where only the peak value matters
✅ Nested loop scans tracking window max with O(N * k) complexity

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires continuous lookup of the extreme element (max or min) within a moving contiguous window, reach for the Monotonic Deque immediately.
slides.transition: Let's review the nested-loop approach and why it struggles.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive sliding scan:

For each starting index `i = 0` to `N - k`, scan the next `k` elements to locate the maximum value. Write the maximum to the output array.

⏱️ Time: O(N * k) due to nested window scans
📦 Space: O(1) auxiliary space

This is slow because we are re-scanning overlapping elements repeatedly. We can cache the active candidates in a sorted queue.
slides.analogy: Re-counting the height of everyone in a moving line from scratch every single time a new person enters the queue.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal Monotonic Deque breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Monotonic Deque Breakthrough
slides.body:
The monotonic decreasing deque optimization:

✅ Use a **Double-Ended Queue (Deque)** storing indices
✅ Remove indices from front that are out of the active window (`dq.front() < i - k + 1`)
✅ Remove indices from back of elements smaller than current (`nums[dq.back()] <= nums[i]`) (they are obsolete!)
✅ Push current index `i`. The front of the deque is now the window maximum!

Each element enters and exits the deque at most once, making the overall cost a blazing fast O(N)!
slides.goldenLine: A newcomer that is both younger and taller makes older, shorter candidates completely obsolete.
slides.transition: Let's watch this dynamic obsolescence filter in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: i=2 (-1): -1 < 3 -> push 2. dq = [1, 2]. Window complete! Max = nums[dq.front() (1)] = 3.
slides.keyObservation: When 5 enters, it completely flushes the deque because it outclasses all previous elements in value and recency.
slides.transition: Why is storing indices inside the Deque mandatory rather than storing element values?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why We Must Store Indices
slides.body:
Why does the deque store indices instead of raw values?

✅ Values alone cannot tell us if a candidate has slid out of the active window bounds
✅ By storing indices, we check `dq.front() < i - k + 1` to prune expired elements in O(1)
✅ We can still easily retrieve the value using `nums[dq.front()]`

This simple choice couples chronological tracking with extreme value pruning.
slides.interviewerTrap: Forgetting to check if the window has reached size `k` (index `i >= k - 1`) before appending maximums to the result array.
slides.transition: Let's implement this elegant monotonic deque in C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Declare a `std::deque<int> dq` to store indices and a result vector `res`
Loop `i` from `0` to `nums.size() - 1`
Prune front: if front index is out of bounds (`i - k + 1`), pop front
slides.mentalCompression: Prune front (expired). Prune back (smaller). Push current. Front is the maximum.

slides.body: A dynamic group where older members retire, and younger, stronger members kick out all weaker seniors from the queue.
slides.memoryHook: Stronger youngsters evict weaker seniors.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Storing values in the deque, which breaks the ability to check if a value has slid out of window
Checking `dq.front() < i - k` instead of `i - k + 1` (off-by-one window bounds error)
interviewerQuestions: Can you solve this in O(N) using a balanced binary search tree? What is the complexity tradeoff?
How would you modify this to find the sliding window minimum?

recall.5sec: Deque of indices. Pop front if out of window. Pop back if <= current. Front is max.
recall.30sec: Sliding Window Maximum uses a Monotonic Deque to prune expired and smaller elements, maintaining maximum in O(1).
recall.1min: Amortized O(N) time sliding window solver. Leverages double-ended queue mechanics to bypass the classic O(N * k) search limits.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates clearly prove why the time complexity is strictly linear O(N) despite the nested while loop. Point out that every index is pushed onto the deque exactly once and popped at most once, meaning the inner loop runs at most N times across the entire execution.
slides.closingLine: Amortized analysis is the secret to proving linear execution boundaries.

revisionCards.title: Min Stack
revisionCards.explanation: Design a stack that supports retrieving the minimum element in O(1) time.
examples: Push values. Min stack tracks the minimums. Returns min in O(1) time.

slides.headline: Min Stack
slides.body:
⚡ Can you retrieve the minimum element of a stack in constant **O(1)** time?

Design a stack that supports `push`, `pop`, `top`, and retrieving the minimum element in constant time, without scanning the stack.

🧠 Recall:
- Stack operations must remain O(1)
- Minimum element query must be O(1)
- Solved elegantly by coupling values with their historical minimums!
slides.visualCue: A vertical stack where each slot holds two values: the item itself and the minimum seen up to that point.
slides.memoryHook: A stack of papers, each stamped with the lowest grade in the pile.
slides.transition: Let's first understand why tracking a single minimum variable fails on pop operations.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Need standard LIFO stack API
✅ Must query the minimum (or maximum) value of all active elements in constant time
✅ Value history must support rapid restorations when elements are removed

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem demands tracking a running state (min, max, sum) that must automatically revert to its exact historical state on pop, cache the state history alongside stack elements.
slides.transition: Let's review why a single `minVal` variable fails.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The single variable approach:

Maintain a single variable `currentMin`. On `push(x)`, update `currentMin = min(currentMin, x)`. Fails on `pop()` because if the popped element *was* the `currentMin`, we have to scan the remaining stack to find the new minimum.

⏱️ Time: push = O(1), pop = O(N) to re-evaluate minimum
📦 Space: O(1) auxiliary space

We must remember the minimum at *every* step of the stack's growth.
slides.analogy: Writing the cheapest item in a store on a blackboard, but having to search the entire store again when that cheapest item is sold.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal state-dependent historical minimum breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Historical Pair Breakthrough
slides.body:
The historical state pair breakthrough:

✅ Store **pairs** in the stack: `{value, currentMin}`
✅ On `push(val)`: look at the top of the stack. If stack is empty, `currentMin = val`. Otherwise, `currentMin = min(val, stack.top().second)`
✅ Push `{val, currentMin}` onto the stack!

When you pop, the historical minimum of the remaining elements is already safely sitting at the top of the stack, ready to be read in O(1) time!
slides.goldenLine: By nesting history inside each node, popping elements automatically restores past states.
slides.transition: Let's watch this history-paired stack in action.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Initialize MinStack. st = []. push(5): st.empty() -> min = 5. Push {5, 5}. st = [{5, 5}]
getMin() returns st.top().second (3). pop() removes {7, 3}. New top is {3, 3}. getMin() still returns 3!
slides.keyObservation: Popping {3, 3} instantly restores the previous minimum of 5, which is safely stored inside the {5, 5} pair below.
slides.transition: Why are stack pairs extremely safe and robust compared to single variable formulas?

slides.headline: 🔍 Stack Pairs vs Math Formulas
slides.body:
Is there a formula to save space?

✅ Yes, by storing the difference: `2 * val - min`
❌ However, this formula triggers integer overflow issues in C++ and requires cast operations
✅ Using `{value, min}` pairs is highly robust, safe from math overflow, and immediately readable

Storing history in pairs is the gold standard for highly stable, production-grade systems.
slides.interviewerTrap: Attempting to call `st.top()` on an empty stack during `getMin()` or `top()` queries, leading to crash errors.
slides.transition: Let's implement this robust pair-based Min Stack in C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Declare a `std::stack<std::pair<int, int>> st` to store `{value, min}` pairs
Implement push: if stack is empty, push `{val, val}`
Else, calculate `currentMin = min(val, st.top().second)` and push `{val, currentMin}`
slides.mentalCompression: Push pairs of {value, runningMin}. Pop restores the previous runningMin automatically.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Class layout and push logic utilizing pairs.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: A double-barreled shotgun where one barrel holds the actual bullets and the other holds a shield indicating the strongest armor level seen so far.
slides.memoryHook: Coupled values hold historical minimums.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to check if the stack is empty before pushing, leading to segmentation faults
Only pushing onto the min-tracking stack when a smaller element is seen, which gets out of sync on duplicates
interviewerQuestions: How would you optimize the space if many duplicate minimums are pushed?
Can you implement a Max Stack using the exact same principles?

recall.5sec: Stack of pairs: {val, currentMin}. push evaluates min. Pop automatically restores previous min.
recall.30sec: Min Stack stores historical state pairs to preserve the running minimum at every step, avoiding costly re-evaluations.
recall.1min: O(1) time complexity stack. Couples active values with their historical minimum boundaries, eliminating dynamic search overhead.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Stand out by proactively mentioning the trade-offs of the single-stack pair method vs the two-stack method! The two-stack method saves space by only pushing to the min stack when a new minimum is found, while the pair method is simpler and has cleaner memory layouts. Demonstrating knowledge of both is elite.
slides.closingLine: State history is the easiest way to avoid costly re-evaluations.

revisionCards.title: Rotten Oranges
revisionCards.explanation: Find the minimum time to rot all oranges in a grid.
examples: Multi-source BFS traversal. Return time when fresh count reaches 0.

slides.headline: Rotten Oranges
slides.body:
⚡ An infectious outbreak: how long before the entire grid is contaminated?

You are given a 2D grid where `0` represents empty cell, `1` fresh orange, and `2` rotten orange. Every minute, any fresh orange adjacent to a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the minimum minutes to rot all oranges, or `-1`.

🧠 Recall:
- Grid contamination spreads step-by-step to neighbors
- Shortest time to reach nodes: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
- Multi-source BFS solves this in linear time!
slides.visualCue: A grid where a few infected cells spread outward like circles in water, turning fresh cells red step-by-step.
slides.memoryHook: An expanding wave of forest fire.
slides.transition: Why does Depth-First Search (DFS) fail completely, and why is multi-source BFS mandatory?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the triggers instantly:

✅ Contamination, fire, or infection spreading over a grid step-by-step
✅ Finding the minimum time or shortest path to fully cover a graph
✅ Multiple starting sources active simultaneously

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires tracking simultaneous expansion from multiple coordinates, think Multi-Source BFS immediately.
slides.transition: Let's first understand why depth-first paths are highly inefficient.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The DFS approach:

For each rotten orange, run DFS to find the shortest time it takes to reach each fresh orange, and update grid cells. Fails because paths overlap, causing redundant updates and high computational waste.

⏱️ Time: O((R * C)^2) due to path overlaps
📦 Space: O(R * C) recursion stack

This is slow because DFS goes deep first, which evaluates paths rather than chronological levels. We need a level-by-level BFS sweep.
slides.analogy: Sending one firefighter to run through every single room in a burning building sequentially, instead of using a sprinkler system that activates all rooms at once.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal multi-source BFS level-by-level breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Multi-Source BFS Breakthrough
slides.body:
The multi-source level-by-level BFS optimization:

✅ Count all fresh oranges initially, and enqueue all rotten orange coordinates
✅ Perform BFS. On each level loop, pop all active coordinates, check 4 directions
✅ If neighbor is fresh (`1`), make it rotten (`2`), decrement fresh count, and push it to queue
✅ Increment minute count after processing all elements in the current level

If fresh count reaches `0`, return the minutes! Otherwise return `-1`.
slides.goldenLine: Multi-source BFS models a physical wave, ensuring every orange is reached in the absolute shortest time.
slides.transition: Let's watch this infection wave sweep through a grid.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Grid has rotten at (0,0) and 5 fresh. Initial: Q = [(0,0)], minutes = 0, fresh = 5.
Minute 1: Pop (0,0). Rot neighbors (0,1) and (1,0). Set grid to 2. Q = [(0,1), (1,0)]. fresh = 3. minutes = 1.
Minute 2: Pop (0,1) and (1,0). Rot (1,1). Q = [(1,1)]. fresh = 2. minutes = 2.
Minute 3: Pop (1,1). Rot (2,1). Q = [(2,1)]. fresh = 1. minutes = 3.
slides.keyObservation: By checking queue size inside the loop, we process all active infection fronts simultaneously per minute.
slides.transition: Why is BFS structurally guaranteed to find the absolute minimum time?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why BFS Guarantees Min Time
slides.body:
Why does Breadth-First Search work so perfectly for timing streams?

✅ BFS expands outward radially like a wave
✅ It guarantees that a node is reached at level `L` only when there is no path of length `< L`
✅ Multi-source BFS is equivalent to having a dummy 'Super Node' connected to all starting points, maintaining mathematical consistency

This makes BFS the absolute standard for grid expansion modeling.
slides.interviewerTrap: Incrementing the minutes counter when the queue is already empty at the end, leading to an answer that is off-by-one.
slides.transition: Let's translate this infection wave into clean C++.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize queue `q` and counter `fresh = 0`
Scan grid: push `{i, j}` of all `2`s onto `q`, increment `fresh` for `1`s
If `fresh == 0` return 0
slides.mentalCompression: Enqueue all sources. Count fresh. Loop level-by-level, rot neighbors, decrement fresh count. Return time when fresh is 0.

slides.body: Outbreak scanning and queue setup.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code (Part 2/2)
slides.body: Outbreak scanning and queue setup. (Continued)

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Water dropping at multiple points on a grid paper simultaneously: the wet spots expand in concentric squares until all dry paper is gone.
slides.memoryHook: Concentric expansion of infected fronts.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Not checking if fresh == 0 at the start, returning minutes = 1 for a completely rotten grid
Incrementing the minute counter on the very last iteration when no fresh oranges were rotted
interviewerQuestions: Can you solve this using a single queue without checking level size? (Hint: Sentinel nodes)
What is the space complexity if the grid is massive?
