Call preorder(2.left) to arrive at [1].
Process [1] immediately. res = [2, 1].
Call preorder(1.left) and preorder(1.right) - both are NULL, return.
slides.keyObservation: We record [2] first, then its left child [1], and only then its right child [3].
slides.transition: Why are some candidates tripped up by the stack layout?

slides.headline: 🔍 Top-Down Path Propagation
slides.body:
Why does preorder serve top-down problems so well?

✅ Values are inherited from top to bottom.
✅ Perfect for questions like 'does a path from root to leaf sum to target?'.

⚠️ The Trap:
Thinking iterative preorder requires a queue. Since stacks are LIFO, to process Left before Right, you must push the Right child onto the stack first, then the Left child!
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'How do you do this iteratively?' Explain that pushing root, then popping, pushing right then left ensures the correct LIFO order.

recall.30sec: Record the current node value, recursive call left, recursive call right. Space O(H), Time O(N).
recall.1min: Pass the result vector by reference to avoid copying. Returns immediately if root is NULL.

revisionCards.title: Postorder Traversal
revisionCards.explanation: Traverse a Binary Tree in Postorder sequence: Left subtree, Right subtree, then Root node.

slides.headline: ⚡ Postorder Traversal Blueprint
slides.body:
How do you safely delete a binary tree without leaving orphaned nodes? Or compute properties that depend entirely on subtrees (like height or diameter)?

You must process children first, and only then evaluate the parent.

🎯 The ultimate challenge:
Backtracking only after both left and right options are completely exhausted.
slides.visualCue: A binary tree being traversed bottom-up, starting from leaves and meeting at the root.
slides.memoryHook: Left -> Right -> Root: Children first, parent last.
slides.transition: When does an interviewer expect you to instantly use Postorder?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Tree deletion (deallocating memory bottom-up)
✅ Calculating subtree properties (sum, height, balance status)
✅ Evaluating algebraic expression trees (operators are roots, operands are leaves)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a parent's calculation depends directly on results computed from its left and right subtrees, think Postorder.
slides.transition: Let's explore the bottom-up recursive intuition.

slides.headline: 📦 Bottom-Up Dependency Thinking
slides.body:
You cannot evaluate the root until you know what both branches returned:

1. Traverse the left child recursively.
2. Traverse the right child recursively.
3. Process the current parent node.

⏱️ Time: O(N) since we visit every node once.
📦 Space: O(H) recursion stack space (H = height of tree).

Why this is slow iteratively: You have to visit a node twice before processing it.
slides.analogy: A manager who cannot compile a division report until both regional sub-managers submit their metrics.
slides.transition: Let's look at the core recursive optimization.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Bottom-Up Engine
slides.body:
Postorder is the core engine for all bottom-up algorithms:

✅ Safely free child memory before the parent disappears.
✅ Bubbles up calculated states (like subtree height) directly.
✅ Ensures parent node only executes with full local context.

This makes tree properties like Balanced or Symmetric incredibly efficient to compute.
slides.goldenLine: Verify both children first, then decide for the parent.
slides.transition: Let's watch this execute in a simulation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Start at root [2]. Call postorder(2.left) to arrive at [1].
Call postorder(1.left) and postorder(1.right) - both NULL, return.
Process leaf [1] because its children are done. res = [1].
Return to [2], then call postorder(2.right) to arrive at [3].
slides.keyObservation: The root [2] is processed absolutely last after all its descendants are finished.
slides.transition: Why is the iterative implementation of postorder considered one of the hardest basic traversals?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Two-Visit Stack Hurdle
slides.body:
Why is iterative postorder challenging?

✅ In preorder/inorder, we process a node on the first or second visit.
✅ In postorder, we must visit a node, check the right subtree, and only process it when returning from the right subtree.

⚠️ The Trap:
Iterating requires tracking whether we've already visited the right child. To bypass this, we can perform a modified preorder (Root-Right-Left) and reverse the entire final output!
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'How do you do iterative postorder with a single stack?' Talk about keeping track of the previously visited node to check if we are ascending from the right child.
slides.transition: Let's look at the clean implementation blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Base Case: If node is NULL, return.
Recursive Step 1: Postorder traverse the left subtree.
Recursive Step 2: Postorder traverse the right subtree.
slides.mentalCompression: L-R-Root: Resolve left, resolve right, process home.
slides.transition: Let's lock it in with clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Beautiful recursive postorder traversal in standard C++.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Imagine a tree shedding its leaves: the leaves must drop off first, branch by branch, until finally the bare root is processed last.
slides.memoryHook: Leaves drop first, branches second, trunk last.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Trying to delete a node before its children are deleted (memory leak or crash).
Reversing the wrong array structure during the iterative two-stack shortcut.
interviewerQuestions: How does Postorder Traversal relate to Postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) expressions?
Can you implement iterative postorder traversal using only one stack?

recall.30sec: Traverse left subtree, traverse right subtree, process root. Time O(N), Space O(H) recursive stack.
recall.1min: Used for bottom-up queries (height, diameter). Pass vector by reference to avoid copying. Base case checks NULL.

slides.headline: 🏆 Showcasing Mastery
slides.body: Elite candidates instantly link Postorder to bottom-up dynamic programming on trees. They demonstrate how problems like calculating the diameter or checking balance can be solved in a single postorder pass, avoiding redundant O(N^2) parent-child traversals.
slides.closingLine: Success is built from the bottom up, one leaf at a time.

revisionCards.title: Left View of Binary Tree
revisionCards.explanation: Return the nodes visible when looking at the tree from the left side. Visually, the first node of each level.

slides.headline: ⚡ Left View of Binary Tree
slides.body:
Imagine standing on the left side of a massive binary tree in a dense forest. Which nodes would block your vision?

You will see only the first node of every level.

🎯 The real challenge:
Can you do this recursively in a single DFS sweep, without storing entire levels in memory?
slides.visualCue: A profile view of a tree with a spotlight shining from the left, highlighting the leftmost nodes.
slides.memoryHook: First encounter at each level of a Left-First DFS traversal.
slides.transition: How do we immediately recognize a profile/view type problem?

slides.headline: 🧠 Profile View Trigger
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Visible boundary nodes from a specific perspective
✅ Level-by-level representative node selection
✅ Shadowing problems where nodes block other nodes

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks for the first or last node at each depth level, think Depth-First Search with depth-tracked array insertion.
slides.transition: Let's review the standard queue-based brute-force approach first.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Level Order
slides.body:
The direct approach uses Breadth-First Search (BFS):

1. Do a standard level order traversal with a queue.
2. For each level, record only the very first node.

⏱️ Time: O(N) to process all nodes.
📦 Space: O(W) queue space, where W is the maximum width of the tree.

This works, but storing entire levels in a queue is space-heavy. We can do better with recursion!
slides.analogy: Taking a group photo row-by-row and only writing down the name of the person standing on the absolute left of each row.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the recursion optimization using the result array size.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Depth-Reference Trick
slides.body:
Use a Left-First DFS with a depth parameter:

✅ Visit Left child before Right child.
✅ Use the size of your result vector as a sentinel.

If `depth == res.size()`, it means this is the *first* time we have ever visited a node at this specific depth! We push it. Otherwise, it is shadowed, so we ignore it.
slides.goldenLine: Let the array size track our maximum depth horizon.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this elegant DFS technique.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Start at root [1] (depth 0). res.size() is 0. Since depth == 0, push [1]. res = [1].
DFS Left to [2] (depth 1). res.size() is 1. Since depth == 1, push [2]. res = [1, 2].
DFS Left from [2] is NULL, return. DFS Right from [2] is [4] (depth 2).
At [4] (depth 2). res.size() is 2. Since depth == 2, push [4]. res = [1, 2, 4].
slides.keyObservation: Because we visit left first, the leftmost node at any depth always gets recorded, blocking all subsequent nodes at that depth.
slides.transition: Why is visiting Left before Right absolutely crucial?

slides.headline: 🔍 DFS Left-to-Right Guarantee
slides.body:
Why is Left-First DFS 100% correct?

✅ DFS guarantees we search path-by-path.
✅ Left-first ensures the leftmost node of any level is visited before any other node on that same level.
✅ Hence, the check `depth == res.size()` will only be true for that first leftmost node.

To get the Right View instead, we would simply visit the Right child before the Left child!
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'What happens if a level has no left child but has a right child?' Left-first DFS will naturally fall back to the right child on that level, which correctly represents the left view!
slides.transition: Let's examine the blueprint of this recursive traversal.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create a recursive helper function taking a node and its current depth.
Base Case: If node is NULL, return immediately.
Check: If depth equals the size of the result vector, push current node value.
slides.mentalCompression: Compare depth to size: if they match, you've hit the leftmost node of a new level.
slides.transition: Let's lock it in with clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Clean recursive DFS Left View in Standard C++.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: DFS downward left-first: if the depth level has never been reached, the current node is the left sentinel.
slides.memoryHook: Depth matching size means new left frontier.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Recursively calling right before left, which generates the Right View instead.
Forgetting to increment depth in recursive calls, placing all nodes on level 0.
interviewerQuestions: How would you modify this to solve the Right View of a binary tree?
Can you write a BFS solution and explain its space complexity compared to DFS?

recall.5sec: Left-first DFS, push when `depth == res.size()`.
recall.30sec: Traverse left child then right child, carrying depth + 1. If depth equals result vector size, record node. Time O(N), Space O(H).
recall.1min: Avoids overhead of queues in BFS. Easily adjustable to Right View by swapping the recursive call order.

slides.headline: 🏆 Showcasing Mastery
slides.body: Elite candidates don't just jump to BFS. They explain how DFS with depth-tracking uses far less memory: O(H) auxiliary space vs O(W) in BFS. They point out that a tree's width can be up to N/2, making BFS memory-inefficient on large, balanced trees.
slides.closingLine: Perspective is everything: the left view is just a left-first walk in disguise.

revisionCards.title: Bottom View of Binary Tree
revisionCards.explanation: Return the nodes visible from the bottom. Multi-level nodes at the same horizontal distance shadow upper ones; rightmost node is picked on conflict.

slides.headline: ⚡ Bottom View of Binary Tree
slides.body:
Imagine standing directly underneath a binary tree looking straight up. Which nodes are visible, and which are blocked by branches higher up?

You see nodes arranged by their horizontal columns. Lower nodes shadow higher ones.

🎯 The real challenge:
Accurately mapping vertical columns and ensuring the latest level nodes overwrite upper ones.
slides.visualCue: A binary tree divided into vertical column strips, highlighting the bottom-most node in each strip.
slides.memoryHook: Horizontal coordinates map to the final node seen per column.
slides.transition: What coordinate system helps us partition a tree into columns?

slides.headline: 🧠 Column-Wise Partition Trigger
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Vertical column tracking or vertical alignment
✅ Shadowing along a coordinate axis (top/bottom views)
✅ Grouping nodes by horizontal distance from the root

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires grouping or selecting nodes based on vertical column slices, think Vertical Grid Coordinates: Root is `0`, Left child is `col-1`, Right child is `col+1`.
slides.transition: Why does recursive DFS complicate the bottom view compared to BFS?

slides.headline: 📦 BFS vs DFS Coordinate Mapping
slides.body:
With DFS, a node visited later might be higher up than one visited earlier. BFS naturally processes level-by-level:

1. Do a level-order traversal carrying horizontal distance (`hd`) columns.
2. Overwrite the column's value in a map at each node visit.
3. Since BFS goes level-by-level, the last node processed in a column is guaranteed to be the lowest.

⏱️ Time: O(N log N) using a map to keep columns sorted.
📦 Space: O(N) to store nodes in queue and map.
slides.analogy: Pouring sand down column slots: the last grain poured in each column rests on top, blocking everything underneath.
slides.transition: How do we implement this level-by-level column assignment?

slides.headline: 🚀 Column Overwrite Engine
slides.body:
The core breakthrough lies in mapping BFS to Sorted Columns:

✅ Track column offsets: `Left = col - 1`, `Right = col + 1`.
✅ Use a hash map or ordered map to record `map[col] = node->val`.
✅ BFS ensures that lower-level nodes are processed *after* higher-level nodes, automatically overwriting them in the map.

This guarantees that the final state of `map[col]` holds the absolute bottom-most node for that vertical column.
slides.goldenLine: BFS guarantees depth priority, while the map organizes horizontal sorting.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this column overwrite process.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Process [5] at col -2. map[-2] = 5.
slides.keyObservation: Node [3] at col 0 and Node [10] at col -1 successfully overwrote their predecessors because they occurred deeper in the level order traversal.
slides.transition: Let's check the code split to handle this logic cleanly.

slides.headline: 🔍 Why BFS is the Optimal Choice
slides.body:
Why BFS over DFS here?

✅ DFS can visit bottom nodes *before* top nodes depending on traversal direction. To do DFS, you'd have to track depth alongside columns and only overwrite if `curr_depth >= map_depth`.
✅ BFS processes top-down, meaning simple unconditional overwriting works perfectly.

⚠️ The Trap:
Using unordered_map requires a separate step to find the min and max column range to print in sorted order. An ordered map (`std::map`) sorts keys automatically in O(log N) per operation.
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'How do you avoid the O(log N) map overhead?' Answer: Keep track of min/max column index during BFS and use a standard hash map, then loop from min to max.
slides.transition: Let's review the code structure across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize an ordered map `map<int, int>` to store the last node at each column.
Set up a BFS queue storing pairs of `(TreeNode*, column_coordinate)`.
Enqueue root at column 0.
slides.mentalCompression: Map columns to values via level-by-level BFS, letting later layers naturally overwrite earlier ones.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the first part of the C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Part 1: Performing column-tracked Breadth-First Search using a queue and an ordered map.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Run a level-order sweep, label nodes with horizontal offsets, and let lower elements overwrite the map at their horizontal offset.
slides.memoryHook: Level order sweep, last-write wins per column.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Using DFS without tracking node depth, causing incorrect higher nodes to overwrite lower ones.
Using an unordered_map without keeping track of min/max boundaries, resulting in unsorted output.
interviewerQuestions: What is the time complexity difference if you use std::map vs std::unordered_map?
How would you solve the Top View of a Binary Tree using a similar structure?

recall.30sec: Queue records `{node, col}`. Left goes `col - 1`, right goes `col + 1`. Map `nodes[col] = node->val`. Time O(N log N) due to map sorting.
recall.1min: Extract values from the ordered map to guarantee left-to-right sorting. O(N) space for queue and map. Base case returns empty array.

slides.headline: 🏆 Showcasing Mastery
slides.body: Elite candidates explain both BFS and DFS approaches, noting that while BFS is simpler due to level-by-level guarantee, DFS can be optimized to O(H) space if we maintain both column and depth. They also mention that `std::unordered_map` with active tracking of `minCol` and `maxCol` improves time complexity to a clean linear O(N).
slides.closingLine: A solid coordinate system makes the most complex views simple.

revisionCards.title: Top View of Binary Tree
revisionCards.explanation: Return the nodes visible from the top. The first node encountered at each horizontal column from left to right.

slides.headline: ⚡ Top View of Binary Tree
slides.body:
If you looked at a binary tree from the sky, which nodes would be visible?

You will see only the first (highest) node at each horizontal offset (column).

🎯 The real challenge:
Making sure lower nodes are completely blocked and never overwrite nodes that were already visible above them.
slides.visualCue: A binary tree viewed from the top with vertical columns, highlighting the topmost node in each vertical slice.
slides.memoryHook: First node to claim a column coordinate is the only one seen from above.
slides.transition: What coordinate tracking mechanism helps us partition columns?

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Skyline or top-down horizontal projection mapping
✅ Filtering nodes by first-appearance in vertical columns
✅ Blocking or shadowing vertical paths

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires selecting only the highest or earliest representative node of each vertical column, think Column-Tracked Level Order Traversal.
slides.transition: Let's review why Level Order Traversal makes column-blocking easy.

slides.headline: 📦 First-Write Level Order
slides.body:
A level order traversal processes top-down, level-by-level:

1. Do a standard BFS carrying vertical columns `col`.
2. When processing a node, check if its column already exists in our map.
3. If it doesn't exist, this node is the highest in its column! Record it.
4. If it does exist, it is blocked by a higher node. Ignore it.

⏱️ Time: O(N log N) using standard ordered map.
📦 Space: O(N) to store queue and map nodes.
slides.analogy: Setting up umbrellas: once an umbrella is placed at a horizontal spot, it blocks all raindrops (nodes) falling underneath it.
slides.transition: How do we implement this first-write block in our BFS queue?

slides.headline: 🚀 The First-Write Sentinel
slides.body:
The core optimization is the **First-Write Sentinel**:

✅ BFS ensures we visit shallower depths before deeper depths.
✅ An ordered map stores `map[col] = node->val`.
✅ By checking `if (map.find(col) == map.end())`, we write *only* if the column is completely vacant.

This guarantees the first node to reach column `col` is locked in, blocking all lower descendants.
slides.goldenLine: First come, first served: the topmost nodes lock their vertical coordinates.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this skyline simulation.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Root [1] at col 0. map[0] is empty -> map[0] = 1. Queue: [(2, -1), (3, 1)].
Process [2] at col -1. map[-1] is empty -> map[-1] = 2. Queue pushes [(4, -2), (5, 0)].
Process [3] at col 1. map[1] is empty -> map[1] = 3. Queue pushes [(6, 0), (7, 2)].
Process [4] at col -2. map[-2] is empty -> map[-2] = 4.
slides.keyObservation: Nodes [5] and [6] both map to col 0, but they are completely shadowed because root [1] reached col 0 first.
slides.transition: Let's split the code into neat, clean chunks.

slides.headline: 🔍 Why BFS is the Safest Pathway
slides.body:
Why is BFS superior to DFS for the Top View?

✅ BFS visits nodes strictly in order of depth. A simple 'is column vacant?' check is sufficient.
✅ With DFS, a deeper node on the left might be visited before a shallower node on the right, which would require complex depth-checks to resolve.

⚠️ The Trap:
Attempting DFS without comparing depth will lead to deep nodes blocking shallow ones if they happen to be on the same column coordinate.
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'How can you do this in DFS?' Answer: You must track `(node_val, depth)` in the map and only overwrite if the new node has a smaller depth than the one currently recorded.
slides.transition: Let's review the code across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize an ordered map `map<int, int>` to store the first node at each column.
Set up a BFS queue storing pairs of `(TreeNode*, column_coordinate)`.
Enqueue root at column 0.
slides.mentalCompression: BFS ensures top-down flow. Write to map ONLY if the column has never been claimed.
slides.transition: Let's view the C++ code structure.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Part 1: Running column-tracked Breadth-First Search using a queue and an ordered map to record topmost nodes.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: A level-order scan where columns are filled once and locked forever, preventing deeper layers from claiming them.
slides.memoryHook: First-write locks the column skyline.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Overwriting columns in BFS (which results in the Bottom View instead of Top View).
Using DFS without depth-checks, letting deep nodes block shallow ones.
interviewerQuestions: How can you optimize this to run in O(N) time instead of O(N log N)?
What happens to the top view if the tree is highly skewed?

slides.body: Elite candidates explain why standard BFS is optimal here compared to DFS (DFS requires maintaining depth variables and comparing them). They also mention that keeping track of `minCol` and `maxCol` values lets us use a simple `std::unordered_map` to drop the time complexity from O(N log N) to linear O(N)!
slides.closingLine: Lock the top, ignore the bottom, and sorting completes the view.

revisionCards.title: Preorder Inorder Postorder in Single Traversal
revisionCards.explanation: Perform Preorder, Inorder, and Postorder traversals in a single pass using a std::stack to track tree states.
examples: Standard binary tree -> returns all three traversal arrays

slides.headline: ⚡ The 3-in-1 Traversal
slides.body:
Can you gather Preorder, Inorder, and Postorder sequences of a binary tree in a single iterative sweep?

Instead of making three separate recursive runs, you can process every node in three states using a single stack.

🎯 The real challenge:
Accurately managing the state changes of each stack element as it simulates backtracking.
slides.visualCue: A single stack containing nodes paired with state counters (1, 2, or 3).
slides.memoryHook: State 1 = Pre, State 2 = In, State 3 = Post.
slides.transition: When should we use this 3-in-1 traversal trigger?

slides.headline: 🧠 Multi-Traversal Trigger
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Interviewer asks for all 3 traversals in a single pass
✅ Manual stack-based DFS simulation is requested
✅ Need to compile structural information of a tree in one clean crawl

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem demands processing nodes at three distinct lifecycle points (on entry, between subtrees, and on exit), think State-Tracked Iterative Stack DFS.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple brute-force multi-pass approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Multi-Pass
slides.body:
The direct approach is to run three separate functions:

1. Run `preorder()` recursively.
2. Run `inorder()` recursively.
3. Run `postorder()` recursively.

⏱️ Time: O(3N) = O(N) but traverses the tree 3 times.
📦 Space: O(3H) call stack space.

While correct, it is highly redundant and shows lack of deep stack-lifecycle control.
slides.analogy: A courier visiting three houses three separate times instead of dropping off all three packages in one trip.
slides.transition: How do we make the single-pass stack state breakthrough?

slides.headline: 🚀 The State-Machine Stack
slides.body:
Track the lifecycle of a node using a state counter:

✅ State 1 (Preorder): Record value, increment state to 2, push left child.
✅ State 2 (Inorder): Record value, increment state to 3, push right child.
✅ State 3 (Postorder): Record value, pop the node off the stack.

This simple state machine elegantly maps the recursive call stack inside a standard stack.
slides.goldenLine: Increment the state as you crawl around the node.
slides.transition: Let's watch this state machine simulate a dry run.

slides.headline: 🎬 State Transition Simulation
steps: Push root [1] with State 1: Stack = [(1, 1)].
Pop (1, 1). It is State 1: Push val [1] to PRE. Push state-increment (1, 2). Push left child (2, 1). Stack = [(1, 2), (2, 1)].
Pop (2, 1). State 1: Push [2] to PRE. Push (2, 2). Left is NULL. Stack = [(1, 2), (2, 2)].
Pop (2, 2). State 2: Push [2] to IN. Push (2, 3). Right is NULL. Stack = [(1, 2), (2, 3)].
slides.keyObservation: Every node is popped and pushed up to 3 times, reflecting its state transitions.
slides.transition: Why are some candidates confused by the order of pushes?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why LIFO Governs the Push Order
slides.body:
Why does the iterative stack push order work this way?

✅ Stacks are Last-In, First-Out (LIFO).
✅ In State 1, we push `(node, 2)` then `(node->left, 1)` so that the left child is popped and processed next.
✅ In State 2, we push `(node, 3)` then `(node->right, 1)` so that the right child is popped and processed next.

This keeps the exact execution sequence identical to recursion.
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'Does this save memory over recursion?' Answer: Theoretically no (both O(H)), but it avoids stack overflow by using the heap instead of the call stack.
slides.transition: Let's review the step-by-step algorithm blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create a stack of pairs: `stack<pair<TreeNode*, int>>`.
Push root onto the stack with state = 1.
Loop while stack is not empty: pop the top node.
slides.mentalCompression: Pre, In, Post matches state 1, 2, 3. Push children LIFO style.
slides.transition: Let's examine the clean C++ code in detail.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Part 1: Setting up the stack and handling State 1 (Preorder) logic.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Every node undergoes a 3-step state cycle on a single stack, outputting to Pre, In, and Post lists accordingly.
slides.memoryHook: Stack state counter: 1 (Pre), 2 (In), 3 (Post).

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to push the parent node back onto the stack after incrementing its state.
Pushing children with state 2 or 3 instead of resetting their initial state to 1.
interviewerQuestions: How does this state machine structure compare to compiler-level stack frame generation?
Can you modify this to traverse N-ary trees?

recall.30sec: Pop `(node, state)`. State 1: PRE, push `(node, 2)`, push `(left, 1)`. State 2: IN, push `(node, 3)`, push `(right, 1)`. State 3: POST.
recall.1min: Simulates all 3 recursive crawls in exactly O(N) time and O(H) space without redundant sweeps.

revisionCards.title: Level Order Traversal
revisionCards.explanation: Perform Breadth-First Search (BFS) to visit nodes level-by-level, returning a 2D array of level-wise nodes.

slides.headline: ⚡ Level Order Traversal
slides.body:
How do you scan a tree row-by-row, like reading lines of text in a book?

You need to exhaustively visit all nodes at depth `d` before touching a single node at depth `d+1`.

🎯 The real challenge:
Tracking level boundaries without letting children from different depths mix in the queue.
slides.visualCue: A horizontal scanner sweeping down a tree level-by-level.
slides.memoryHook: BFS Queue: FIFO queue processes the current width cleanly.
slides.transition: When is Level Order Traversal an absolute must in interviews?

slides.headline: 🧠 Row-Wise Search Trigger
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Level-by-level grouping or processing of nodes
✅ Shortest path in unweighted tree structure
✅ Connected component breadth search

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires checking properties row-by-row or finding relationships within the same horizontal layer, think BFS Queue with a level-size snapshot.
slides.transition: Let's review the simple queue setup.

slides.headline: 📦 Breadth-First Thinking
slides.body:
DFS dives deep, BFS spreads wide:

1. Place the root in a queue.
2. In a loop, check the current size of the queue. This is the count of nodes on this level!
3. Pop exactly that many nodes, record their values, and queue their children.

⏱️ Time: O(N) to visit each node once.
📦 Space: O(W) maximum width of the tree (can be up to N/2 nodes).
slides.analogy: Ripples in a pond expanding outward in perfect concentric circles.
slides.transition: How does the level-boundary size snapshot work?

slides.headline: 🚀 The Level-Boundary Snapshot
slides.body:
The core breakthrough is locking the queue size:

✅ Read `size = q.size()` at the start of each outer loop.
✅ Use a nested loop to pop exactly `size` elements.

This keeps child nodes queued during this step safely insulated in the back of the queue, making level boundaries crystal clear.
slides.goldenLine: Lock the row count before you begin popping, so future layers don't bleed into the present.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this snapshot approach.

slides.headline: 🎬 Level-Order Dry Run
steps: Queue root [1]. q = [1].
Level 0: size = 1. Pop [1], push to level vector. Push children [2], [3]. q = [2, 3]. res = [[1]].
Level 1: size = 2. Loop i = 0 to 1.
Pop [2], push to level. Push children [4], [5]. q = [3, 4, 5].
slides.keyObservation: Even though [4] and [5] were pushed while processing [2], they were not popped in Level 1 because the boundary size was locked to 2.
slides.transition: Let's split the code into beautiful chunks.

slides.headline: 🔍 Why BFS Memory Differs from DFS
slides.body:
Why does BFS consume more memory on balanced trees?

✅ In a balanced tree of depth D, the leaf level contains N/2 nodes.
✅ BFS queue stores the entire leaf level at once, taking O(N) space.
✅ DFS only stores one branch path, taking O(log N) space.

⚠️ The Trap:
Forgetting to handle the empty/NULL root check, which immediately triggers a crash when accessing queue front on an empty structure.
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'Can you implement Level Order Traversal using recursion?' Answer: Yes, using DFS with a depth index, appending nodes to matching vector indexes.
slides.transition: Let's review the code across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Base Case: If root is NULL, return empty vector.
Create a queue `queue<TreeNode*>` and enqueue root.
While queue is not empty: read `size = q.size()`.
slides.mentalCompression: Queue the root. Lock size, pop size elements, enqueue children, repeat.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Evaluating `q.size()` directly inside the loop condition instead of storing it beforehand.
Forgetting to push children to the queue.

revisionCards.title: Vertical Order Traversal
revisionCards.explanation: Traverse a binary tree vertically. Nodes are grouped by columns and rows; overlapping nodes must be sorted by value.

slides.headline: ⚡ Vertical Order Traversal
slides.body:
How do you group tree nodes into vertical columns, sorting them from left to right, top to bottom?

And what if two nodes overlap in the exact same col and row? They must be sorted by value!

🎯 The real challenge:
Combining horizontal columns, vertical rows, and value sorting into a unified data structure.
slides.visualCue: A vertical grid mapping tree nodes onto 2D coordinate blocks.
slides.memoryHook: 3D Coordinates: Column -> Row -> Sorted Values.
slides.transition: When should we invoke this powerful 3D coordinates map?

slides.headline: 🧠 Column-Row Sort Trigger
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Grid-based tree mapping
✅ Precise top-to-bottom vertical column alignment
✅ Custom tie-breaking rules for overlapping tree nodes

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires vertical column groupings where top-to-bottom and value sorting constraints co-exist, think Column-Row-Value nested mapping.
slides.transition: Let's review why basic BFS is insufficient for overlapping nodes.

slides.headline: 📦 The Overlap Conundrum
slides.body:
Basic vertical traversal only tracks columns. But to handle overlaps cleanly:

1. Track both column and row coordinates for every node.
2. Store coordinates in a structure that sorts columns first, then rows second, then node values third.

⏱️ Time: O(N log N) due to map and multiset sorting overhead.
📦 Space: O(N) to store node coordinates.
slides.analogy: Organizing spreadsheet files: folder by column, subfolder by row, and files alphabetically by name.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the ultimate nested map breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The 3D Coordinate Engine
slides.body:
Unlock the power of nested STL maps:

✅ `map<col, map<row, multiset<val>>>`
✅ Columns sort naturally from left to right.
✅ Rows sort naturally from top to bottom.
✅ `multiset` handles duplicate values in sorted order.

This structures the coordinates to automatically handle sorting as we traverse the tree.
slides.goldenLine: Let the map hierarchy handle the complex sorting rules for you.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this nested coordinate tracking.

slides.headline: 🎬 Coordinate Dry Run
steps: Root [1] at (col 0, row 0). map[0][0] = {1}.
Queue left [2] at (-1, 1), right [3] at (1, 1).
slides.keyObservation: Nodes [5] and [6] overlapped at (col 0, row 2) and were correctly sorted by value inside the multiset.
slides.transition: Let's check the code split across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Multiset is Crucial
slides.body:
Why use `std::multiset` instead of `std::vector`?

✅ A standard `set` deletes duplicates. If the tree contains two nodes with value `5` at the same spot, a `set` would erase one.
✅ `multiset` preserves duplicates while keeping them perfectly sorted.

⚠️ The Trap:
Failing to coordinate left and right children updates correctly (`col - 1` vs `col + 1` and `row + 1`).
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'How do you avoid using a complex nested map?' Answer: Collect all nodes in a flat vector of custom structs `(col, row, val)` and write a custom 3-parameter comparator, sorting in O(N log N) at the end.
slides.transition: Let's review the code across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Define the nested coordinate map structure.
Initialize BFS queue tracking pairs of `(TreeNode*, pair<col, row>)`.
Enqueue root at coordinate (0, 0).
slides.mentalCompression: Track (col, row) coordinates during BFS. Let nested maps + multisets sort columns, rows, and values.

slides.body: Part 1: Running BFS using a queue to populate our nested coordinate maps.

slides.body: Project each node on a 2D coordinate grid, and let the C++ ordered map hierarchy sort columns, rows, and overlapping values.
slides.memoryHook: Map columns -> Map rows -> Sorted multisets.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Using a standard `set` instead of `multiset`, which deduplicates same-value nodes.
Confusing row additions (decrementing row instead of incrementing bottom-up).
interviewerQuestions: How would you change this to only return the Left View?
Can we implement this with a single DFS pass instead of BFS?

recall.30sec: Queue carries `(col, row)`. Left is `col-1, row+1`, right is `col+1, row+1`. Store in nested map. Time O(N log N), Space O(N).
recall.1min: Multiset resolves overlaps by keeping duplicate values sorted. Iterate through maps to build the final list of columns.

slides.body: Elite candidates instantly realize why standard BFS level indices are not enough (overlap conditions require strict coordinate tracking). They explain the difference between sorting via nested maps vs flat vectors with custom lambda comparators, showing complete mastery of C++ STL structures.
slides.closingLine: When order is multi-dimensional, a structured map holds the universe in place.

revisionCards.title: Root to Node Path
revisionCards.explanation: Find the sequence of node values forming the path from the root node to a target node in a binary tree.

slides.headline: ⚡ Root to Node Path
slides.body:
How do you trace the exact trail of branches leading from the root of a tree directly to a target node?

You must explore paths recursively, keeping a diary of the journey and erasing missteps.

🎯 The real challenge:
Efficiently backtracking to remove incorrect subtrees from your path vector without copying arrays.
slides.visualCue: A glowing red line tracing a path down a tree, backtracking where it hits a dead end.
slides.memoryHook: DFS Backtracking: Push on entry, pop on dead end.
slides.transition: When is tracing this path useful in interview scenarios?

slides.headline: 🧠 Trail Tracing Trigger
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Need the exact list of nodes from the top to a target
✅ Finding the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) via path comparison
✅ Distance between two nodes query

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires recording the route from root to leaf or target and requires backtracking from dead-ends, think DFS Boolean Path-Accumulator.
slides.transition: Let's review the sub-optimal brute-force way.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Path Copying
slides.body:
A sub-optimal approach returns paths at each level:

1. Let recursive functions return a full array of the current path.
2. Copy the array when passing it up or merging it.

⏱️ Time: O(N * H) due to copying vectors repeatedly.
📦 Space: O(H^2) array clones.

This is highly slow! We can do it in linear time by passing a single vector by reference.
slides.analogy: Taking a photocopy of your entire journal every time you turn a corner in a maze.
slides.transition: How do we implement the optimal boolean backtracking engine?

slides.headline: 🚀 The Boolean Backtracker
slides.body:
Use a single vector passed by reference combined with a boolean return:

✅ Push current node: `path.push_back(root->val)`.
✅ If node is target: return `true` immediately!
✅ Recurse Left and Right. If either returns `true`, propagate `true` up.
✅ If both return `false`, we popped: `path.pop_back()` and return `false`.

This keeps memory copying to exactly zero, maintaining a single active path.
slides.goldenLine: If the path ahead leads to a dead end, erase your footprints.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this backtracking engine.

slides.headline: 🎬 Backtracking Dry Run
steps: Start at root [1]. Push [1] to path. path = [1].
Call getPath(1.left) to arrive at [2]. Push [2] to path. path = [1, 2].
Check [2] != target. Call getPath(2.left) and getPath(2.right) -> both NULL (return false).
Backtrack at [2]: Pop [2] from path. path = [1]. Return false.
slides.keyObservation: Node [2] was temporarily added but successfully erased once it was identified as a dead end.
slides.transition: Let's check the deep reasoning behind passing by reference.

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Reference Vectors Excel
slides.body:
Why is a reference vector with boolean return optimal?

✅ Only one vector is allocated in memory.
✅ Pop operations are O(1) constant time.
✅ Boolean returns short-circuit immediately once target is found, avoiding exploring remaining branches.

⚠️ The Trap:
Forgetting to pop the node when returning false, which leaves dead-end nodes inside the final path vector.
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'How would you find the path between two arbitrary nodes?' Answer: Generate root-to-node path for both, then find the last common node in their paths (LCA) and concatenate.
slides.transition: Let's review the clean algorithm blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Base Case: If root is NULL, return false.
Action: Push current node's value to the reference path vector.
Check: If `root->val == target`, return true.
slides.mentalCompression: Push node, check target, explore subtrees, pop node on failure.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Clean recursive backtracking in C++ using a single reference vector.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Keep a single active path trail. If you reach a dead end, reel the line back by one node.
slides.memoryHook: Trace and erase: push deep, pop on defeat.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to backtrack (pop_back) when returning false.
Passing the vector by value, turning a linear algorithm into O(N^2) memory copier.
interviewerQuestions: What is the space complexity of this approach in worst vs best cases?
How can this be adapted to find all root-to-leaf paths?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: DFS push, check, pop if false.
recall.30sec: Push current node to path. If target, return true. If left/right DFS is true, return true. Otherwise pop and return false. Time O(N), Space O(H).
recall.1min: Pass vector by reference to avoid copies. Boolean return ensures we halt exploration immediately on success.

patternConnections: All Paths from Source to Target

slides.headline: 🏆 Showcasing Mastery
slides.body: Elite candidates don't just solve the path retrieval. They demonstrate how passing vectors by reference achieves O(H) space, discuss immediate short-circuiting on success, and describe how this forms the foundation for solving the Lowest Common Ancestor problem in linear time.
slides.closingLine: Every wrong path taken is progress, as long as you erase the error.

revisionCards.title: Maximum Width of Binary Tree
revisionCards.explanation: Calculate the maximum width of a binary tree, defined as the maximum number of nodes between end-points per level (including null nodes).

slides.headline: ⚡ Maximum Width of Binary Tree
slides.body:
What is the maximum span of a binary tree across all its horizontal levels?

The width is the number of nodes between the leftmost and rightmost non-NULL nodes, including intermediate NULL nodes!

🎯 The real challenge:
Representing indices of nodes mathematically to handle gaps without storing actual NULL elements.
slides.visualCue: A tree diagram with node indexes marked, highlighting the widest horizontal level span.
slides.memoryHook: Heap Indexing: Left = 2*i, Right = 2*i + 1.
slides.transition: What indexing rules let us map tree gaps mathematically?

slides.headline: 🧠 Gap-Inclusive Width Trigger
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Measuring span of horizontal levels inclusive of empty spots
✅ Heap-like array indexing in tree structures
✅ Coordinate distance tracking per level

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires calculating width or distance between extreme boundary nodes at each depth level, think Heap Indexing with dynamic column tracking.
slides.transition: Why does storing NULL nodes in BFS fail?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force NULL Insertion
slides.body:
The direct approach is to queue all actual and null nodes:

1. Do a standard BFS.
2. Queue dummy NULL nodes to represent gaps.

⏱️ Time: O(2^H) where H is the height of the tree.
📦 Space: O(2^H) memory.

For deep, skewed trees, this causes an instant Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error! We must index nodes mathematically instead.
slides.analogy: Measuring a parking lot's span by parking empty cars in empty slots instead of just checking the row number of the first and last car.
slides.transition: How do we use heap indexing to solve this optimally?

slides.headline: 🚀 Heap-Index Math Breakthrough
slides.body:
Represent the tree as a binary heap array:

✅ If parent index is `i`, Left child is `2*i`, Right child is `2*i + 1`.
✅ Level width is simply: `last_index - first_index + 1`.

⚠️ Integer Overflow Remedy:
Subtract the level's minimum index `first` from each node's index `idx` (`cur_idx = idx - first`) before calculating children coordinates. This keeps indexes small, preventing 64-bit overflow!
slides.goldenLine: Normalize indices at the start of each level to reset the coordinate origin.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this overflow-proof index math.

slides.headline: 🎬 Heap-Index Dry Run
steps: Root [1] at index 0. q = [(1, 0)].
Level 0: first = 0, last = 0. Width = 0 - 0 + 1 = 1. cur_idx = 0. Queue pushes [(3, 0), (2, 1)].
Level 1: first = 0, last = 1. Width = 1 - 0 + 1 = 2.
Process (3, 0): normalized = 0 - 0 = 0. Push left [(5, 2*0) = (5, 0)].
slides.keyObservation: Normalizing index of [2] to 1 ensured that child [9] was indexed at 3, correctly capturing the 2 missing NULL slots between [5] and [9] without storing them.
slides.transition: Let's check the code split across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Normalization Prevents Overflow
slides.body:
Why is normalization mandatory?

✅ At level 30, indices can reach `2^30` (over 1 billion).
✅ In skewed or sparse trees, indices grow exponentially and overflow even a `long long` variable.
✅ By subtracting the first node's index on each level, we reset the baseline to `0`, ensuring coordinate numbers only span the maximum active width of that level.

This guarantees safe math without any extra memory.
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'Why do we use `idx - first` rather than just letting it overflow?' Explain that signed integer overflow is undefined behavior in C++, while unsigned overflow can lead to incorrect width calculations.
slides.transition: Let's review the code across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize `maxWidth = 0`.
Set up BFS queue storing pairs of `(TreeNode*, index)` using `long long`.
Enqueue root at index 0.
slides.mentalCompression: Track level boundaries. Reset parent index to 0, calculate children at 2*i and 2*i+1.

slides.body: Part 1: Running level order BFS and indexing nodes dynamically while capturing width metrics.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: BFS with heap coordinate indexes, subtracting the level's minimum coordinate at each row to keep indexes small.
slides.memoryHook: Heap indexes, normalized row-by-row.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Failing to normalize parent index, leading to early integer overflow on deep paths.
Using standard integer (`int`) which overflows after only 31 levels.
interviewerQuestions: What is the maximum height a tree can have before even 64-bit indexes overflow?
Can you implement this using recursive DFS?

recall.1min: Heap indexing maps sparse gaps easily. Normalizing prevents coordinate growth. Handles highly skewed layouts cleanly.

slides.body: Elite candidates don't just state the O(N) complexity; they immediately address the integer overflow challenge. They explain *why* subtracting the level's first index prevents signed integer overflows and how this enables the code to run correctly on trees up to 1000 nodes deep.
slides.closingLine: Coordinates are relative; reset your origin and infinity shrinks to zero.

revisionCards.title: Zig-Zag Level Order Traversal
revisionCards.explanation: Perform level order traversal, alternating direction (left-to-right, then right-to-left) at each level.

slides.headline: ⚡ Zig-Zag Level Order
slides.body:
How do you scan a tree in an alternating snake-like pattern: left-to-right, then right-to-left?

You need to traverse level-by-level, but reverse the element order on every second row.

🎯 The real challenge:
Optimizing node insertion to avoid expensive O(N) array reversals at each level boundary.
slides.visualCue: A winding snake-like arrow weaving through horizontal levels of a binary tree.
slides.memoryHook: Zig-Zag BFS: Alternate array index filling or push directions.
slides.transition: When does an interviewer expect you to write a clean Zig-Zag BFS?

slides.headline: 🧠 Alternating Level Trigger
slides.body:
Spot the patterns instantly:

✅ Level-by-level grouping with alternating traversal direction
✅ Spiral or snake-like scanning pattern in grids/trees
✅ Directional alternation queries

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires compiling levels where odd levels go left-to-right and even levels go right-to-left, think Alternated Index BFS.
slides.transition: Let's look at the slow brute-force reversal approach.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Level Reversal
slides.body:
The direct approach uses standard BFS and reverses vectors:

1. Do a standard level order traversal.
2. For every alternate level, reverse the compiled row vector.

⏱️ Time: O(N) but requires traversing each row multiple times.
📦 Space: O(N) to store level outputs.

Reversing arrays is slow and inefficient. We can fill the level array directly in the correct order!
slides.analogy: Writing a sentence backwards by writing it left-to-right first and then erasing and re-writing it letter-by-letter.
slides.transition: How do we implement direct, zero-reversal array indexing?

slides.headline: 🚀 Direct Alternated Indexing
slides.body:
Eliminate O(N) reversals using pre-allocated arrays and index calculations:

✅ Pre-allocate row vector size: `vector<int> level(size)`.
✅ Maintain a boolean flag `leftToRight`.
✅ If `leftToRight == true`, fill from the front: `idx = i`.
✅ If `leftToRight == false`, fill from the back: `idx = size - 1 - i`.

This structures the array perfectly in O(1) per node!
slides.goldenLine: Calculate the landing spot of each node before you place it, avoiding reversals.
slides.transition: Let's dry run this zero-reversal indexing.

slides.headline: 🎬 Zig-Zag Dry Run
steps: Queue root [1]. q = [1], leftToRight = true.
Level 0: size = 1. Pop [1]. Since leftToRight, level[0] = 1. Queue [2, 3]. res = [[1]]. Toggle flag: leftToRight = false.
Level 1: size = 2. level = [_, _]. Pop [2]. Since !leftToRight, level[2-1-0 = 1] = 2. Queue [4, 5].
Pop [3]. Since !leftToRight, level[2-1-1 = 0] = 3. Queue [6, 7]. level = [3, 2]. res = [[1], [3, 2]]. Toggle: leftToRight = true.
slides.keyObservation: By writing to calculated indexes, the second level [3, 2] was created in perfect order without any post-processing.
slides.transition: Let's review the C++ code split across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🔍 Why Direct Insertion Wins
slides.body:
Why is direct index mapping superior?

✅ Avoids memory reallocations during `vector::insert` or reversals.
✅ Maintains strict queue FIFO sequence, keeping tree traversal logic simple.
✅ Flag toggle is extremely fast and simple.

⚠️ The Trap:
Using standard vector `push_back` and then trying to insert at the front of a std::vector, which is a slow O(N) shifting operation.
slides.interviewerTrap: Interviewer asks: 'Can we solve this using two stacks instead of a queue?' Yes! Two stacks naturally reverse order when popped, allowing you to alternate push orders to achieve zig-zag.
slides.transition: Let's review the code across the next two slides.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Base Case: If root is NULL, return empty array.
Set up standard queue, enqueue root, set `leftToRight = true`.
While queue is not empty: read level `size`.
slides.mentalCompression: Maintain queue. Pre-allocate level array, fill from front or back using a toggle flag, toggle flag.
slides.transition: Let's check the first part of the C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Part 1: Running level BFS and pre-allocating the level vector for calculated indexing.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Perform standard queue BFS, but fill pre-allocated level arrays from left-to-right or right-to-left using a toggle flag.
slides.memoryHook: Pre-allocate level size, fill index dynamically.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Not initializing the level vector with a fixed size before using index assignment.
Using slow vector inserts at the front, turning BFS into an O(N^2) operation.
interviewerQuestions: Can you implement this iteratively using two stacks?
How would you change this to only collect leaf nodes in a zig-zag order?
