slides.closingLine: Reversing edges is the lens that highlights hidden circular loops.

revisionCards.title: Maximum Product Subarray
revisionCards.explanation: Find the contiguous subarray within a 1D numerical array that has the largest product.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Find the contiguous subarray that maximizes the product of its numbers.

Unlike sum-based subarrays where numbers are either positive or negative, products can swing wildly. A single negative number turns a huge positive product into a deep negative, but another negative can instantly multiply it into a monumental positive!

🎯 The puzzle:
How do we track these sudden polar flips without recalculating everything from scratch?
slides.visualCue: A path of numbers with positive and negative signs, where a double negative acts like an explosive multiplier.
slides.memoryHook: A negative value is a magnifying mirror that swaps wealth and debt.
slides.transition: Let's see the triggers to identify this pattern instantly in interviews.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Problem asks for a contiguous subset (subarray) maximizing product
✅ The elements include negative integers, meaning double negatives yield positives
✅ Swapping extreme states (min becomes max, max becomes min)

💡 Interview Signal:
When current choices depend on two polar opposite extremes (highest positive and lowest negative), think Min-Max Dual DP.
slides.transition: How does a naive approach try to tackle this?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive way:

Compute the product of every possible subarray using nested loops.
- Loop starting index i from 0 to n-1.
- Loop ending index j from i to n-1 and maintain a running product.

⏱️ Time: O(N²)
📦 Space: O(1)

Extremely slow for large arrays. We can do it in a single linear pass!
slides.analogy: Calculating every pair of products is like checking every path in a maze instead of following the coordinates.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the optimal linear time breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Use the dual-tracking mechanism:

✅ Maintain two running values: maxProd (largest positive product) and minProd (smallest negative product) up to the current index.
✅ When encountering a negative number, maxProd and minProd swap roles before updating!

This completely bypasses redundant subarray searches by utilizing simple state transitions.
slides.goldenLine: A negative magnifier turns your largest debt into your greatest fortune.
slides.transition: Let's simulate this polar swap step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Init: res = 2, maxProd = 2, minProd = 2
Index 1 (val=3): maxProd = max(3, 6) = 6. minProd = min(3, 6) = 3. res = 6.
Index 2 (val=-2): Negative! Swap maxProd & minProd: maxProd becomes 3, minProd becomes 6. Then: maxProd = max(-2, -6) = -2. minProd = min(-2, -12) = -12. res remains 6.
Index 3 (val=4): maxProd = max(4, -8) = 4. minProd = min(4, -48) = -48. res remains 6.
slides.keyObservation: Swapping the products on negative elements instantly kept the negative multiplier correct without extra loops.
slides.transition: Why is tracking the minimum product mathematically correct?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why It Works
slides.body:
At any index i, the maximum product ending here must be one of:
- The number itself (starting a new subarray)
- The number multiplied by the previous maxProd
- The number multiplied by the previous minProd (in case of a negative times a negative)

By tracking both extremes, we guarantee no potential product is missed, regardless of signs.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by only tracking the maximum product, missing the double negative swap entirely.
slides.transition: Let's look at the implementation blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize res, maxProd, and minProd with the first element of the array.
Iterate through the array starting from index 1.
If the current number is negative, swap maxProd and minProd.
slides.mentalCompression: Iterate and swap min/max on negative; keep updating global best.
slides.transition: Let's check the ultra-clean C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal O(N) Time and O(1) Space C++ Implementation.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: A double negative creates a massive positive, so keep tracking both maximum gains and minimum losses and swap them on negative values.
slides.memoryHook: Polar Swap on Negatives.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Not handling zero properly, which resets the product to zero
Only tracking maxProd and ignoring minProd
interviewerQuestions: How would you modify this to return the actual subarray?
How do we handle decimal fractions in the array?

recall.5sec: Track minProd and maxProd, swap them on negative numbers.
recall.30sec: Iterate once. If nums[i] < 0, swap maxProd and minProd. Update both with max/min of nums[i] and product.
recall.1min: Optimal O(N) time and O(1) space Dynamic Programming algorithm that avoids O(N^2) subarray products.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates point out immediately that standard Kadane's algorithm doesn't work directly due to signs. They discuss handling of zeros and suggest checking for potential integer overflows upfront, showing real production-level awareness.
slides.closingLine: Dual-tracking is the key to mastering sign-sensitive array patterns.

revisionCards.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
revisionCards.explanation: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence in an array.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Find the length of the longest subsequence in an array such that all elements are strictly increasing.

Subsequences do not need to be contiguous! They can skip elements as they march forward.

🎯 The real challenge:
How do we choose which numbers to keep and which to skip without checking all 2^N combinations?
slides.visualCue: A series of heights where you want to build the longest set of upward stepping stones.
slides.memoryHook: Stepping stones that only go up.
slides.transition: Let's look at the triggers to identify LIS pattern instantly in interviews.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Ordered elements where order must be preserved, but elements can be skipped
✅ Strict relationship like increasing, nested boxes, or non-overlapping intervals
✅ Finding longest chain of decisions

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever elements can be chained in a strictly increasing sequence, think LIS DP.
slides.transition: How does a standard O(N^2) DP approach look?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive O(N^2) DP approach:

Define dp[i] as the LIS length ending at index i.
For each element at i, look back at all elements j < i and if nums[i] > nums[j], update dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1).

⏱️ Time: O(N²)
📦 Space: O(N)

We can optimize this to O(N log N) using a smart Patience Sorting technique!
slides.analogy: Checking all previous elements is like looking back at every step you took to decide the next, instead of just keeping track of your best boundaries.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the O(N log N) patience sorting breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Use the patience sorting/binary search strategy:

✅ Maintain an active list tails where tails[i] stores the smallest tail of all increasing subsequences of length i+1.
✅ For each number x, use binary search (lower_bound) to find its insertion point in tails.
✅ Replace the element or extend the list.

This dramatically compresses the search from O(N) to O(log N) for each element!
slides.goldenLine: Replacing elements in-place dynamically constructs the boundaries of all valid subsequences.
slides.transition: Let's simulate this active list step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Init: tails = []
Process 10: tails becomes [10]
Process 9: 9 <= 10, replaces 10. tails becomes [9]
Process 2: 2 <= 9, replaces 9. tails becomes [2]
slides.keyObservation: The tails array might not represent the actual LIS path (e.g. [2,3,7,18]), but its length is mathematically guaranteed to be correct!
slides.transition: Why is this replacement correct?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why It Works
slides.body:
By replacing tails[i] with a smaller element x, we increase the chances of extending this subsequence in the future with smaller numbers.

This is a greedy optimization layered on top of dynamic programming: we keep the smallest possible end element for every subsequence length.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by trying to build the actual LIS instead of tracking the tail boundaries.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create an empty array tails.
For each element x in nums, find the first element in tails that is >= x using binary search.
If no such element exists, append x to tails.
slides.mentalCompression: For each number, binary search to update tails in-place. Size of tails is the answer.
slides.transition: Let's look at the ultra-clean C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Highly optimized O(N log N) Time and O(N) Space C++ Implementation using std::lower_bound.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Think of stacking playing cards into piles: always place a card on the first pile it can fit on top of, or start a new pile.
slides.memoryHook: Piles of Patience Sorting.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Using upper_bound instead of lower_bound (which fails strictly increasing criteria)
Thinking the tails array holds the actual LIS sequence at the end
interviewerQuestions: How do you print the actual LIS?
Can we use this method for non-decreasing subsequences (use upper_bound)?

recall.5sec: Binary search insertion points in a tails array to get length in O(N log N).
recall.30sec: Iterate numbers. Use lower_bound to find placement in tails vector. Replace or append. Returns tails.size().
recall.1min: O(N log N) solution based on Patience Sorting that maintains optimal endings for subsequences of each length.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates immediately explain Patience Sorting and distinguish between O(N^2) DP and O(N log N) Binary Search. They also proactively explain why the tails array is not the actual LIS path but shares its length.
slides.closingLine: Patience sorting turns a quadratic search into logarithmic elegance.

revisionCards.title: Longest Common Subsequence
revisionCards.explanation: Find the length of the longest subsequence common to two strings.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given two strings, find the length of their longest common subsequence (LCS).

A subsequence is a sequence that appears in the same relative order, but not necessarily contiguously.

🎯 The challenge:
Aligning two sequences containing insertions, deletions, and substitutions to find the longest matching path.
slides.visualCue: Two strings side-by-side with lines connecting matching letters in the same relative order.
slides.memoryHook: Diagonal matches step forward, mismatches split paths.
slides.transition: Let's see the triggers to identify LCS patterns instantly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Comparing two strings/sequences
✅ Finding a shared pattern where elements can be skipped
✅ Minimizing character insertions/deletions to align them

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you need to match two sequences and are allowed to skip elements, think LCS 2D Grid DP.
slides.transition: What is the intuition behind the bottom-up table?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

For each character, either we match them (if equal) or try skipping a character from text1 or text2 recursively.

⏱️ Time: O(2^(M+N)) due to double branching
📦 Space: O(M+N) call stack

Bottom-up dynamic programming stores the solutions to subproblems to avoid this exponential explosion!
slides.analogy: Trying every combination of character alignment is like comparing two books letter-by-letter in every possible shift instead of highlighting matching sentences.
slides.transition: Let's look at the optimal 1D space DP breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
We use a 1D DP array instead of a 2D matrix:

✅ Since dp[i][j] only depends on dp[i-1][j-1] (previous diagonal) and dp[i-1][j] (directly above), we can compress space to O(N) by keeping a single row!
✅ Maintain a prev variable to store the diagonal value before it gets overwritten.

This yields O(M * N) time while reducing memory to O(N) space!
slides.goldenLine: A single row of memory is all that is needed to carry the history of string alignments.
slides.transition: Let's watch this dynamic space update step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Strings: t1 = 'abcde', t2 = 'ace'
Row 1 ('a'): Matches 'a', dp becomes [0, 1, 1, 1]
Row 2 ('b'): No match, dp remains [0, 1, 1, 1]
Row 3 ('c'): Matches 'c', dp becomes [0, 1, 2, 2] (prev diagonal was 1, so 1+1=2)
slides.keyObservation: Saving the cell state before updating allowed us to perfectly simulate a 2D diagonal transition inside a 1D array.
slides.transition: Why is the diagonal transition correct?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why It Works
slides.body:
The recurrence relations are mathematically elegant:
- If t1[i-1] == t2[j-1]: The characters match! The best answer is 1 + LCS(prefix1, prefix2).
- Otherwise: Mismatch! The best answer is the max of skipping a character from t1 or t2, i.e., max(LCS(i-1, j), LCS(i, j-1)).

This simple choice guarantees global optimality.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail to optimize space from O(N*M) to O(min(N,M)), which is highly valued in elite loops.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize dp vector of size t2.size() + 1 with 0.
Outer loop through t1 from index 1.
Set prev to 0 (represents dp[i-1][0]).
slides.mentalCompression: Loop both strings. If chars match: diagonal + 1. Else: max of left and top. Compress to 1D array.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the clean, compressed C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Space-Optimized O(N) Space and O(M*N) Time LCS Implementation.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Diagonal match steps forward by 1, while a mismatch inherits the best of its immediate left and top neighbors.
slides.memoryHook: Match? Diagonal + 1. Mismatch? Left vs Top.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to store the diagonal value in a temp variable before overwriting
Off-by-one errors due to mismatch between 0-based string indexing and 1-based DP indexing
interviewerQuestions: How do we reconstruct the actual LCS string using O(min(N,M)) space?
How does this relate to Edit Distance?

recall.5sec: If match: diagonal + 1. If mismatch: max(left, top).
recall.30sec: Bottom-up 1D DP table. Loop strings. Maintain a running prev to store the top-left diagonal cell. Update cell in-place.
recall.1min: O(N) space and O(M*N) time bottom-up dynamic programming approach that eliminates full 2D table footprint.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates always start by mentioning space complexity optimizations. They proactively suggest that if string lengths differ significantly, passing the shorter string as the inner loop parameter reduces space to O(min(M, N)).
slides.closingLine: Elegant space compression shows true mastery of state variables.

revisionCards.title: 0-1 Knapsack Problem
revisionCards.explanation: Find the maximum value possible by filling a knapsack of capacity W with complete items.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
You have a knapsack of capacity W and n items, each with a weight and a value.

You must decide whether to pack each item entirely (1) or leave it (0) to maximize total value without exceeding capacity.

🎯 The real challenge:
Every item we pack consumes capacity, blocking future high-value items. How do we balance this trade-off optimally?
slides.visualCue: A knapsack with weight constraints and items of varying shapes (weight) and colors (value).
slides.memoryHook: Take it or leave it, scanning backwards.
slides.transition: Let's check the triggers that identify 0-1 Knapsack instantly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Decision to include or exclude elements with constraint limits
✅ Subsets of items that sum up to or under a target weight/capacity
✅ No fractional parts allowed (unlike Fractional Knapsack, which is Greedy)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you are picking items under a constraint and can't use fractions or reuse items, think 0-1 Knapsack 1D Backwards DP.
slides.transition: Why is the brute force recursion highly sub-optimal?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

Try all subsets of items. For each item, branch into two paths: either take it (if weight allows) or skip it. Return the maximum.

⏱️ Time: O(2^N) due to binary branching
📦 Space: O(N) stack depth

Bottom-up tabulation caches values to resolve this in pseudo-polynomial time.
slides.analogy: Trying every subset is like packing every possible bag combinations from scratch, instead of just checking if replacing one item with another adds value.
slides.transition: Let's see the 1D space optimization breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Use 1D space-optimized DP:

✅ Maintain a 1D array dp of size W + 1, where dp[w] is the maximum value for capacity w.
✅ Update the dp array backwards from W to wt[i]!

This prevents using the same item twice: since we calculate from right to left, dp[w - wt[i]] still holds the state of the previous items, not the current one!
slides.goldenLine: Scanning backwards preserves history, locking each item into a single choice.
slides.transition: Let's watch this backward sweep step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Setup: W=4, wt=[1, 2, 3], val=[6, 10, 12]. dp size 5 initialized to 0.
Item 0 (wt=1, val=6): Sweep backwards: dp[4]=max(0, 6+dp[3])=6... dp becomes [0, 6, 6, 6, 6]
Item 1 (wt=2, val=10): Sweep backwards from 4 to 2: dp[4]=max(6, 10+dp[2])=16. dp[3]=max(6, 10+dp[1])=16. dp[2]=max(6, 10+dp[0])=10. dp becomes [0, 6, 10, 16, 16]
Item 2 (wt=3, val=12): Sweep backwards from 4 to 3: dp[4]=max(16, 12+dp[1])=18. dp[3]=max(16, 12+dp[0])=16. dp becomes [0, 6, 10, 16, 18]
slides.keyObservation: Updating the array from right to left made it impossible for an item to compound its own weight.
slides.transition: Why does the backward loop prevent double usage?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Backward Sweep Secret
slides.body:
In 2D DP, dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], val[i] + dp[i-1][w-wt[i]]).
Notice both terms on the right come from row i-1 (the previous item).

If we update a 1D array forwards, dp[w-wt[i]] would have already been updated with item i, causing unbounded duplicates. Updating backwards ensures dp[w-wt[i]] is still purely from row i-1.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by looping weights forwards, converting 0-1 Knapsack into Unbounded Knapsack.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize dp vector of size W + 1 with 0.
Loop through items from 0 to n-1.
For each item, loop weight w backwards from W down to wt[i].
slides.mentalCompression: 1D DP of size W+1. Inner weight loop runs backwards to prevent item re-use.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Space-Optimized O(W) Space and O(N*W) Time C++ Solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Store values in a 1D array, and update from right to left so each item decision is based on undisturbed previous states.
slides.memoryHook: Right-to-Left locks the choice.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Looping weight forward, which permits item reuse
Off-by-one errors on indices when matching weights and values
interviewerQuestions: What is the difference between 0-1 Knapsack and Unbounded Knapsack?
Why is this algorithm classified as pseudo-polynomial?

recall.5sec: Loop backwards: dp[w] = max(dp[w], val[i] + dp[w-wt[i]]).
recall.30sec: Maintain O(W) DP array. Iterate items. Update weights backwards to secure 0-1 selection semantics.
recall.1min: O(N * W) time and O(W) space pseudo-polynomial dynamic programming solution for subset constraint optimization.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates highlight that 0-1 Knapsack is NP-Complete, and the DP solution runs in O(N * W) which is pseudo-polynomial. They explain clearly why the backward sweep is mathematically required to collapse the 2D state into 1D.
slides.closingLine: Understanding the direction of state dependency is the mark of a senior engineer.

revisionCards.title: Edit Distance
revisionCards.explanation: Find the minimum operations (insert, delete, replace) required to convert word1 to word2.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given two words word1 and word2, find the minimum number of operations required to convert word1 to word2.

You have three allowed operations:
- Insert a character
- Delete a character
- Replace a character

🎯 The real challenge:
Finding the cheapest sequence of edits across all possible alignment permutations.
slides.visualCue: A letters grid aligning 'horse' to 'ros' with color-coded arrows showing insert, delete, and replace operations.
slides.memoryHook: Three branches of choice on character mismatch.
slides.transition: Let's identify the interview signals for Edit Distance.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Transforming one string into another string
✅ Allowed operations are Insert, Delete, Replace
✅ Looking for minimum operations or distance metric

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever you are computing similarity metrics or alignment steps between two sequences, think Edit Distance (Levenshtein) DP.
slides.transition: Let's review the sub-optimal brute force before looking at the grid.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

Compare characters from the end. If they match, step back. Otherwise, explore all three choices: Insert, Delete, or Replace recursively.

⏱️ Time: O(3^(M+N)) due to three-way branching
📦 Space: O(M+N) recursion stack

This brute-force search is extremely slow. We can cache intermediate results in a 2D table!
slides.analogy: Trying every mutation sequence randomly is like throwing letters at a word until it matches, instead of fixing errors character by character.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant bottom-up grid optimization.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Use bottom-up 2D Dynamic Programming:

✅ Define dp[i][j] as the minimum edits to convert prefix word1[0...i-1] to word2[0...j-1].
✅ Base Cases: Empty string conversions: dp[i][0] = i (i deletes) and dp[0][j] = j (j inserts).
✅ Transitions: If matching, inherit diagonal dp[i-1][j-1]. Else, take 1 + min of Insert, Delete, and Replace.

This structures the search into an elegant, structured table calculation!
slides.goldenLine: The minimum path in our grid represents the most efficient alignment history.
slides.transition: Let's trace this step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Compare 'cat' and 'cut'. dp matrix is initialized with base distances.
Row 2 ('a'): mismatches 'u'. min(Delete(dp[1][2]), Insert(dp[2][1]), Replace(dp[1][1])) + 1 = 1.
slides.keyObservation: Initializing borders correctly with increasing indices handles empty string base states automatically.
slides.transition: Why do the three terms correspond to insert, delete, and replace?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Operations Unveiled
slides.body:
Let's analyze the mismatch transitions:
- dp[i-1][j] + 1 (Delete): Removing a char from word1 to match word2.
- dp[i][j-1] + 1 (Insert): Adding a char to word1 (which matches current word2 char).
- dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 (Replace): Changing current char to match word2 char.

Taking the minimum of these choices guarantees correctness.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by not understanding which neighbor represents which operation, or by making index off-by-one errors.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize dp matrix of size (m+1) x (n+1).
Fill first column dp[i][0] = i and first row dp[0][j] = j.
Loop through both strings from index 1.
slides.mentalCompression: Grid DP. Base cases are index counts. Mismatch? Take 1 + min of left, top, diagonal.
slides.transition: Let's check the clean C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Highly clean C++ Implementation of 2D bottom-up Edit Distance.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Draw a grid. Initialize borders with step counts. On mismatch, take the best of your left, top, and top-left diagonal neighbors and add 1.
slides.memoryHook: Borders count up, center takes min + 1.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Off-by-one errors due to indexing strings at i-1 and dp at i
Forgetting to initialize first row and column with index values
interviewerQuestions: Can we optimize space to O(N) by keeping only two rows?
How would you support custom operation costs (e.g. replace costs 2, delete costs 1)?

recall.5sec: If match: diagonal. If mismatch: 1 + min(left, top, diagonal).
recall.30sec: Use 2D bottom-up DP. Set boundaries dp[i][0]=i and dp[0][j]=j. Run nested loops over strings and pick minimum of edits.

slides.body: Elite candidates stand out by clearly explaining which DP state corresponds to which edit operation. They also explain how to compress space to O(N) using two rows, and mention applications in spell checkers and DNA alignment.
slides.closingLine: Visualizing string transformations as grid traversals is the key to mastering string DP.

revisionCards.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
revisionCards.explanation: Determine if an array can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sums.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Determine if a given non-empty array of positive integers can be partitioned into two subsets such that the sum of elements in both subsets is equal.

🎯 The core challenge:
Can we find a subset of numbers that sums to exactly half of the total sum of the array? If total sum is odd, partitioning is instantly impossible!
slides.visualCue: An array splitting into two balance scales that perfectly balance their weight sums.
slides.memoryHook: Find a subset summing to half of total sum.
slides.transition: Let's identify the interview signals for Partition Equal Subset Sum.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Dividing an array into two subsets with identical properties
✅ Finding a subset that matches a specific target sum
✅ Unweighted, binary selection decisions (take/leave)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires partitioning into equal halves or matching target weights, think 0-1 Knapsack Target DP.
slides.transition: Why does brute force check fail?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

Calculate the total sum. If odd, return false. Otherwise, target = totalSum / 2.
Try all subset combinations using recursion (for each index, choose to include it in the subset or not) to see if any subset sums to the target.

⏱️ Time: O(2^N)
📦 Space: O(N) stack depth

We can optimize this to O(N * target) using a bottom-up target matching array!
slides.analogy: Checking all possible combinations of subset partitioning is like picking random groups of items hoping they match on a scale, instead of building sums incrementally.
slides.transition: Let's check the 1D space optimization breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
This is a direct adaptation of the Subset Sum Problem:

✅ Target is sum / 2. If sum is odd, return false instantly.
✅ Maintain a boolean 1D array dp where dp[j] represents whether sum j is achievable.
✅ Initialize dp[0] = true and update the array backwards from target down to n for each number n!

This avoids element reuse and resolves the query in simple linear target steps!
slides.goldenLine: Targeting half of the sum turns partitioning into a single subset sum check.
slides.transition: Let's watch the target state updates step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Setup: nums = [1, 5, 11, 5]. Total sum = 22, Target = 11. dp initialized with size 12, dp[0]=true, rest false.
Process 1: dp[1]=dp[1]||dp[0]=true. dp becomes [T, T, F, F, F, F, F, F, F, F, F, F]
Process 5: Update backwards: dp[6]=dp[1]=true, dp[5]=dp[0]=true. dp becomes [T, T, F, F, F, T, T, F, F, F, F, F]
Process 11: dp[11]=dp[0]=true. Target reached! dp[11] is true.
slides.keyObservation: Exiting early or skipping calculations when target becomes achievable boosts performance.
slides.transition: Why does the backward loop prevent element duplication?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why It Works
slides.body:
If we update the 1D array forwards (from n to target), we would use the same number multiple times. For example, if dp[0] is true, dp[n] becomes true, then dp[2n] becomes true in the same step!

Updating backwards ensures each number is processed exactly once, preserving the 0-1 subset rules.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by updating forwards, enabling multiple selections of the same element, which violates the subset partition rules.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Calculate total sum of array.
If sum is odd, return false.
Set target = sum / 2.
slides.mentalCompression: Odd sum? False. Target = Sum/2. Solve Subset Sum with target using backward 1D boolean DP.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Space-Optimized O(Target) Space and O(N*Target) Time C++ Solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: If total sum is odd, it's impossible. Otherwise, try to find a subset that sums up to half the total sum by sliding target states backwards.
slides.memoryHook: Check odd, target half, sweep back.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Forgetting to check if the total sum is odd upfront
Using forward loops which duplicate the same element inside the sum
interviewerQuestions: What is the complexity if target sum is extremely large?
Can we use bitset optimization to speed this up?

recall.5sec: If sum % 2 != 0 return false. Solve subset sum for sum / 2.
recall.30sec: Initialize boolean dp size target+1. Set dp[0]=true. For each number, iterate weights backwards and mark achievable states.
recall.1min: O(N * Target) time and O(Target) space DP algorithm that reduces partitioning into a subset sum check.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates immediately mention bitset optimization. They explain that in C++, std::bitset allows updating all sum states in parallel using bitwise shifts: dp |= (dp << n). This reduces the runtime factor by a constant of 32 or 64!
slides.closingLine: Bitwise updates turn dynamic programming into pure hardware execution.

revisionCards.title: Matrix Chain Multiplication
revisionCards.explanation: Find the most efficient way to multiply a chain of matrices.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given a chain of matrices, find the most efficient way to multiply them.

Multiplying matrices is associative, meaning the grouping (parenthesization) changes the total multiplications required. For example, (A*B)*C can require 10 times fewer operations than A*(B*C)!

🎯 The goal:
Identify the nesting structure that yields the absolute minimum multiplication cost.
slides.visualCue: A chain of matrices with different dimensions being bracketed in different permutations to count math operations.
slides.memoryHook: Split the chain at every index 'k' to find the minimum.
slides.transition: Let's check the triggers that identify Partition DP instantly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Multi-stage grouping or parenthesization problem
✅ Merging adjacent items into one (matrix multiplication, stone merging, balloon bursting)
✅ Optimal split coordinates required to minimize intermediate cost

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires choosing optimal splitting points in a range [i, j], think Matrix Chain / Partition DP.
slides.transition: Let's review the sub-optimal brute force recursion.

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

For a range [i, j], try splitting the chain at every index k from i to j-1.
Recursively calculate the cost of multiplying the left part [i, k], the right part [k+1, j], and merging them: arr[i-1] * arr[k] * arr[j].

⏱️ Time: O(2^N) or exponential
📦 Space: O(N) recursion stack

This leads to massive overlapping calculations. We can solve this with bottom-up range tabulation!
slides.analogy: Evaluating every parenthesization pattern from scratch is like checking every permutation of brackets in an algebraic expression instead of multiplying sub-equations once.
slides.transition: Let's look at the optimal bottom-up range DP breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Bottom-up Range DP:

✅ Define dp[i][j] as the minimum cost to multiply matrices from index i to j.
✅ Loop through lengths of the chain from 2 to N.
✅ Loop through the starting index i, finding the ending index j = i + len - 1.
✅ Check all splitting points k in between, selecting the split that minimizes total cost.

This structures the solution in O(N³) time and O(N²) space!
slides.goldenLine: Building range by range, we solve smaller chains to perfectly bracket the entire sequence.
slides.transition: Let's trace this range building step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Setup: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40] (3 matrices: A1=10x20, A2=20x30, A3=30x40). dp size 4x4.
Length 2 (2 matrices):
slides.keyObservation: Solving smaller matrix chain lengths first is mandatory because larger chains build directly upon their optimal divisions.
slides.transition: Why does the loop structure require outer loop by length?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Range Constraint
slides.body:
In standard grid DP, we iterate row by row or col by col. But in Range DP, dp[i][j] depends on dp[i][k] and dp[k+1][j]. These are sub-problems of smaller lengths!

Therefore, we must solve for smaller lengths first, ensuring when we query dp[i][k] or dp[k+1][j], they are already perfectly computed.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by using standard row/column nested loops instead of length-based range updates.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize dp matrix of size N x N with 0.
Loop through chain length len from 2 to N-1.
Loop through starting index i from 1 to N - len.
slides.mentalCompression: Range DP. Loop by chain length, then start index. Test all split points k in between. Select min cost.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Standard Bottom-up Range Dynamic Programming Implementation.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Define range boundaries, grow the chain length incrementally, and try every splitting index to merge subproblems optimally.
slides.memoryHook: Grow length, split at k.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Incorrect matrix indices: forgetting that matrix i dimension is arr[i-1] x arr[i]
Looping k up to j instead of j-1 (causing out of bounds/empty subproblem)
interviewerQuestions: How do we print the actual optimal bracketing structure?
What is the connection between this and Burst Balloons?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Loop by length. Test splits k: dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + mergeCost).
recall.30sec: 2D DP of size NxN. Solve ranges of increasing lengths. Check all partition splits k in the range to minimize multiplication cost.
recall.1min: O(N^3) time and O(N^2) space bottom-up Range Dynamic Programming standard solution for chain associations.

patternConnections: Minimum Cost Tree From Leaf Values

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates distinguish between standard multi-stage DP and Range DP. They explain how the subproblem dependency is non-linear and requires building states sorted by range length, demonstrating deep algorithmic intelligence.
slides.closingLine: Mastering Range DP unlocks a beautiful class of associative boundary problems.

revisionCards.title: Minimum Sum Path in a Matrix
revisionCards.explanation: Find a path from top-left to bottom-right in a grid which minimizes the sum of numbers along its path.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given a grid filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from top-left to bottom-right which minimizes the sum of all numbers along its path.

You can only move either down or right at any point in time.

🎯 The goal:
Finding the absolute path of least resistance across a 2D terrain.
slides.visualCue: A 2D grid with numbers and a highlighted glowing trail running from top-left to bottom-right, picking smaller numbers.
slides.memoryHook: Step from the smaller neighbor: left or top.
slides.transition: Let's check the triggers that identify Grid Path DP instantly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ 2D Grid structure with movement constraints (only down or right)
✅ Finding a path that minimizes or maximizes a running sum
✅ Decisions at each coordinate depend purely on adjacent grid neighbors

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem restricts navigation to forward-only grid steps, think Grid-Path Bottom-Up DP.
slides.transition: Why is brute force recursive path exploration bad?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

From cell (i, j), explore both choices: move down (i+1, j) or move right (i, j+1) and return the minimum path cost.

⏱️ Time: O(2^(R+C)) due to double branching at each cell
📦 Space: O(R+C) recursion stack

We can solve this in O(R * C) time and O(1) auxiliary space by using the grid itself to cache sums!
slides.analogy: Checking all paths is like a traveller drawing every possible road on a map before choosing, rather than just remembering the shortest distance to each junction.
slides.transition: Let's look at the in-place grid optimization breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
In-place grid update:

✅ For any cell (i, j), the minimum path sum to reach it must come from either the left (i, j-1) or the top (i-1, j).
✅ Transition: grid[i][j] += min(grid[i-1][j], grid[i][j-1]).
✅ Handled boundaries: The first row can only be reached from the left; the first column can only be reached from the top.

By overwriting the grid, we consume absolutely zero extra memory!
slides.goldenLine: The terrain itself becomes the memory of our shortest journey.
slides.transition: Let's watch the grid update step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: First Row: grid[0][1] += grid[0][0] -> 4. grid[0][2] += grid[0][1] -> 5. Row 0 becomes [1, 4, 5].
First Col: grid[1][0] += grid[0][0] -> 2. grid[2][0] += grid[1][0] -> 6. Col 0 becomes [1, 2, 6].
slides.keyObservation: Updating borders first handles edge cases seamlessly and avoids messy if conditions in the inner loop.
slides.transition: Why is updating the original grid safe here?

slides.headline: 🔍 Safe In-Place Updates
slides.body:
Since cell (i, j) only depends on cells to its top and left, and we iterate top-to-bottom, left-to-right, the values grid[i-1][j] and grid[i][j-1] are guaranteed to have already been updated.

Since we never need original values again once a cell is updated, overwriting in-place is 100% correct and saves huge allocation overheads.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by not handling the first row/column boundaries correctly, causing out-of-bound errors.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Determine row count r and column count c.
Loop i from 0 to r-1 and j from 0 to c-1.
If i == 0 && j > 0, set grid[i][j] += grid[i][j-1] (first row).
slides.mentalCompression: Iterate grid. Update borders from previous elements; update middle cells from min of top and left.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant in-place C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Highly optimized O(R*C) Time and O(1) Space In-place Grid DP Solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Flow through the grid top-to-bottom and left-to-right, accumulating each cell with the smaller of its top or left neighbors.
slides.memoryHook: Flow with the smaller neighbor.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Accessing negative indices when i=0 or j=0 without guards
Modifying the grid when the interviewer explicitly requests not to mutate input data (create a separate O(C) space row in that case)
interviewerQuestions: How would you solve this if you are not allowed to modify the input grid?
Can we optimize space to O(C) using a single 1D row?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Accumulate cells: grid[i][j] += min(top, left).
recall.30sec: In-place traversal. Treat boundaries separately (add accumulated values). Set inner cells to minimum of left or top coordinates.
recall.1min: O(R * C) time and O(1) space bottom-up Dynamic Programming grid navigation algorithm.

patternConnections: Minimum Path Sum in a Grid (Variant)

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates proactively discuss input mutability. They ask the interviewer if modifying the grid is allowed. If not, they instantly write a space-efficient O(C) 1-row buffer solution, showcasing advanced system thinking.
slides.closingLine: Caring about input side-effects is the signature of a professional engineer.

revisionCards.title: Coin Change
revisionCards.explanation: Find the minimum number of coins to make up an amount.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given an array of coin denominations and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins needed to make up that amount.

You have an infinite supply of each coin type.

🎯 The real challenge:
Every coin we pick reduces our remaining amount. How do we pick the optimal set without falling into the trap of a greedy approach that might fail?
slides.visualCue: Coins of values [1, 2, 5] targeting an amount of 11, with a decision tree choosing coin paths.
slides.memoryHook: Amount steps back by coin value.
slides.transition: Let's check the triggers that identify Coin Change instantly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Combining items of fixed sizes to match an exact target sum
✅ Infinite supplies of items allowed (Unbounded Knapsack variant)
✅ Finding the minimum number of items to achieve the target

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires matching a target sum with minimal items and infinite reuse, think Coin Change 1D DP.
slides.transition: Why does a greedy approach fail on custom coin sets?

slides.headline: 📦 Why Greedy Fails
slides.body:
Why not just take the largest coin first?

Consider coins = [1, 3, 4] and amount = 6.
- Greedy: takes 4, then 1, then 1 (3 coins).
- Optimal: takes 3 and 3 (2 coins).

⏱️ Brute Force: O(S^N) where S is amount
📦 Space: O(Amount) recursion depth

Tabulating minimum coins per amount up to target solves this in O(Coins * Amount) time!
slides.analogy: Greedy is like running towards the destination using only the largest leaps, which might force you to take tiny, wasteful steps at the very end.
slides.transition: Let's see the 1D bottom-up tabulation breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Use 1D bottom-up tabulation:

✅ Maintain a 1D array dp of size amount + 1 initialized to infinity (1e9), with dp[0] = 0.
✅ Loop through each coin denomination.
✅ Loop amount i forwards from coin to amount and update: dp[i] = min(dp[i], 1 + dp[i - coin]).

Looping forwards allows coins to be reused indefinitely, matching unbounded selection rules!
slides.goldenLine: Matching amount-by-amount, each state builds on previously optimized coin combinations.
slides.transition: Let's watch this unbounded sweep step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Setup: coins = [1, 2, 5], amount = 6. dp initialized to [0, inf, inf, inf, inf, inf, inf].
Process coin 1: dp[1]=min(inf, 1+dp[0])=1, dp[2]=min(inf, 1+dp[1])=2... dp becomes [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
Process coin 5: dp[5]=min(3, 1+dp[0])=1, dp[6]=min(3, 1+dp[1])=2. dp becomes [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2].
slides.keyObservation: Looping weights forwards allowed a coin to build upon its own usage in the same step, perfectly capturing 'infinite supply'.
slides.transition: Why does the forward loop enable infinite supply?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Forward Loop Secret
slides.body:
In 0-1 Knapsack, we loop backwards to base our choices on past states (without the current item).
In Unbounded Knapsack (Coin Change), we loop forwards so that dp[i - coin] represents a state that could already include this coin. This mathematically mirrors the ability to pick the coin again and again.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by returning -1 on unreachable amounts, or by confusing 0-1 backward and Unbounded forward loops.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create vector dp of size amount + 1 pre-filled with infinity (1e9). Set dp[0] = 0.
Iterate through each coin denomination coin.
For each coin, iterate i forwards from coin up to amount.
slides.mentalCompression: 1D DP size amount+1. Pre-fill with infinity. Set dp[0]=0. Loop coins, loop amount forwards. Return -1 if unreachable.
slides.transition: Let's look at the clean C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Optimal O(Amount) Space and O(Coins * Amount) Time C++ Solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Pre-fill the amount path with infinity. Step forward through the amounts, building from the cheapest historical coin step.
slides.memoryHook: Forward step from historical coin.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Using INT_MAX directly, which triggers integer overflow when doing 1 + dp[i - coin]
Looping backwards, which restricts coin usage to 0-1 limits
interviewerQuestions: How would you return the actual coin combinations used?
How would you find the total number of ways to make the amount? (Coin Change II)

recall.5sec: Forward loop: dp[i] = min(dp[i], 1 + dp[i-coin]).
recall.30sec: Initialize DP size amount+1 with large constant. Set dp[0]=0. Outer loop coins; inner loop amount forwards to enable reuse.
recall.1min: O(C * A) time and O(A) space bottom-up Dynamic Programming algorithm solving the Unbounded Knapsack coin minimization problem.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates stand out by instantly explaining the difference between forward loop (unbounded reuse) and backward loop (0-1 selection). They also point out why INT_MAX triggers arithmetic overflows and elegantly bypass it using a safe infinity like 1e9.
slides.closingLine: A tiny constant boundary fix distinguishes senior code from buggy loops.

revisionCards.title: Subset Sum Problem
revisionCards.explanation: Determine if there exists a subset of an array that sums to target.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given an array of non-negative integers and a target sum, determine if there exists a subset of elements whose sum is exactly equal to the target.

🎯 The core challenge:
Can we select a subset of these numbers such that their combined weight is exactly target, without reusing any element?
slides.visualCue: A set of weights and a scale set to 'target'. We want to turn on/off individual weights to balance it.
slides.memoryHook: Achieve target by flipping boolean states backwards.
slides.transition: Let's check the triggers that identify Subset Sum instantly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Selecting a sub-group of numbers to sum to a exact target sum
✅ Binary choice for each item (take/leave, no reuse)
✅ Returns a boolean answer (yes/no, true/false)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks if a subset can sum up to a specific value without element reuse, think Subset Sum 1D Backward DP.
slides.transition: How does brute-force recursion fail?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

For each index, branch: either include arr[i] in the sum (if arr[i] <= sum) or exclude it. Return true if either path achieves the sum.

⏱️ Time: O(2^N) due to binary branching
📦 Space: O(N) stack depth

Bottom-up tabulation caches achievable sums to solve this in O(N * Sum) time and O(Sum) space!
slides.analogy: Checking all subsets is like testing every combination of weights on a scale instead of tracking which weights are achievable incrementally.
slides.transition: Let's check the 1D space optimization breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Space-Optimized 1D DP:

✅ Maintain a boolean array dp of size sum + 1 initialized to false, with dp[0] = true (0 is always achievable with empty subset).
✅ Update the dp array backwards from sum down to arr[i]!

This prevents using the same number twice in the sum. If dp[j - arr[i]] is true, we mark dp[j] = true.
slides.goldenLine: Sweeping backwards preserves previous subset achievements, preventing numbers from duplicating themselves.
slides.transition: Let's simulate this backwards update step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Setup: arr = [3, 4], sum = 4. dp initialized size 5: [T, F, F, F, F].
Process 3: Sweep backwards from 4 to 3: dp[4]=dp[4]||dp[1]=F. dp[3]=dp[3]||dp[0]=T. dp becomes [T, F, F, T, F].
Process 4: Sweep backwards from 4 to 4: dp[4]=dp[4]||dp[0]=T. dp becomes [T, F, F, T, T].
End: dp[4] is true (subsets: [4]).
slides.keyObservation: Scanning backwards guarantees that the activation of dp[3] in step 1 does not trigger dp[6] in the same step.
slides.transition: Why does the backward sweep lock in single-use logic?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why It Works
slides.body:
If we loop forwards, dp[j - arr[i]] would represent a state that already processed arr[i] in this row. Marking dp[j] = true would mean we added arr[i] multiple times.

Looping backwards ensures that we only build upon sum states from before we considered arr[i], perfectly executing 0-1 selection rules.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by updating forwards, transforming a 0-1 subset problem into an unbounded sum problem.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create boolean vector dp of size sum + 1 filled with false.
Set dp[0] = true.
Loop index i from 0 to N-1 through the array elements.
slides.mentalCompression: 1D boolean DP size sum+1. Set dp[0]=true. Outer loop elements, inner loop weights backwards. Return dp[sum].
slides.transition: Let's check the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Space-Optimized O(Sum) Space and O(N*Sum) Time C++ Solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Start with target sum as a boolean trail. For each number, step backwards and flag all sums that can be unlocked by adding it.
slides.memoryHook: Sweep back to unlock sum states.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Looping weight forwards, which allows element reuse
Off-by-one errors on index sizes
interviewerQuestions: How would you output the indices of the subset?
How does this relate to Partition Equal Subset Sum?

recall.5sec: Sweep backwards: if dp[j - arr[i]] is true, mark dp[j] = true.
recall.30sec: Maintain O(Sum) boolean array. Set dp[0]=true. Iterate elements. Update sums backwards to secure single-use 0-1 subset logic.
recall.1min: O(N * Sum) time and O(Sum) space Dynamic Programming algorithm for exact target sum matching.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates mention how the space-optimized boolean array mirrors 0-1 knapsack states. They also discuss bitset optimizations (dp |= (dp << arr[i])) which compress the entire inner loop into single CPU instruction cycles, highlighting world-class efficiency.
slides.closingLine: Bitwise updates turn dynamic programming into pure hardware execution.

revisionCards.title: Rod Cutting
revisionCards.explanation: Find the maximum value possible by cutting a rod of length N into pieces and selling them.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given a rod of length n and an array of prices that contains prices of all pieces of size smaller than n.

Determine the maximum value obtainable by cutting up the rod and selling the pieces.

🎯 The goal:
Finding the combination of cuts that yields the absolute highest profit, with the ability to reuse piece sizes as much as we want!
slides.visualCue: A rod of length 4 marked with cuts, showing different combinations of piece prices summing to the maximum.
slides.memoryHook: Amount steps forward, piece sizes can be reused.
slides.transition: Let's identify the triggers for Rod Cutting.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Cutting a resource of length n into multiple pieces
✅ Ability to reuse piece sizes infinitely (Unbounded Knapsack variant)
✅ Maximizing total profit or value

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem requires partitioning a resource into integer lengths to maximize value, think Rod Cutting / Unbounded Knapsack DP.
slides.transition: Why is brute force recursive division slow?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

For a rod of length n, try making a cut of length i (from 1 to n) and recursively solve for the remaining rod n-i. Return the maximum profit.

⏱️ Time: O(2^N) due to exponential branching
📦 Space: O(N) recursion stack

We can tabulate maximum profit for all rod lengths up to n in O(N²) time and O(N) space!
slides.analogy: Trying every split randomly is like sawing a log into random configurations without checking if you've already sold that exact configuration before.
slides.transition: Let's see the 1D space optimization breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Use 1D bottom-up tabulation:

✅ Maintain a 1D array dp of size n + 1 pre-filled with 0.
✅ Outer loop through piece sizes i from 1 to n.
✅ Inner loop through rod length j forwards from i to n!
✅ Update: dp[j] = max(dp[j], price[i - 1] + dp[j - i]).

Looping forwards allows us to reuse pieces of length i multiple times, perfectly matching Unbounded Knapsack semantics.
slides.goldenLine: By building profit step-by-step forwards, pieces of any length can be chosen repeatedly.
slides.transition: Let's simulate this forward update step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Setup: price = [1, 5, 8, 9], n = 4. dp size 5 initialized with 0.
Process piece i=1 (price 1): Loop j from 1 to 4: dp[j]=max(dp[j], 1+dp[j-1]). dp becomes [0, 1, 2, 3, 4].
Process piece i=2 (price 5): Loop j from 2 to 4: dp[2]=max(2, 5+dp[0])=5, dp[3]=max(3, 5+dp[1])=6, dp[4]=max(4, 5+dp[2])=10. dp becomes [0, 1, 5, 6, 10].
Process piece i=3 (price 8): Loop j from 3 to 4: dp[3]=max(6, 8+dp[0])=8, dp[4]=max(10, 8+dp[1])=9. dp becomes [0, 1, 5, 8, 10].
slides.keyObservation: Looping forwards in step 2 allowed piece of length 2 to be chosen twice, yielding maximum profit of 10 at length 4.
slides.transition: Why does the forward loop represent infinite supply?

slides.headline: 🔍 Safe Forward Loops
slides.body:
In 0-1 Knapsack, we loop backwards to avoid picking the current item twice.
In Unbounded Knapsack (Rod Cutting), we loop forwards because we want to be able to pick the current piece multiple times. Overwriting the cell forwards naturally incorporates the current piece's newly optimized value in the same loop step.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by looping backwards, limiting each piece length to at most one selection.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Create vector dp of size n + 1 pre-filled with 0.
Loop piece size i from 1 to n.
For each piece size, loop rod length j forwards from i up to n.
slides.mentalCompression: 1D DP size n+1. Loop pieces, loop rod length forwards. Update maximum achievable profit.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Highly optimized O(N) Space and O(N^2) Time C++ Solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Build rod profits incrementally from left to right, allowing each new cut size to compound on previous lengths' maximum values.
slides.memoryHook: Compound profits forwards.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Looping length backwards, preventing multiple cuts of same size
Off-by-one errors mapping piece length i to price[i-1]
interviewerQuestions: How would you track the actual cuts made?
How does this problem compare to the Integer Break problem?

recall.5sec: Forward loop: dp[j] = max(dp[j], price[i-1] + dp[j-i]).
recall.30sec: Initialize DP size n+1. Set dp[0]=0. Loop pieces from 1 to n, and update rod lengths forwards to enable multiple cuts of same size.
recall.1min: O(N^2) time and O(N) space dynamic programming algorithm for maximum utility cut partitioning.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates stand out by immediately classifying Rod Cutting as Unbounded Knapsack. They explain why the forward iteration order matches unbounded selection mathematically, showing deep structural knowledge.
slides.closingLine: Recognizing standard templates in varied descriptions is the key to instant solutions.

revisionCards.title: Egg Dropping Puzzle
revisionCards.explanation: Find the minimum number of attempts needed to find the threshold floor in a building of N floors using K eggs.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given k eggs and a building with n floors, find the minimum number of attempts needed in the worst case to identify the critical threshold floor below which eggs don't break.

If an egg breaks, you lose it. If it doesn't break, you can reuse it.

🎯 The real challenge:
How to balance risk and information. Too aggressive, and you run out of eggs. Too conservative, and you waste attempts.
slides.visualCue: Eggs dropped from a building with a grid showing threshold outcomes and remaining eggs.
slides.memoryHook: Maximize floors with 'attempts' and 'eggs' backwards.
slides.transition: Let's check the triggers that identify Egg Dropping Puzzle instantly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Finding minimum attempts in the worst case (Minimax problem)
✅ Limited resources that break upon failure (constrained query search)
✅ Tradeoff between high risk (many floors skipped) and low risk (step-by-step check)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks for optimal worst-case search strategies under limited resource breakage, think Egg Dropping DP.
slides.transition: Why is standard O(K * N^2) DP too slow?

slides.headline: 📦 Standard DP vs Elite Dual DP
slides.body:
The classic DP defines dp[i][j] as the min drops for i eggs and j floors. This requires checking every floor x: 1 + max(break, no_break), taking O(K * N²) time.

We can invert this! Let dp[attempts][k] be the maximum floors we can test with attempts and k eggs.

⏱️ Time: O(K log N) instead of O(K * N²)
📦 Space: O(K) instead of O(K * N)

This completely bypasses massive nested loops!
slides.analogy: Classic DP is like checking every path step-by-step; Inverted DP is like checking how far a map can stretch for each step we are willing to take.
slides.transition: Let's unlock the O(K) space inverted DP breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 The Optimal Inversion
slides.body:
Invert the question:

✅ Instead of finding drops for N floors, find how many floors we can test with attempts drops and K eggs.
✅ Transition: dp[j] = dp[j] + dp[j - 1] + 1 (if egg breaks we search below, if egg survives we search above, plus 1 for current floor).

We loop attempts and update the egg states backwards to compress space to O(K)!
Once dp[K] >= N, the current attempts count is the answer.
slides.goldenLine: Inverting the problem turns a quadratic search into a lightning-fast logarithmic sweep.
slides.transition: Let's simulate this inverted state update step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Setup: K = 2 eggs, N = 6 floors. dp size 3 initialized to 0.
Attempt 1: Loop eggs j from 2 down to 1:
slides.keyObservation: Updating egg counts backwards ensured that the new attempt counts did not compound within the same drop step.
slides.transition: Why is the transition dp[k] + dp[k-1] + 1 mathematically correct?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Math of Egg Dropping
slides.body:
When we drop an egg from a floor:
- Egg breaks: We can test at most dp[attempts - 1][k - 1] floors below.
- Egg survives: We can test at most dp[attempts - 1][k] floors above.
- The current floor counts as 1 floor.

Adding these three terms: dp[attempts - 1][k] + dp[attempts - 1][k - 1] + 1 yields the total coverage. Since we only need the previous attempt's values, we can store it in a single 1D array of size K + 1 updated backwards.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by writing O(K*N^2) or O(K*N) DP, which is rejected by top companies for large inputs.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Initialize dp vector of size K + 1 with 0.
Set attempts = 0.
While dp[K] < N:
slides.mentalCompression: Invert the DP. Find max floors for given attempts and eggs. Loop attempts, update eggs backwards: dp[j] = dp[j] + dp[j-1] + 1.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Highly optimized O(K) Space and O(K log N) Time Inverted DP Solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Find the maximum floors you can check with each step: sum egg-broken coverage, egg-survived coverage, and the current floor.
slides.memoryHook: Sum broken, survived, plus one.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Using standard O(K*N^2) DP which times out on N >= 10^4
Looping egg counts forwards, causing egg counts to propagate incorrect attempt states
interviewerQuestions: Why is this inverted method O(K log N) time?
How would you implement this using binary search on the standard DP transition?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Loop attempts: dp[j] = dp[j] + dp[j-1] + 1 backwards. Exit when dp[K] >= N.
recall.30sec: Invert standard problem. Track maximum floors coverable for attempts and eggs. Compress to O(K) array and loop egg counts backwards.
recall.1min: O(K log N) time and O(K) space highly optimal minimax dynamic programming algorithm.

patternConnections: Guess Number Higher or Lower II

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates instantly bypass standard quadratic DP and explain the inverted DP formulation. They discuss why the time complexity becomes O(K log N) because attempts are bounded by O(log N) for multiple eggs, proving deep mathematical insight.
slides.closingLine: Inverting states is the ultimate breakthrough in complex minimax challenges.

revisionCards.title: Word Break
revisionCards.explanation: Determine if a string can be segmented into space-separated dictionary words.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given a string and a dictionary of words, determine if the string can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of dictionary words.

You can reuse words from the dictionary multiple times.

🎯 The real challenge:
Deciding where to place segmentation breaks so that all pieces form valid words without leaving orphans.
slides.visualCue: A string 'leetcode' being sliced into 'leet' and 'code' using arrows matching dictionary lookups.
slides.memoryHook: Check prefix validity, lookup dictionary suffixes.
slides.transition: Let's see the triggers to identify Word Break instantly.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ Splitting a string into valid contiguous segments
✅ Dictionary search or word validation within a sequence
✅ Reusable subsets of sub-elements (dictionary words)

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem asks if a string can be constructed by chaining dictionary sub-segments, think Prefix validation DP.
slides.transition: Why is brute-force recursive slicing slow?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

For each index i, try splitting the string. If the prefix is a valid dictionary word, recursively solve for the remaining suffix.

⏱️ Time: O(2^N) due to exponential branching
📦 Space: O(N) recursion depth

We can solve this in O(N²) time and O(N) space using a 1D boolean array to track validated prefix break points!
slides.analogy: Slicing randomly is like trying to read a sentence by guessing every word combination from scratch instead of verifying spaces left-to-right.
slides.transition: Let's see the 1D bottom-up prefix matching breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
Use 1D bottom-up tabulation:

✅ Maintain a boolean array dp of size s.size() + 1, where dp[i] represents whether prefix s[0...i-1] is segmentable.
✅ Set dp[0] = true (empty string is always valid).
✅ For each index i from 1 to s.size(), check if there exists some split j < i such that dp[j] is true AND the suffix s[j...i-1] is in the dictionary.

This locks prefix achievements, completely bypassing redundant suffix searches!
slides.goldenLine: A segmentable prefix acts as a valid jumping board to test future word boundaries.
slides.transition: Let's trace this prefix matching step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: Setup: s = 'leetcode', dict = {'leet', 'code'}. dp initialized size 9 to false, dp[0]=true.
Index 1 to 3: No valid dictionary words starting from dp[0]=true.
Index 4: Suffix s[0...3] ('leet') is in dict. dp[4] = true. dp is [T, F, F, F, T, F, F, F, F].
Index 5 to 7: No splits j with dp[j]=true yielding dictionary words for s[j...i-1].
slides.keyObservation: Having dp[4] set to true allowed us to immediately focus on testing only suffixes starting at index 4, avoiding other dead ends.
slides.transition: Why does prefix validation guarantee correctness?

slides.headline: 🔍 The Prefix Jumping Board
slides.body:
If a string can be segmented, there must be a valid cut at some index j such that the prefix before j is valid (dp[j] == true) and the remaining word s[j...i-1] is a valid dictionary entry.

By building these checkpoints, we convert an exponential search into a quadratic sequence of lookups, guaranteed to be safe and accurate.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by copying strings inside loops, leading to O(N³) times instead of keeping it strictly O(N²).
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Convert dictionary vector into unordered_set for O(1) lookups.
Initialize boolean vector dp of size s.size() + 1 with false, and set dp[0] = true.
Loop i from 1 up to s.size().
slides.mentalCompression: 1D DP size s.size()+1. Mark dp[0]=true. If dp[j] is valid and suffix is in dictionary, mark dp[i]=true. Break inner loop early.
slides.transition: Let's inspect the clean C++ code.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Highly optimized O(N^2) Time and O(N) Space C++ Solution using unordered_set.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Mark valid word ending coordinates in a boolean trail, and use them as active launching pads to test the next segment.
slides.memoryHook: Check prefix, jump to suffix.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Using standard vector search instead of unordered_set, increasing complexity to O(N^2 * D)
Incorrect substring parameters: substr(start, length) in C++ vs substring(start, end) in JS
interviewerQuestions: How would you print the actual segmented sentences? (Word Break II)
Can we optimize lookups further using a Trie?

recall.5sec: If dp[j] is true and s[j...i-1] in dict, set dp[i] = true.
recall.30sec: Create boolean dp size s.size()+1. Set dp[0]=true. For each index i, search for a split index j where dp[j] is true and suffix is in set.
recall.1min: O(N^2) time and O(N) space dynamic programming algorithm for string partition segmentation.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates explain how to optimize word matching using a Trie instead of an unordered_set, or they mention length-restricted jumps (only searching j back to i - max_word_len) which keeps the runtime linear when dictionary words are short.
slides.closingLine: Restricting search windows based on real constraints shows brilliant practical optimization.

revisionCards.title: Maximum Path Sum in a Grid
revisionCards.explanation: Find a path from top-left to bottom-right that maximizes the sum of values.

slides.headline: ⚡ The Core Challenge
slides.body:
Given a grid of numbers, find a path from top-left to bottom-right that maximizes the sum of all values along its path.

You can only move either down or right at any step.

🎯 The goal:
Finding the path of maximum collection, absorbing as much value as possible from each visited coordinate.
slides.visualCue: A 2D matrix of treasures, with a path picking up the highest numbers from top-left to bottom-right.
slides.memoryHook: Step from the larger neighbor: left or top.
slides.transition: Let's check the triggers that identify Grid Max Path DP.

slides.headline: 🧠 Interview Trigger Recognition
slides.body:
Spot the indicators:

✅ 2D Grid navigation with down and right constraints
✅ Finding a path that maximizes a running sum
✅ Decisions at coordinate (i, j) depend on neighbors

💡 Interview Signal:
Whenever a problem restricts navigation to forward-only grid steps to maximize collection, think Grid-Path Max DP.
slides.transition: Why is brute force recursive path exploration bad?

slides.headline: 📦 Brute Force Thinking
slides.body:
The naive recursive way:

From cell (i, j), explore both choices: move down (i+1, j) or move right (i, j+1) and return the maximum path sum.

⏱️ Time: O(2^(R+C)) due to double branching
📦 Space: O(R+C) recursion stack

We can solve this in O(R * C) time and O(1) auxiliary space by updating the grid in-place!
slides.analogy: Checking all paths is like calculating every possible path value on a map from scratch, instead of tracking the highest accumulated treasure at each junction.
slides.transition: Let's look at the in-place grid optimization breakthrough.

slides.headline: 🚀 Optimal Approach
slides.body:
In-place grid update:

✅ The maximum path sum to reach cell (i, j) must come from either left (i, j-1) or top (i-1, j).
✅ Transition: grid[i][j] += max(grid[i-1][j], grid[i][j-1]).
✅ Handled boundaries: First row accumulates from left; first column accumulates from top.

By overwriting the grid, we consume absolutely zero extra memory!
slides.goldenLine: Rewriting coordinates in-place stores the highest accumulated rewards directly in our path.
slides.transition: Let's watch the grid update step-by-step.

slides.headline: 🎬 Dry Run Simulation
steps: First Row: grid[0][1] += grid[0][0] -> 3. grid[0][2] += grid[0][1] -> 8. Row 0 becomes [1, 3, 8].
First Col: grid[1][0] += grid[0][0] -> 4. grid[2][0] += grid[1][0] -> 5. Col 0 becomes [1, 4, 5].
slides.keyObservation: Pre-processing borders prevents checking boundary guards inside the inner cell loops.
slides.transition: Why is in-place updates mathematically safe?

slides.headline: 🔍 Why In-Place is Safe
slides.body:
Since cell (i, j) only depends on cells to its top and left, and we iterate top-to-bottom, left-to-right, the values grid[i-1][j] and grid[i][j-1] are guaranteed to have already been updated.

Since we never need original values again once a cell is updated, overwriting in-place is 100% correct and saves huge allocation overheads.
slides.interviewerTrap: Candidates fail by not handling the first row/column boundaries correctly, causing out-of-bound errors.
slides.transition: Let's review the blueprint.

slides.headline: 🧩 Algorithm Blueprint
steps: Determine row count r and column count c.
Loop i from 0 to r-1 and j from 0 to c-1.
If i == 0 && j > 0, set grid[i][j] += grid[i][j-1] (first row).
slides.mentalCompression: Iterate grid. Update borders from previous elements; update middle cells from max of top and left.
slides.transition: Let's check the elegant in-place C++ implementation.

slides.headline: 💻 C++ Code
slides.body: Highly optimized O(R*C) Time and O(1) Space In-place Grid DP Solution.

slides.headline: 🧠 One-Line Mental Model
slides.body: Flow through the grid top-to-bottom and left-to-right, accumulating each cell with the larger of its top or left neighbors.
slides.memoryHook: Flow with the larger neighbor.

slides.headline: ⚠️ Common Bugs & Interview Traps
mistakes: Accessing negative indices when i=0 or j=0 without guards
Modifying the grid when the interviewer explicitly requests not to mutate input data (create a separate O(C) space row in that case)
interviewerQuestions: How would you solve this if you are not allowed to modify the input grid?
Can we optimize space to O(C) using a single 1D row?

slides.headline: ⚡ 10-Second Recall

recall.5sec: Accumulate cells: grid[i][j] += max(top, left).
recall.30sec: In-place traversal. Treat boundaries separately (add accumulated values). Set inner cells to maximum of left or top coordinates.
recall.1min: O(R * C) time and O(1) space bottom-up Dynamic Programming grid navigation algorithm.

slides.headline: 🏆 What Makes Candidates Stand Out
slides.body: Elite candidates proactively discuss input mutability. They ask the interviewer if modifying the grid is allowed. If not, they instantly write a space-efficient O(C) 1-row buffer solution, showcasing advanced system thinking.
slides.closingLine: Caring about input side-effects is the signature of a professional engineer.
